# To the Most Reverend in God
## The Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince and Lord
Lord ERNEST, Elected and Confirmed Archbishop of Cologne and Prince-
Elector; Bishop of Liège; <term>Administrator</term> <note>A title for a high-ranking official who manages a diocese without being its consecrated bishop.</note> of the Sees of Münster, Hildesheim, and Freising; Prince of Sta-
velot; Count Palatine of the Rhine; Duke of Upper and Lower Bavaria, of Westphalia, Angria, and Bouillon;
Margrave of Francimont; Count of Loon and Horne, etc., our most gracious
Prince-Elector and Lord.

<image-desc>Decorative floral drop cap initial 'H' featuring elaborate scrollwork and leafy patterns.</image-desc>
Most Reverend in God, Most Illustrious and High-Born
Prince-Elector, Gracious Lord: Whereas Your Electoral Prince’s Grace <note>original: "E. C. F. G." (Eure Churfürstliche Gnaden), a formal address used for high nobility.</note>, as a lover
and promoter of divine and natural light, previously
and most graciously requested of our late father Johann Huser (may he rest in peace)
that—since the writings of the precious and well-founded German
<term>Philosopher</term> <note>A seeker of natural wisdom.</note> and <term>Physician</term> <note>A doctor of medicine.</note>, Theophrastus Paracelsus, have for the most part not yet
been brought to light, and others published here and there by various people
have been printed so <term>incorrectly</term> <note>original: "mendose"; full of errors.</note>, falsely, and defectively that often no meaning, or a completely
distorted one, contrary to the <term>Author's</term> intention, could be drawn from them: as
the <term>comparison</term> <note>original: "collatio"</note> of the old and current copies clearly proves—that he
should take the effort upon himself to track down the remaining books as much as possible,
correct the published ones from the original manuscripts, and then prepare them all together
for public printing. Which he then, for Your Electoral Prince’s Grace’s most humble honor and
pleasure, and out of love for the common good (which he was always diligent to promote to
the best of his ability), willingly took upon himself and <unclear>performed</unclear>, and put into effect
as much as he was able.

And although many and various <term>difficulties</term>, great labor, and the expenditure of
unexpected costs were encountered in promoting this work, nothing more burdensome
happened to him in all this than that the printers who had previously undertaken to produce
such a work unfairly delayed him, and after the death of the aforementioned Johann Huser,
contrary to their promise, sent the <term>Surgical Works</term> <note>original: "Chirurgica"; books focusing on the practical art of surgery.</note> back to us, Huser’s heirs,
unfinished. But since nothing else seemed proper to us than to fulfill our father's promise
and word as much as possible, we have therefore exerted ourselves in other ways
to bring such a work to print: yet we could not succeed until finally the
honorable and distinguished Lazarus Zetzner, bookseller and citizen in Strasbourg,
declared himself ready to complete the printing of such a work (for which he is
well worthy of fame and praise). How highly useful and necessary these books will be
for the common good, experience will show. For (<term>with all due respect to others</term> <note>original: "pace aliorum dictum"; a polite disclaimer when making a strong claim.</note>)
in the art of surgery, nothing more fundamental or proven has ever been brought to light
by anyone at any time. But what our aforementioned father Johann Huser brought
together and <term>added</term> from new <term>writings</term> beyond the books previously
<term>most faultily published</term> <note>original: "mendosissimè evulgirten"</note>, the <term>catalog</term> in
each part will demonstrate.

All of this, then, we hereby <term>offer</term> and <term>dedicate</term> to Your Electoral Prince’s Grace,
as we did the previous ones, most humbly and with a devout plea that you would be pleased
with your Paracelsus and our father’s great effort, expense, and applied diligence herein. And
regarding the long delay—the cause of which was not Huser, but the printers who unfairly
delayed him and us—may you take no displeasure, but rather remain and continue to be
our most gracious Prince-Elector and Lord, just as you were to our father and now to us his heirs.
Commending Your Electoral Prince’s Grace herewith to divine protection and shelter for
a long and healthy life and a peaceful reign. Dated Great Glogau, December 1, 1604.

# To the highly learned Lord Wolfgang Thalhauser,
# Doctor of Medicine, Physician, and City Doctor of the praiseworthy City of Augsburg, his favorable Lord, THEOPHRASTUS von Hohenheim, Doctor of both Medicines, wishes his greetings.

There are three things, especially dear friend, that cause me to write here and to compile a book on <term>Wound-Medicine</term> <note>Surgery and the treatment of external injuries.</note>, regardless of the supposedly grand knowledge and skills of other physicians—and not without reason. For I have applied myself to the benefit of the art more than others known to me, my good lords and friends, Doctors and Masters. The first is that the books of the ancients who came before us—as many as have come to light—are composed upon such an imperfect foundation that no true hope regarding the power of nature can be found in them. The second is the unjust and ruinous damage caused to the sick and injured through the incompetence and misunderstanding of those who call themselves surgeons. The third concerns the <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "Zufall"; here meaning medical complications or secondary symptoms that arise during the healing of a wound.</note> that occur with the wounded, which are matters of the highest consideration and are the greatest treasure of this art, yet they have never been considered by either the ancients or the moderns.

Such folly, I say, causes me to write based on my manifold experience and, for the benefit of those in need, to remain silent no longer. Although I take a burden upon myself herewith—for my opposition is a heavy yoke—I hope and am certain that what is built upon sand cannot endure. Nor am I such a young wolf that I have not heard or grown accustomed to such howling. I commend this to your consideration, as one who loves the true foundation and seeks it with diligence. Judge therefore in this matter according to your custom, impartially.

I would have liked to adorn this book with great and subtle arts—of which you partially possess a good foundation and knowledge—and to approach it in the most beautiful way. However, since wound medicine is practiced by those who do not understand such things, I did not wish to compose it in a higher style than they could understand and bear. Therefore, I intend to demonstrate and complete the higher arts of this wound medicine in a special little book called the *Small Surgery* [<term>Klein Artzney</term>], and in others concerning injuries and the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "Frantzosen"; a common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>. I doubt not that this will be especially pleasing to you, given the great benefit to the sick, which you pursue daily. Would to God that every physician carried such a spirit and applied himself to contemplating the foundation of his patients in such a way, as is only right. Then the physicians and the art would not be spoken of so ill. In this regard, I desire that you will be an undisturbed judge and defender against my opposition in this matter. With that, I commend you to God. Given at Augsburg, the 23rd of July, in the year 1536.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous page's dedication (written by Paracelsus to Wolfgang Thalhauser) to a reciprocal dedication or preface written by Thalhauser back to Paracelsus. This demonstrates the mutual respect and professional alliance between the two medical reformers.</meta>

# To the Highly Renowned and Widely Experienced Lord THEOPHRASTUS von Hohenheim,
## Doctor of both Medicines, his especially beloved friend,
### WOLFGANG Thalhauser, Doctor of Medicine and appointed Physician to the City of Augsburg, wishes grace from
### God and happy welfare for the benefit of everyone in all good undertakings.

<image-desc>A large ornamental historiated initial "D" at the beginning of the text, featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Although medicine—especially dear Lord and Friend—was created and invented by God from the earth for the benefit of mankind (who is subject to daily infirmity) so that he might not despair in times of need: yet by God’s permission, and solely through the misuse of ungrateful men who could not or would not attribute His gifts directly to the Merciful God, it has become so diminished and weak that it seems to require a physician itself. This is to see if perhaps in these "final times," <note>A common 16th-century belief that they were living in the last age of the world, characterized by both great corruption and the rediscovery of ancient knowledge.</note> in which men have undertaken to repeat or restore all the arts, medicine might also unfortunately rise again, and appear healthy and sensible before those who have long called it sick and even insane. That should rightly be our desire from God, with a good and purposeful will: that if we were to receive it once more, properly purged and healthy, we would not so carelessly let it fall ill again or sink into decay. Many in our times have labored in various ways toward such a restoration of our weak art. However, for the most part, it has been carried out with useless chatter—which many of us nevertheless regard as great ornament and mastery—with only a few exceptions, such as what the dear and praiseworthy <term>Johannes Manardus</term> <note>Giovanni Manardi (1462–1536), an Italian physician who was a pioneer in criticizing the errors of medieval medicine and Arab authorities.</note> of Ferrara achieved. But I believe that God, because of the great ungratefulness of men, did not wish to grant him to us longer on this earth. For no matter how much he, Manardus, labored for the common good of medicine, rooting out errors and pointing toward more useful things, it was all a source of mockery and contempt for the majority of these so-called doctors. Because of this, I have been troubled not a little, and until now stood in no small worry that our art must continue to proceed in a bungling—I would even say groundless or completely senseless—manner. This was until I now recognized, from your writing in this *Wound-Medicine* of yours, and also in the discussion you held with me regarding other matters—namely, regarding <term>lesions</term> and the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "Schäden vnd Franzosen"; "Franzosen" was the common term for Syphilis at the time.</note> and, in short, everything concerning the whole art of surgery—I see that God finally wishes to begin the restoration of this noble art through His experienced men. This art of surgery possesses demonstrations far more thorough and sensible than those of internal medicine. For this, we should first be grateful to Him as our Merciful God, and thereafter give you the praise you deserve as one chosen by God for such a useful task, and show you a favorable and kind will. For things are going so miserably and pitifully everywhere for the sick that I wonder greatly how the authorities everywhere can simply tolerate or endure it.

The Romans once, for much lesser reasons, banished all their physicians from the city. <note>Referencing a historical claim made by the Roman author Pliny the Elder that Rome functioned without physicians for 600 years after expelling them.</note> Should that same authority live today, I fear they would not tolerate the current doctors in the whole Empire; for there is no longer any art, any understanding, and no order left in medicine. Whatever happens to succeed by chance, that they praise—though it is little enough. Then the "master" puffs himself up, grows warm in his "art," and presumes to deal with people according to his own whim without any foundation, as if they were mere <term>beasts</term> <note>original: "Bestiæ"; Latin for wild animals.</note>. He perhaps thinks it does no harm to "cut straps from someone else's leather." <note>A German idiom meaning to be reckless or extravagant at someone else's expense—in this case, experimenting on a patient's body.</note> I consider the <term>Physicos</term> <note>University-trained physicians who focused on internal medicine and theory, often looking down on manual surgery.</note> or personal physicians to be the root cause of this ruin and inhumane damage. For while there are three things in which the whole art of medicine is comprised and conducted—namely the body, the disease, and the medicine with which one may help—it is necessary that every doctor should have a certain and correct knowledge of those three. But how "certain" they have been for a long time now is more obvious than I like to hear said. It follows from this that, whereas in former times the shearers, bath-masters, blood-letters, barbers, and the rest of that crew were the servants and ministers of the physician, knowing nothing of how to treat the sick except what the Doctors commanded or ordered; now, however, since becoming a "Doctor" for a small amount of money has become so common and cheap, it does not surprise me that the Art itself has become precious and rare. For no one pursues the art anymore; they merely head from the High Schools to the nearest city where there is hope of winning money, armed with a few hundred recipes copied from books or otherwise inherited—and what a man does not already know...

<summary>In this dedication, the Augsburg physician Wolfgang Thalhauser praises Paracelsus for restoring the "sick" art of medicine. He criticizes the incompetence of contemporary university-trained physicians, whom he accuses of treating patients like animals and lacking true foundational knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface written by Wolfgang Thalhauser, the city physician of Augsburg, addressed to Paracelsus (Theophrastus von Hohenheim). Thalhauser is critiquing the current state of medical education and the incompetence of practitioners who lack proper training in surgery.</meta>

he can still boast. For it is now so common among physicians that no one pays it any mind anymore: he only sees to it that he can flatter well and let everyone be right; for if the churchyard is well-manured <note>A dark joke implying that a doctor becomes wealthy when his patients die and fill the cemetery.</note>, the physician is all the richer. If an injury arises that requires <term>wound-surgery</term> <note>original: "Wundarzney"; the practice of surgery, which was often treated as separate from internal medicine in the 16th century</note>, such a Doctor can say nothing about it. Then comes a <term>barber</term> <note>original: "Scherer"; barber-surgeons were craftsmen who performed minor surgeries, bloodletting, and tooth extractions</note> or a <term>bath-keeper</term> <note>original: "Bader"; practitioners who managed public baths and offered basic medical treatments</note> who knows no more of the human <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four "humors" or bodily fluids that was believed to determine a person's health and temperament</note> than a butcher knows of a sow. He cuts, burns, patches, and tears at his pleasure, and no one can challenge him as to why he does so. For the Doctor has not learned it, nor ever seen it before—even though they now style themselves "Doctors of both medicines" <note>Referring to "Physic" (internal medicine) and "Surgery" (manual operations)</note> in Germany. At which university one might actually study wound-surgery, you know best, for you have experienced enough of it.

Thus it happens that the barber, who has been an apprentice for a year or two and then becomes a master in a single night by taking a wife <note>Refers to the practice of gaining a master's title by marrying the widow or daughter of a deceased guild master</note>, is considered to have handled everything correctly, even if it has cost hands and feet, body and life.

Therefore, it gladdens me that you, undoubtedly ordained by God for this purpose, have begun to stir up this mess, to challenge, decry, and expose this "executioner-like" torture. I am in good hope that through your manifold and long experience in true wound-surgery, you will lay a foundation in many good-hearted people and provoke in them a rightful zeal for human health—regardless of the fact that the entire mob of physicians is hostile to you out of envy. But I regard your work like a new house that someone builds on the street: all who see it talk about it, offer advice, and teach in many ways. Yet he who understands it recognizes the master by the work. One must let people talk, for as they say, dogs cannot do anything but bark. Those who wish to be better will accept this writing of yours with the highest gratitude; the others will reveal their own lack of understanding through their judgment. But you should not mind that: "Time brings roses" <note>A proverb meaning that patience and time will eventually bring results or reveal the truth</note>. He who thinks all fruits ripen at the same time as strawberries knows nothing of the grape harvest. But I hope that some will learn to recognize your fruits, leave behind that which is outdated, and reflect on something better—which they may truly find with you, as they shall confess.

-> That I wish to offer my service herewith, and have commended you as my <-
-> dear Lord and Friend. Dated from my <-
-> lodging in Augsburg, the 24th of July, in the year <-
-> 1536. <-

<meta>This page transitions from the preface by Wolfgang Thalhauser, which criticized the lack of surgical training in universities, to the formal dedication of the work by Paracelsus himself to King Ferdinand I.</meta>

# To the Most Powerful / Most Illustrious Prince and Lord / Lord
## Ferdinand / by God’s Grace, King of the Romans / of Hungary and Bohemia / etc. Our Most Gracious
### Lord / DOCTOR PARACELSUS’S Presentation of the Great Surgery.

Since now, Most Gracious Lord, Almighty God has no respect for personhood <note>meaning God treats everyone equally regardless of their social rank or status</note> in the frailty of nature, but has instead made every human subject to all diseases and death just like any other, and in this regard looks upon nothing nor spares anyone, but has created the greatest and the least with equal softness and gentleness: so too has Divine Providence, before the creation of man, considered such human frailty. Moved by mercy to prevent and turn away such occurring sicknesses from humanity, God ordained and created the physician along with medicine from the earth. From this it follows that man should have regard for the physician and medicine, for the wise man does not despise them: so that when the hour of need appears, he has those who can help him out after he has fallen into the ditch. For woe to him who lies there and has no one to help him up. Therefore, no one may exempt or exclude themselves from medicine.

Since now, Most Powerful Prince and Lord, such a heavy care is bound to humanity, forced by the accidents of disease: I have gathered here into a book the least and the fewest of the diseases, namely, regarding <term>wound-surgery</term> <note>original: "Wundarzney"; in the 16th century, surgery was often considered a manual trade distinct from "Physic" or internal medicine</note>, which increases and spreads more firmly the longer it goes, wounding the greatest as much as the least. This is a burden laid upon every person to take care regarding the healing of how such wounds occur. Since man carries such care through his innate nature, it is necessary that this art be ascribed and dedicated to the most powerful and highest of all men among us mortals on earth. This is for many reasons: namely, that the greatest as well as the least await it; also that the truth of the art be presented by the greatest and highest head to the least and most humble. Therefore, I rightly dedicate this to Your Roman Royal Majesty, as the most gracious and highest head.

As Your Roman Royal Majesty appears as and is the supreme head—in which I trust myself to be Your Majesty’s servant and a servant to all people, to everyone, no one excepted, present and future, for eternity—even though much has been written [on this subject], Your Majesty shall hold judgment herein between those writers and me, regarding how great an error has crept in. For when I consider your innate, faithful, and royal spirit, I have no doubt that Your Majesty will be a father to the whole land and consider the heavy and harsh deception that occurs through the "pretended physicians" against all the sick, which clearly leads to their ruin. You should prevent them and not let the truth of medicine be hindered, but rather provide protection and maintain the upper hand over it. Perhaps time might allow the false medicine of such destroyers and "pretended physicians" to be extinguished and vanish. Since it is innate by nature for every animal to take care of its own, so that the wolf or the hawk does not break in and take their young: how much more care should Your Majesty have for your subjects, whose bodies are the lodging of the soul, that they are not harmed or strangled by such ruinous physicians.

Since Your Majesty is ordained by Divine Providence to root out and throw into the fire that which is worthless, and to plant only that which is useful and good: I have, upon this basis, taken the care upon myself for the foundation of true medicine—as it reaches us from the righteous physicians—though I am weak. However, along with the daily new discoveries which show themselves now in this time more than ever, and with which God has gifted me through nature and prepared me with such experience, I present myself in my recipes and descriptions as an experienced man. So far as I boast, there is nothing here that has not been tested above all gold and made sharper than silver, through poverty, anxieties, wars, and needs. I have thus delayed my writing and teaching for so long for the sake of sufficient testing, so that I might present and offer not chatter, not a false fiction, not an unprepared art, not "guessing and opining," but a "Yes" and certain knowledge.

Since I have now fulfilled the care that I have carried for a long time—and the first care is mine—it follows that the second care belongs to Your Majesty: namely, to protect and uphold experience and truth, as the greatest head is indebted to his subjects. This is so that the flippancy of the incidental physicians, who do not belong in medicine, may not use their falsehood and obstruction of the truth, nor let them thrive. Although I give forth all art according to the truth without payment, uncovered and simply according to the foundation, I will not regret whoever eats of my will, since the same is won with the truth.

The crowd is large, Most Gracious Lord, that sets itself against me; but small is their understanding and art, therefore they shall win nothing from me in battle, for they have too little proof. Their following is large, but it scatters more and more the longer it goes due to the failure of their arts. If Your Majesty alone protects experience—of which there is no doubt—and bears the gracious will to promote the common good in every way, I have no doubt that a great deal of rubbish will fall from the throne, through which many sick people have been ruined. For when a thing reaches its height, it falls very quickly to the ground. If the art of wound-surgery is found to be truthful, without any flaws, and thoroughly discovered and proven, as recorded in this book: it is good to remember, since the truth lets itself be felt and noticed, that its enemy will lose the battle. I thus trust and hope, as a most humble servant, that I have served and worked well for Your Majesty and the whole wide world for a long time, showing thankfulness, honor, and praise—and that imperishably, until a better [art] arises and springs forth (according to the course and path of the current heavens, when the same is brought into something entirely new). I herewith commend myself to Your Majesty as a most humble servant, and also to the whole common good of the world, and hope without doubt to have obtained favor through Your Majesty’s spirit, under which I humbly commend myself. Given at Münchrath <note>likely referring to Mindelheim or a nearby locality where Paracelsus was staying</note> on the 7th of May, in the lesser count in the 36th year <note>1536</note>.

<header>Preface</header>

# DOCTOR PARA-
# CELSI,

## Into the First Treatise.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a scholar or physician seated at a table with an armillary sphere or globe and various books.</image-desc>

I have always and ever, with great attentiveness and diligent labor, strived to learn the foundation of medicine—to see if it might truly be called an art, or if it exists at all, or what might be within it. For many reasons moved me to this: namely, the uncertainty of its purpose. Specifically, I saw that so little praise and honor accompanied the actual works, and that so many sick people were ruined, killed, lamed, and utterly abandoned—not only in one disease, but in nearly all of them. It was so uncertain that in my time there has been no physician who could certainly cure even a toothache, let alone something smaller, to say nothing of great diseases. Furthermore, I found such folly in the writings of all the ancients. And alongside this, I saw in the great cities and among the wealthy that they were willing to offer great wealth for a cure, and yet were abandoned by all the doctors in their time of need—doctors who nevertheless went about in silk and gold rings, etc., with no small reputation, pomp, and chatter. Because of this, I several times resolved to abandon this art. For when considering its foundation, it seemed certain to no one else either; it appeared to be a work of fables and a "sweet luring-out of the penny" <note>an idiomatic way of saying the doctors were just tricking people out of their money</note>. It seemed an art based only on faith—so that if someone by chance happened upon the hour of improvement on their own, the credit was given (unjustly) to the art, to which it did not actually belong. I often left the profession and dealt in it with great resentment.

Yet, I did not entirely give in to my own feelings, but attributed the failure to my own <term>simplicity</term> <note>original: "Einfalt"; here meaning a lack of specialized knowledge or humble understanding</note>. Thus, for many years, I explored the high schools <note>the universities</note> among the Germans, the Italians, and the French, seeking the foundation of medicine. I did not wish to surrender myself only to their teachings, writings, and books, but wandered further to Granada, to Lisbon, through Spain, through England, through the Mark, through Prussia, Lithuania, Poland, Hungary, Wallachia, Transylvania, Croatia, the Windic March <note>a historical region in modern-day Slovenia</note>, and other lands as well, not all of which need to be recounted. In all these ends and places, I diligently and industriously inquired and researched for certain and experienced truthful arts of medicine. I sought this not only from the doctors, but also from the <term>barber-surgeons</term> <note>original: "Scherern"</note>, the <term>bath-keepers</term> <note>original: "Badern"; these men often performed minor surgeries and bloodletting</note>, learned physicians, women, practitioners of the black arts <note>original: "Schwartzkünstlern"</note> who practice such things, from the alchemists, from the monasteries, from the noble and the ignoble, from the clever and the simple. But I could not learn anything so thoroughly as to be certain, no matter what the disease might be. I thought much on how medicine seemed an uncertain art that was not fit to be used; it was not right to rely on luck, to make one person healthy while ruining ten others in exchange. This gave me cause to believe it was a deception of spirits intended to mislead and belittle humanity. Again, I left the profession and fell into other affairs. However, I was pushed back into this art once more. I found the <term>saying of Christ</term>: *The healthy have no need of a physician, only the sick.* <note>original: "Die gesunden dörffen keins Artzts / allein die Krancken" - Matthew 9:12</note> This moved me so much that I had to set another purpose for myself: namely, that the art, according to the content of Christ’s saying, must be truthful, just, certain, perfect, and whole. In it, there should be nothing of spirits for deception, nor should it be the fault of luck, but rather a proven and necessary art in times of need, useful and helpful to all the sick for their health. When I took this upon myself and grasped it, it was necessary to reconsider what the medicine was that I had heard of from books and others. I found that not one of them ever certainly knew, experienced, or understood this art at its foundation. They walked around the art of medicine like "a cat around porridge" <note>a German idiom meaning to avoid the heart of the matter or to approach something hesitantly without getting to the point</note>. They taught what they themselves did not know; they did not understand their own disputations. They visited the sick and gave counsel, yet they recognized neither the disease nor the art required for it. Thus, the fault lay solely in those who practiced it. Though much was and is said, they were merely shouters and chatterers in their pomp and splendor, and

# Preface.

there was nothing in them but a dead man’s grave, which is beautiful on the outside, but inside a stinking, rotten carcass, full of worms <note>A biblical allusion to the "whitewashed tombs" of the Pharisees (Matthew 23:27)</note>. Because of this, I was forced to search further, to leave behind the reading of the aforementioned evil lies, and to pursue another foundation that would be undefiled by the mentioned fables and chatter—firstly in surgery <term>Wundarkney: literally "wound-medicine," the historical term for surgery and external treatment</term>, which I have experienced as the most certain thus far. How I possess experience in this follows hereafter.

Now, it is no less true that in my time I will not be able to overthrow this work of fables, for they are old, unruly dogs; they learn nothing further and are ashamed to step down into the recognition of their folly. However, that matters little; rather, it depends on this: I hope the young will "step into another skin" <note>An idiom meaning to adopt a new way of thinking or being</note> when the old pass away. They will leave their delusions behind, and in time, the foundation will make progress. I must also mention this: in surgery, they are accustomed to holding great consultations; Doctors, barbers <term>Scherer: barber-surgeons who performed surgeries, bloodletting, and tooth extractions</term>, bath-masters <term>Bader: bath-house keepers who performed minor medical procedures</term>, etc., come together, and yet among them all there is no understanding. I will show and prove by their own conscience <note>original: "Conscienß"</note> that at this time there is no Doctor who could even heal a wound, let alone advise a remedy, yet they sign themselves as "Doctor of Both Medicines" <note>likely referring to internal medicine and surgery, though mocking the title 'Doctor of Both Laws'</note>. It is the same among the barbers and bath-masters; they are sworn masters of a city and swear an oath they cannot uphold, for they do not possess the art they swear upon. So much I say to you: it requires no consultation, but it is a certain and true art, just as ready as a carpenter in his carpentry. He must learn to build correctly, then he can do it rightly and needs no consultation. But if he cannot do it right, let him consult every day, and still nothing good will come of it; in the end, it all collapses. So it is with the medicine of wounds: what I say is a certain art; that is how it is.

Therefore, for the love of the art, I have made this book for you, so that you may see that you are taught rightly in this book. And although it is a rare cause—medicine is no rhetoric <term>Rethorica: the art of persuasive speech</term>—it will go well for you, and medicine will proceed for you just as a potter makes a pot. Therefore remember: if God created the potter <term>Hafner: potter</term> and his clay, which serves only for the stove and the pot, how much more did He create the physician and his medicine, which is greater than all arts and crafts.

Therefore, my book is for all physicians, whoever they may be, bearded or unbearded; they should not take it ill (for your own conscience and certainty proves me right). I know many of you, and in nearly many lands, and many are among you who are not entirely without skill; some even have "little pieces" of knowledge—one has one piece, another one and a half, some two whole ones, more or less. Whatever each one can do, I begrudge him not at all. I only want to teach those things that I mention and indicate in this book. The learned and those who are already capable do not need my teaching; I do not mean them in my writing, nor do I want the learned, the righteous, or the proven to be included here, but only the others who wish to understand. It would not be against me or my writing if the better way were always brought forth, and not the worse. Even if the worse way is helpful, it is still burdened with so much failure; to prevent this, as much as is possible for the body, promises can be made and kept—with the instruction and distinction that follows hereafter in the first treatise, and following that, the healing in the final two. And begin this with the fear of God, and seek first His kingdom; ask, seek, and knock in the name of God, and all your needs will be given to you in overflowing abundance. For in His name, and through Him, all things happen. And strive to be perfect in your

->art, for God created it perfect, so that<-
->your work may praise, honor,<-
->and glorify God.<-

# Catalogue and Register of all Books and Treatises
## contained in the following three parts of the Surgical Books and Writings
->By Theophrastus, and contained in the Appendix.<-

### In the First Part.

I. **The First Book of Great Surgery, containing three treatises.** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist. "Great Surgery" (Die grosse Wundartzney) was his most successful publication during his lifetime.</note>
1. What pertains to a surgeon, and what is necessary for him to know regarding wounds.
2. Treatise on medicine: its recipes, descriptions, and everything to be made and known by which wounds, stabs, arrow-shots, and the like are healed.
3. Treatise on all kinds of animal venom and bites occurring externally: also the healing of bone fractures, and all kinds of burns according to the manner of craftsmen—among miners, salt-boilers, weather-exposed workers, gunners, powder-makers, and the like; likewise, clotted blood and frostbite.
II. **The Second Book: on the origin, signs, and nature of open lesions of the whole body, and contains within itself three treatises.**
1. How the first physicians, both the righteous and the unrighteous, dealt with open lesions through arts and medicines.
2. On the various origins and natural beginnings of open lesions.
3. On the three types of healing for open lesions: one universal and two particular.
III. **The Third Book: on the French Disease <term>Frantzösischen Kranckheiten: a historical term for syphilis, which spread rapidly through Europe in the late 15th century</term>, pustules, sores, paralysis, spots, and other growths that arise from them.**

---

### In the Second Part.

I. **On the deceptions used in treating the French Disease: likewise on the correction and abolition of the same:** Divided into three books.
II. **On the origin and source of the French Disease, eight books: together with the healing of the same.**
III. **On the pustules, paralysis, boils, holes, and tremors caused by the French Disease and their like, containing ten beautiful books, within which the "Small Surgery" <note>original: "CHIRVRGIA parva"</note> is comprised.**
IV. **The Hospital Book of Theophrastus, in which the entire cure for the French Disease is contained.**
V. **A little book on Guaiacum wood <note>original: "De ligno Gvaiaco"</note>: that is, how the French Disease should be healed through Guaiacum wood.** <note>Guaiacum, or "holy wood," was imported from the Americas and was a popular, though often ineffective, 16th-century treatment for syphilis.</note>
VI. **A little book on wood: which was perhaps collected from other writings of Theophrastus in this manner.**

---

### In the Third Part.

I. **The Bertheoneae, three books, dealing with wounds, open lesions, and ulcers.**
II. **The book of all open lesions born out of nature: divided into seven beautiful books.**
III. **On the opening of the skin, and its natural displacement, two books from Theophrastus’s own manuscript.** <note>original: "eigner handschrifft"</note>
IV. **Three other surgical books, the titles of which were found in the original manuscript as: Book 3 on the French Disease, Book 4 on Ulcers, Book 5 on Abscesses.** <note>original: "Liber 3. de Morbo Gallico, Liber 4. de Vlceribvs. Liber 5. de Apostematibus"</note>
V. **On abscesses, ulcers, open lesions, and other growths on the body, one book, containing 62 chapters.**
VI. **Theophrastus’s surgical lectures on wounds: never before issued in print.** <note>original: "prælectiones Chirurgicæ de Vulneribus"</note>
VII. **Three other books of surgery: the 1st on wounds, the 2nd on open lesions, the 3rd on the French Disease.**
VIII. **Small Surgery, on the cure of wounds, from the original manuscript of Theophrastus.** <note>original: "Chirurgia parva, De cura vulnerum, ex Autographo"</note>

---

I. **A draft or collection <term>Rhapsodia: a term Paracelsus used for a miscellaneous collection of notes or fragments</term> of a surgical book on wounds (and what pertains to them) which have been ruined by bad surgeons: likewise, those mixed with other bodily internal illnesses. It is divided into 6 books: but not all are present.**

# TO THE DISTINGUISHED AND MOST LEARNED
## MASTER JOHANNES HUSER, PHYSICIAN; JOHANNES POLITUS OF LIÈGE, DOCTOR OF BOTH LAWS, ON THE RESTORATION OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.

<note>This is a Latin poem of praise for Johannes Huser, the editor who spent decades collecting and printing Paracelsus's scattered manuscripts to "restore" his legacy.</note>

> Why, German, do you marvel at Italy or famous Athens?
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When your own glory is by no fate lesser.
> All things change in cycles: but the gifts of Nature,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Flowing from a single source, are accessible to all lands.
> Behold, PARACELSUS triumphs! He who is high-born,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shows the way to the arduous peaks of things with a wondrous light.
> Among doctors, he has raised his head so far above all others,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Teaching the medical art more surely than the ancient craft:
> As much as Apollo <note>original: "Latous"; the son of Leto</note> surpassed you, Marsyas, in song,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And as much as Dardanian Rome surpasses other cities.
> But you ask: why, after so many writings of the ancients,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Does this new man take his path through the arts by an unknown track?
>
> <column-break/>
>
> It is no wonder: Nature is fertile, and the seeds of things
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are provident: known only in their own proper times.
> He is deservedly praised who, through many wanderings,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Was first able to approach the Indians by a conquered sea.
> But he is also to be praised who, avoiding the bends and curves,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Followed after him by a more convenient way.
> Therefore, HUSER, what do your friendly mind, your good deeds,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And your labor for the human race not deserve?
> Go then, and please ERNST, <note>Ernst of Bavaria (1554–1612), Archbishop-Elector of Cologne and Huser's patron.</note> great man; by his sagacious
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Genius, the envious crowd shall fall.
> He favors the learned Muses <note>original: "Camænis"</note>, being most learned himself,

# The First Book of Doctor Paracelsus / of the Great Surgery / Begins in the Name of the Lord / Amen.

## The First Treatise teaches and instructs / What belongs to a Surgeon / and what is necessary for him to know.

### CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the first inspection of wounds / what a physician should know / and recognize in them.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or physician) seated at a desk with a child or student nearby.</image-desc>

Every surgeon <note>original: "Wundarzt"; literally "wound-doctor." In this era, surgeons were often distinct from academic physicians, focusing on external treatments and operations.</note> should first be prepared with this point / and know at the first inspection of the wounds / what is there before his eyes and lies before him / as soon as he looks upon the wounds: Namely / how far he may progress with it / to what end he may bring it / so that he does not blunder at the start / promising more or less than Nature is willing to grant. For he should so undertake the care of wounds / that he places his word within the capability of Nature / not attempting more / than is possible for Nature / or accomplishing less / than Nature could well have achieved. Whatever he overlooks in this / is a heavy shame to him / and a great mockery. For if you promise too much / and Nature cannot fulfill it / it is not within her power / so you pay and struggle toward a point / where you cannot arrive: And the longer you pay / the more you ruin in the process / and bring yourself to shame. If you promise little / and achieve more / it is yet a mockery / that you did not understand your own tools and your art: Or if you could have achieved more / but did not / how much greater is your shame. Therefore learn / that you first have a knowledge of Nature and of the Art <note>Paracelsus often treats "Art" (the physician's skill) and "Nature" (the body's healing power) as two necessary partners.</note> / so that you three come together / for if any were lacking / it would ruin the whole game.

You should know / that Nature does not allow herself to be forced / nor driven into another essence / than her nature is: you must follow her / and she not you. Therefore if you bring medicine that is not suitable to Nature / you destroy her: For she does not follow you / you must now follow her. This is the Art / that you recognize the medicine suitable to Nature / then you may easily make haste. A limb that is hacked off from the body / you may never set back on / What however is off / and may be set back on again / that may never come to its old essence / without defect. Likewise what is hacked lame / that may not become straight again / and what is unto death / do not attempt to keep it in life. Likewise do not attempt impossible things / for it is ridiculous. Therefore learn / when a thing lies openly before your eyes / to know what the power of Nature is / also of the Art / and proceed in the same. Although the manual techniques <note>original: "Handtgriff"; literally "hand-grips" or "manipulations."</note> may not be written down / such as the joining of the wounds: You should know the same through your own skill / which you have learned from experience / and do not act against the proper joining / so that you do not bring Nature into a deformity through your lack of skill.

I have many times listened to barbers, bath-keepers <note>original: "Scherern, Badern"; these were practitioners of minor surgery, bloodletting, and tooth extraction, often viewed by Paracelsus as unlearned competitors.</note> / and their like / who boast so crudely of their art / that they have found hacked-off noses / that lay in the snow for three days / hacked-off fingers / and the like even more unbelievable / and after several days / set them back in their old place: Do not accustom yourself to such idle talk. A physician should be truthful / earnest / and brave with his words / not frivolous: Speak what is possible / and consistent with Nature / that a pious man may believe / and praise you. I saw indeed in Brno <note>original: "Berun"</note> / a man had an ear hacked off / and a bath-keeper took it / and set it back on again with stone-mason's cement, cheese-glue <note>original: "Käßleim"; a strong adhesive made from casein/milk protein.</note> / etc. He kept the praise / and a great cry of wonder: On the second day it fell off again / where the pus had eaten beneath it. Thus it happens also to other such reattached limbs. But what kind of praise is that?

You should also be instructed / to recognize good and bad signs of the wounds / whether something adverse might happen in the wounds / so that you recognize them daily / and know their meaning / what they represent / and what evil the signs indicate / so that you may daily prevent such an incident. For a healthy body is not without incident / how much more an injured one. For thus wounds occur / that develop into a stroke <note>original: "Schlag"; apoplexy or paralysis.</note>, into joint-sickness <note>original: "Glidsucht"; often referring to gout or arthritis.</note>, into consumption <note>original: "Schwindsucht"</note> / into the falling sickness <note>original: "Fallendensucht"; epilepsy.</note> / and others more. Where you do not understand such / you mislead yourself / and destroy the sick as an ignorant and inexperienced person. If you despise them / you cast it to the wind / and cannot turn it back / trusting in your art / and yet you do not know it: So see / how you bring the wounded into need / and that which you despise / brings misery and need / worse than the wound in itself: Therefore if you know and are able / and recognize such signs and incidents / so may you prevent future...

# CHAPTER II.

->How and in what way a wound is healed: What heals / and what ruins.<-

<margin>

In order that you may understand what it is / that heals a wound: For without such knowledge you cannot properly recognize any medicine: So you should know / that the nature of the flesh / the body / the veins / the bone has within itself an innate Balsam <term>Balsam: Paracelsus believed the body possessed an internal life-force or "mummy" that performed the actual work of healing.</term> / which heals wounds / stabs / and the like. That is to say / the balsam that naturally lies in the bone / heals the bone-breaks / the balsam that naturally lies in the flesh / heals the flesh. Thus it is to be understood with every limb / that every limb carries its own healing within itself / and thus Nature has her own doctor in her own limb / who heals that / which is wounded in her. Therefore, every surgeon should know / that he is not the one / who heals / but the Balsam in the body is that which heals: If the doctor presumes / he is the one / who heals / then he deceives himself / and does not recognize his own art: But so that you may know why you, the surgeon, are good and useful / and what the art is for / it is this / that you provide protection and defense to Nature in the injured part against adverse enemies / so that the external enemies do not drive back the Balsam of Nature / nor poison nor ruin it / but that it remains in its Balsamic power and effect / through the protection of this shield: For this is certain and evident / if the wound is open / and is not protected or shielded / that it can in no way accomplish its work. Therefore, he who can protect and guard well / he is a good surgeon. Thus the surgeon is, through medicine, a protector of Nature against the external elements / which strive against Nature: And where Nature is found to be ailing / there they <note>the external elements/enemies</note> think to introduce even more ailments. Such enemies and elemental power / the doctor shall drive away through medicine / so that Nature may proceed ready and happily through her Balsam / as she is kept in peace and rest by the shield / and within herself / and when Nature finds herself in such protection / and by your skill in bandaging / she heals herself together and makes the flesh grow / the veins / or whatever it is / according to the capacity that may be in the wound. As an example: What is it that makes the flesh / the barley / the fat / the blood / the marrow / etc. grow? Not man / not food: But Nature has a growing and increasing power within her / which makes the body perfect. But through food and drink, this same power is maintained. Rain and earth do not make wood / but the tree itself makes it / yet without the rain and earth it dies.

For that same medicine gives nourishment to the Balsam / and feeds it / and through that same nourishment it heals all the more strongly and quickly. Therefore, the medicine is a suitable nourishment for the Balsam / and it is healed all the better. For it depends upon this / that the doctor should know to apply good nourishment to Nature / so he may proceed all the more fortunately. # Surgery: The First Treatise.

A <margin>Pus and Discharge</margin> thus you ruin the wounds / and fall into all manner of complications and aggravations of the wound: You might well consider / if you let a wound rot / and it becomes stinking / that it lacks its nourishment / and that it cannot complete its work: Rather, the wound must be kept clean with nourishment / so that nothing rotten or stinking is found within it. And note here a distinction regarding the pus in the wound / for there are two kinds: one comes from the rotting of the wound / the other from the nourishment of the medicine. Thus, one is a <term>pus</term> <note>original: "Eyter"; here referring specifically to infectious or "bad" pus</note> / the other is an <term>excrement</term> <note>original: "Excrementum"; Paracelsus uses this to mean the natural byproduct or "waste" of the body's internal healing force</note>, which is to say: The <term>balsam</term> <note>the body's innate healing power</note> draws its nourishment from the medicine / and what remains / are the <term>waste products</term> <note>original: "Stercora"; literally "dung" or "refuse"</note>, just as every kind of food yields its own waste. Based on this, the surgeon should know / that the wounds should be maintained in their "excrements" / and not in the "pus" / or the rot. Therefore, it is a contrary medicine / where the wounds are stifled and smothered / and not maintained in free nourishment / and this should happen in no way. For not only does one kind of damage follow from it / but many-sided aggravations are to be expected. I would also have you surgeons warned / though it is a common custom among you / yet it is without art and understanding / even with a supposedly certain healing / as you have the custom of sewing wounds / also of gumming them up with egg whites / and thus driving nature by force in its way into something contrary / which is an altogether unfit and ungrounded medicine / as is proven in many ways. For nature desires nothing in its healing / but only that it be rescued from rot / and guided through medicine / as is mentioned above / and that the proper discharges are found at every bandage change. Thus, enough has been said for this time / as to what it is / that heals the wound: And whatever is otherwise / than as has been mentioned / the same ruins the wound.

B <margin>Disease</margin> <note>The source uses a symbol or character that translates to "disease" or "illness," marking the start of a new section on pathology.</note> Therefore know that the medicines / which do not yield "excrements" / are not medicines of the wounds / but rather they ruin them. Based on this, know now / that you should apply yourself to recognize the "excrements" / so that you proceed on the right foundation / for where they do not appear / you must expect misfortune / and the ruin of the sick person. I have many times seen the lack of understanding among you surgeons / when the wound merely stank properly / and gave rotten pus / like a stinking old hole on a thigh <note>original: "Delschenckel"; likely a regional variant for "Diechschenkel," the thigh</note> / that it pleased you well / yet in your folly and ruin. This I tell you / as soon as a wound stinks and rots in that way / like an old sore on a running leg / that should not be—neither you, nor your wound / nor your medicine.

You must have the knowledge / so that you understand which medicine makes "excrements" / and which does not / and how one is better than the other / each according to its kind. Where you have not learned this / your business is blind / whether it turns out well or ill. But you shout loudly / whenever you happen to hit upon something / without your art / if it only happened to be there / then you have a boast <note>original: "plerz"; a loud boast or outcry</note> for many years thereafter. You must know the "excrements" and <term>ichor</term> <note>original: "Sanies"; a thin, watery discharge from a wound</note> of the wounds / and that the healing power / which is within man / heals alone / keep it clean / and protect it from external and incidental enemies. Thus are all wounds healed.

## CHAPTER III.

### Which wounds are deadly or not: concerning lame wounds, and the like.

It is necessary / that you recognize by sight / whether a wound leads to death / or not / whether it is a "lame" wound or <unclear>Mon</unclear> / or how far you may bring it / toward its old and natural essence and power. This happens in this way: First, what is chopped off / will never again be set back on: What is chopped off down to the skin / is also thus. What comes to the tenth part / can come to no more fruitfulness: As when you divide an arm / crosswise / into ten parts / and the nine were chopped off / then the tenth might well bring the arm back together / but without fruit and strength: But what is within the nine parts / the closer to the first / the more useful.

What only affects the flesh / is without harm: Unless the <term>fear</term> <note>original: "Fercht"; likely referring to the vital spirit or "life-force" within the tissue</note>, life / or muscles <note>original: "Mäuß"; literally "mice," a common historical term for muscles</note> were therein / then it may lead to death / to a lameness / or into another worry.

Those which are crosswise wounds / result in "lame" wounds: Unless they are protected with good medicine.

C All vessels <note>original: "Geäder"; referring to veins and arteries</note> that are chopped off / depend entirely on the medicine / whether the person becomes lame, crooked, or not. For through right medicine / no chopped-off nerves / vessels / <term>sinews</term> <note>original: "Altwachs"</note> yield "lame" wounds / unless they are brought to that point by bad medicine / and through accident or the disorder of the sick.

All joint-wounds / be they what they will / as long as they lose no bone or <term>joint-disc</term> <note>original: "Scheiben"</note> / are brought back into their old essence through right medicine / without lameness or crookedness. But where a heat / or swelling strikes / then it can never happen. Also if bone is lost / and where flesh grows in / that is / what is filled with flesh / where bone should be / there "lame" wounds occur.

Thus it is to be known in summary / that in the four limbs / as stabs or wounds occur / crosswise / lengthwise / according to depth / etc. / that through their right medicine they may well be preserved and protected from lameness and crookedness. But through the medicine in the <term>brass boxes</term> <note>original: "Messinen Büchslin"; a derogatory reference to cheap, mass-produced apothecary ointments</note> / it cannot be prevented: for they introduce accidents / and similar troubles / the same ruin them / therefore I do not unjustly despise their medicine and art / since there is a better one / through which such accidents do not occur.

So also there are wounds in the head / which take and bring the stroke / sudden death / epilepsy / speech / hearing / etc. Though it does not happen in all / yet sometimes / according to how the human is natured: To help such as these in the occurring illnesses / depends on the time / the person / the <term>complexion</term> <note>the individual's physical and temperamental makeup</note>...

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus's systematic evaluation of wounds based on their location in the body and the nature of the organs affected. He emphasizes that while some wounds are inherently fatal, others depend on the astrological timing, the patient's temperament, and the skill of the surgeon.</meta>

# The First Book of the Great [Surgery].

...nature, to the property, and according to the nature of the case, so too is the medicine. For thus <margin>A</margin> they sometimes become deaf, insane, and burdened with other such diseases. Furthermore, it is to be known that where the chambers of sight, hearing, and speech are struck, it is no stroke or paralysis, but wounds in themselves; they are never perfectly healed unless they were hit only very slightly.

Smallpox wounds <note>original: "Blatern"; refers to pustules or the pox</note> are fatal, for they accept no healing.

Wounds or stabs in the regions of the heart are fatal, without any exception.

The organ wounds <note>original: "Weydwunden"; wounds affecting the internal soft organs or gut</note> are not fatal; they may be well-managed by skilled doctors in their entry and exit. But where they are severed, they will never be healed. They are also to be judged by where they are hit, whether below or above, or in the middle, and according to how one can reach them.

Wounds or stabs to the spleen are not lethal, nor worrisome in other ways. Their complications are removed through <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "Lässine"; a regional term for phlebotomy used to vent "excess" humors</note> thereafter.

Wounds in the gall <note>the gallbladder</note> are fatal, and lead to a long-drawn-out end.

Wounds in the lungs are not lethal, but they do not pass without subsequent infirmity; for they accept no healing, but rather rot, tightness, coughing, shortness of breath, and the like.

Wounds in the stomach accept no healing. But it often happens that life is maintained for a long time; however, they are all fatal wounds. Depending on how they are, they finish the person quickly or linger; especially those from the side or through the back are bad, and from the front they are fatal.

<margin>B</margin> Liver wounds are not quickly fatal, but fall into long illness. They accept no healing and worsen the longer they last, leading to the wasting away of the whole body, and are subject to many diseases.

Kidney wounds are like liver wounds, yet curable; however, they lose their strength.

Furthermore, you should also know that where "roots" are struck—those places where the main organs are anchored—they are fatal, faster or slower according to the importance of that organ.

Know also that all stabs and wounds inside the body cannot be thoroughly seen; therefore, no certain judgment can be made of them. Sometimes miraculous stabs are healed, etc., and sometimes minor stabs lead to death. It all depends on what they hit and touch. A stab may pass through and be without harm, whether through the ribs or the belly, for it may deflect and slip off, or no damage may occur.

Wounds in the head are all worrisome, both small and large. Much also depends on the patient's nature and strength, and on the skillful medicine. For in the head lie the origins of many fatal diseases; if something is present there, it breaks forth and causes heavy injuries. And none is so small that it passes without harm. If the brain is opened, it is a sign of death, and there is no more healing to be had.

He who is struck in tensed or extended limbs—these are worrisome wounds leading to death, paralysis, and much pain. For anyone who stands with stretched, tensed limbs and is hit in them meets a worrisome end. But where the limb lies loose, soft, gentle, or bent, little misfortune is to be expected.

Likewise, many types of wounds occur that cannot be described. Thus, every surgeon should be experienced, well-traveled, and skillful in himself, to recognize their essence and property from the aforementioned signs.
<margin>C</margin>

Although there are many who persuade themselves they know much, yet know nothing: for such inexperienced ones, it is better to remain idle and stand aside, for their opinions are the ruin of the sick.

Time, the hour, the heavens, the course [of the stars], the nature, the movement, the instances, etc., also produce fatal wounds that would otherwise be nourished without harm. Man is placed in much danger and burdened and surrounded by many evil hours. No one can fathom it all, but every day something new is discovered.

***

### CHAPTER IV.

->What the physician should fear in wounds, and what is hindered by the heavenly stars, and how far capability sets its limit.<-

Every surgeon should also know what he should dread in wounds or not. Even if they have a pleasing appearance, many adversities are to be expected. Namely, those wounds inflicted in anger from the "gall"—those who rage in their bile—these are difficult and worrisome to heal, spoiling the wounds so that it is not well possible to heal them as is proper. Rather, one must let the bile dissipate and wait for the end of its poison. For anger cannot be forestalled until it consumes itself. Women who are wounded in anger are likely to expect <term>labor pains</term> <note>original: "Kindelwehe"</note>, gout <note>original: "Bergicht"</note>, or colic <note>original: "Darmgächt"</note>. And where one finds those of such an angry, sudden nature, it is for them as for "evil women." Those who are <term>Saturnine</term> <note>original: "Saturnisch"; influenced by Saturn, often meaning melancholic or stubborn</note>, envious, hateful, or unfaithful—these same are also predisposed to such incidents, as are the <term>Martial</term> <note>original: "Martialischen"; influenced by Mars, meaning aggressive or hot-tempered</note> ones.

Likewise, there are sometimes such poisonous gazes that if they look into the wounds, they defile the wounds...

# Surgery: The First Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> ...cleansing, and to make them all the more incurable, one must also let them pass away: as in women, and in many others. For there are many sicknesses that expel themselves through sweat, and some that poison through the breath. Likewise, much poison flows out through the sight, directed wherever the gaze is turned.

Also, when wounds are inflicted upon you while the belly is full of food and drink—and should pork or the like have been eaten—it is also a hindrance to healing. For those same foods must be digested and distributed throughout the entire body; where wounds are present, the body is open and susceptible to infection <note>original: "süchtig"; implying a state of being prone to disease or "dropsical" in some contexts</note>.

Also, at times, there are accidental diseases innate to the person, such as <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Vergicht"; a general term for joint pain or paralysis in this period</note> or <term>labor pains</term> <note>original: "Kindelwehe"; refers here to complications or conditions arising from childbirth</note>, which also cause a delay in health. In such accidents, you must know how to protect yourself: for Nature has set no further goal; such things must be dealt with first, for Nature is overmastered by such adverse things and is no longer in control of herself.

Furthermore, it is to be known that where diseases fall into the wound—such as <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "Schweinsucht"; literally "swine-sickness," often referring to wasting diseases or scrofulous swellings</note>, fistula, cancer, cavities, etc.—there Nature allows no further healing until the disease is first taken away from her. Therefore, do not judge the wound alone, but also that which strikes the wound, so that you do not mislead yourself and the sick person. Where such understanding is not with you, it will be a troublesome work.

Therefore, do not undertake anything further than the goal to which Nature reaches. For from such wounds, they cease to be wounds and become other diseases; against this, you should know to protect yourself.

<margin>B</margin> The course of the Heavens is also manifold, and its operation is strong, pressing heavily against us through its impression <note>The "impression" refers to the astrological influence or "astral seal" exerted by planets on earthly bodies</note>. If it is possible for the Heavens to "imprint" the plague, then it is also quite possible for such a celestial accident to poison the wounds, and that in many different ways. But because this is too difficult to discover and present here, I commend it to the <term>Astronomical School</term>. Every surgeon should know, however, that when the Heavens stand unluckily, he should also consider the patient unlucky. Although one cannot act against the stars, one must let them "blow over" <note>original: "versausen"; to let a storm pass or a sound fade</note>. Although change may happen, it will be no more powerful than medicine is against the plague; therefore, do not undertake more than your power allows against the enemies of the wounds. And judge well how they are disposed. If they are too powerful for the medicine, then remember that you cannot overcome the more powerful. Do not boast too much, but keep the advantage in your hand. For man is a very slight thing, and such an inconstant creature, that one cannot place too much trust in him: since such is innate to man, it is necessary to observe him well. It also happens that wounds receive a character of their own, in the same way as wood that is harvested under a bad sign becomes worm-eaten; or like clay that is dug at an improper time is full of <term>crickets</term> <note>original: "Grillen"; likely referring to imperfections, cracks, or perhaps literal insects in the raw material</note> and changes, as there are many such things. If a wound works according to such a [celestial] operation, think nothing else than that you cannot prevent such a force except through special <term>Secret Remedies</term> <note>original: "Arcana"</note>, which are like certain herbs and seeds: where they lie, no cricket remains. Likewise, where some lie, no worm remains in the wood. Through such secret remedies you must work further, so that the common course of healing is maintained. For it is often found that wounds regress even under great medicine, the sole cause of which is the heavenly course: just as sometimes wood is cut down in a bad <term>alignment of stars</term> <note>original: "Constellation"</note> and will never grow back; and for the same reason, a branch that is planted. Thus, although rare, it also happens to wounds of such a kind.

<margin>C</margin> Note: Therefore, you should not exclude yourself from the knowledge of the heavenly course, but be diligent to learn, so that you do not stand there like a shoemaker who can make the whole shoe, right up until it is time to <term>turn it</term> <note>original: "vmbkehren"; in "turnshoe" construction, the shoe is sewn inside out and then flipped. A shoemaker who cannot perform this final, difficult step has a useless product</note>.

->### CHAPTER V.<-

->How to treat fresh wounds, and what to do with corrupt ones, recognizing the difference between their two medicines.<-

It is also of great necessity to know the manner of binding <note>bandaging</note>, so that the wounds are not corrupted, just as corrupt wounds must be kept with binding according to their nature. Now, fresh wounds are to be handled so that you protect them from all accidents from which harm may spring: for if you overlook such, the wounds become corrupted. I indicate this for a reason and dedicate a special chapter to it, though it has been mentioned enough before: because there are so many abuses with fresh wounds, it is necessary to explain them better. And even if the inexperienced doctor might say: "He had also healed wounds without such foresight," he nevertheless keeps silent about the filth he committed in the meantime, and the torment and torture he allowed the patient to suffer. Now, the custom is to stitch wounds, to paste them with egg white, and thus to wait until the third day. That is the **first corruption**. Initially, you should keep the order of the Second Treatise without stitching, and heal the wounds through nourishment; thus you will not fall into the first corruption, from which much harm follows. Furthermore, if you find them already corrupted, then cleanse them, so that they may be freed from the stench and filth into which they were led, as is presented in the Second Treatise. Thus you have the distinction between fresh and corrupted wounds, and how you should...

# Surgery: The First Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> ...handle and accept. Furthermore, proceed with the medicine of the second treatise and bind the wound twice every day—exactly twelve hours apart—and do not neglect the hour. For if you let the medicine lie longer, its power is spent <note>original: "verwürckt"; meaning the medicinal effect is exhausted or spoiled</note>, its nourishment is gone, and the protection from the outer elements is lost. Then the wound falls into mishap and aggravation, worsening as time goes on, attracting all those complications that ought not to be there. Therefore, do not miss the hour, and continue thus until the end. Although, at the very last, as the wound nears its closing, you may well delay for twenty-four hours, yet do not trust it too much.

Also, take note of further corruption: once the first bandage (applied with egg white, as mentioned) is removed, other types of corruption often follow. They bind wounds with resin, sometimes with <term>pine resin</term> <note>original: "Bilharz"</note>, sometimes with unprepared wax, sometimes with tallow, or with oil, all mixed together; and sometimes they add sponges, mastic, incense, etc., or gums. Now, know regarding such medicine that it is not at all suitable for wounds, for it heats them too much. Also, it is so poorly prepared <note>original: "vngering kocht"; literally "undercooked" or poorly concocted</note> in the <term>brass chest</term> <note>original: "Messbüchlein" / "Messinen Büchlein"; refers to a small brass container or the standard apothecary chest of the time, which Paracelsus often criticized</note> that it can provide no nourishment to the wound; it draws to itself what it should not draw, and it cannot act according to the forces of nature. From this follows swelling, extensive rotting, wound-sickness <note>infection</note>, burning inflammation, shooting pains in the limbs, and other worse signs that follow. Where you encounter such a wound, take it to be a corrupted, disgraced wound, and bind it immediately with medicines that heal wounds through cleansing, keeping them clean and at their proper temperature; otherwise, they might certainly be judged as leading to death or other shameful decay. 

There are also some wounds that are fatal in certain persons but not in others; fatal at one time, but not another. Some also become fatal over time through complications, as will be mentioned more in other places. Therefore, a true and certain knowledge of fatal wounds cannot always be found, to judge exactly whether every wound leads to death or life, for they creep in as secretly as a thief. <margin>B</margin> However, those who are struck unto death, and in whom there is no recovery, are these: such as wounds to the brain; where the brain matter itself finds a way out, no life is to be expected. Also, whatever stabs or wounds occur around the <term>pit of the heart</term> <note>the epigastrium or "heart-pit"</note> are also fatal, for the heart wishes its region to be uninjured. Also, wounds to the <term>urinary bladder</term> <note>original: "Wasserblatern"</note> are fatal. Likewise, when <term>gut-wounds</term> <note>original: "Weydwunden"; wounds to the intestines</note> occur and the passage cannot be cleared, they are fatal. Also, whatever damages the windpipe to the lungs is fatal; whatever shatters the neck is fatal; also, what are "dry strokes" <note>blunt force trauma without open bleeding</note> that reach into the region of the heart with congested blood are also fatal. There are also other signs that lead to death, but over a long time; and another sickness may well fall in between, which introduces death in another way, such as in the lungs, liver, etc. Regarding the spleen, there is little to worry about. Where the gallbladder is opened, it is also fatal; likewise, the stomach introduces death over time. Where the veins between the liver and stomach are pierced, it is also fatal. Furthermore, regarding other wounds, know that wounds which are stabbed into the <term>muscle</term> <note>original: "Mauß"; literally "mouse," a common term for a muscle</note> where the life-force <note>original: "Ferch"; an archaic term for the vital spirit or the seat of life</note> resides, are also fatal. And what are "tension wounds"—that is, when someone stretches a limb and is struck while the limb is thus extended—are also fatal, though less worrisome than others. It also happens that sometimes a person is malformed inside the body, so that the veins do not lie in their natural place; such wounds also become fatal. Sometimes wounds happen such that sudden death, or a stroke, or another fatal sickness coincides with them; these are also fatal. Sometimes an "influence" <note>an astrological or environmental "influx"</note> falls into the wound—that is, in an evil sign—and it becomes fatal. Sometimes wounds become fatal out of great fright, sometimes out of neglect, and sometimes after the passage of time. For death comes creeping in many hidden ways, as mentioned in the previous chapter.

<margin>C</margin> Likewise, it is to be noted that very often head wounds cause <term>deafness</term> <note>original: "Taubsucht"; can mean deafness or a state of being dazed/numb</note>. Similarly, if the veins of the sight are struck, they cause blindness; also, if the chamber of hearing is pierced, it takes away the hearing. Likewise, if the genitals are injured, it is sometimes fatal, or sometimes they take away fertility; so too are the organs of the voice, which govern speech. Likewise, it is to be known that wounds which run crosswise, splitting the wound open, are <term>paralyzing wounds</term> <note>original: "lame Wunden"</note>. Wounds struck in other ways depend on the medicine and how diligently they are healed. Where a "cold stroke" <note>likely gangrene or sudden paralysis</note> strikes a wound, it causes lameness, wherever it may be. And any <term>tendon</term> <note>original: "Flachs"</note> that loses its natural "balsam" <note>the body's innate healing fluid</note> also results in a paralyzed wound. Also, any wound that is prone to falling into <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "Schwindsucht"; wasting away</note> results in lameness. There are also many other kinds of paralyzing wounds, such as when the root of the ligaments is struck; this paralyzes an entire limb. There are also many other types of paralysis that occur outside the mentioned places and yet still cause lameness. The cause is the time, the hour, and other accidents whose coming cannot be described. For man is burdened with much misery; therefore, he should not risk his skin so lightly. For so many things happen—more for the worse than for the better—that such complications cannot always be prevented. Thus, the doctor can do nothing against the possibility of Nature; rather, only so far as she permits, in that same measure should he be certain and truly grounded in his knowledge. And although it also happens that through medicine many lamenesses are averted and other accidents healed where Nature accepts it, this is explained in the Second Treatise. And bind the swelling with warm rose vinegar, and throw away the <term>white ointment</term> <note>original: "weiß Selblin"</note> in the brass box, and bind the wounds, once they are cleansed, with the <term>stitch-plasters</term> <note>plasters used to draw wound edges together or extract toxins</note>, and proceed thus until the end of the healing.

Furthermore, there is another corruption present that comes from that same brass box, namely <term>joint-water</term> <note>original: "Glidwasser"; synovial fluid or serous discharge</note>. Should this appear, throw all their medicine from that same brass box out the window—it is truly time—and bind only with the stitch-plaster, and proceed with the same, (also)
