# CHAPTER VI.
## Concerning the Complications of Wounds, according to Time, the Course of the Heavens, and other Unfortunate Afflictions.

<margin>B</margin> It is sufficiently and openly known that the heavens, according to the time, create many kinds of sicknesses and so poison and defile even healthy people that it is beyond counting. This is well known to everyone; no healthy person can protect themselves from it, but must humble themselves before the heavens and wait every day to see what they might send. For the heavens have a wondrous course within them, and humans are also given a wondrous nature; therefore, wondrous complications occur. If the heavens can overcome the healthy, how much more so the wounded? If experience had not proven this, it would be impossible to believe. In this regard, take note: just as the heavens, through their movements, are the father of many fevers in a healthy person, know also that they bring fever into wounds. Thus, at specific hours, the fever begins in the wound <margin>Mattheſſ. 479. Wound pain <note>original: "瘡 痛"; Chinese scholarly annotation</note> Cl. D. 284. x 83. x 388.</margin> and fulfills its work and <term>paroxysm</term> <note>the peak stage of a fever</note> with chills and heat, just as is the nature of fevers—the daily fever, the three-day fever—and it does not leave the person until the wound is healed. In this way, a specific type of sickness develops in the wound, almost like a separate person living within it. A physician must know that such wound-sicknesses are not merely "wound-sickness," but are actually fevers. Furthermore, it has happened that in times of plague, the <term>pestilence</term> has appeared within the wounds—though without the usual buboes—beginning with chills and heat. Some died quickly from this, though they felt nothing else in their entire body except what was caused by the wound. Also, <term>burning stalk-fevers</term> <note>original: "Febres Caulonicæ"; a historical term for a type of malignant, high fever</note> have entered wounds and shown all the usual signs, and some have died from them. It has also occurred several times that a common <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: "Breune"; typically an inflammation of the throat or tonsils, like diphtheria</note> broke out among soldiers, appearing with all its signs inside the wounds. Thick skins would peel off the wounds just as one peels the skin from the tongues of those who have the quinsy; the wound and the mouth looked exactly the same. Such complications are countless, and if they are to be helped, the order of medicine must be applied just as if one were fighting the actual disease. For just as with the plague or the quinsy, the wounds were healed using the same medicines that serve against those diseases. There is no other way to treat such sicknesses in a wound unless one uses the medicine intended for the pestilence or the fever.

<margin>C</margin> It has also often happened that wounds began to bleed, yet it was not truly <margin>Mattheſſ. 479. Dysentery <note>original: "痢 疾"; Chinese scholarly annotation</note></margin> blood, and it could not be stopped by any standard medicine. But because the <term>bloody flux</term> <note>original: "Rotruhr"; dysentery</note> was prevalent in the land at that time, and the discharge from the wound was identical to the stool of that sickness—behaving just like a bowel movement and returning in cycles like one—it was compared to the bloody flux. Consequently, the medicine for dysentery was given, and the wound was helped immediately. It is necessary for every physician to consider this. Since this has happened to me and to several wounded people—and it did not start or end with my practice, but occurred many times—it is well worth reflecting upon. I saw a wounded <term>squire</term> <note>original: "Ersknappen"; could refer to a senior miner or a noble's attendant</note> whose wound shook and trembled three or four times a day, accompanied by a powerful cramp that pulled the limb back and forth, with foam and froth lying upon the wound for a quarter of an hour. When I gave him the medicine for the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>epilepsy</note> to drink, the wound was cured of its paroxysm and his condition improved. That is, when the <term>liquor of vitriol</term> <note>original: "liquor Vitrioli"; a preparation of sulfuric acid or sulfates used in alchemy and medicine</note> was given to him, he recovered, for it was a type of epilepsy of the wound. I point this out so that if such an improper sickness should arrive, one may recognize that there is more than just a wound present; therefore, internal medicine must be sought. Although it would be more proper for a surgeon to know how to heal such wound-necessities without further searching, because of their negligence and laziness, it is right to search further. It also often happens that a sickness falls into the body because of a wound, yet it does not dwell in the wound itself, but becomes a true bodily disease, such as deafness or the falling sickness. Even if the wounds are healed, the sicknesses are not driven out. Therefore, another counsel must be sought in that case—as mentioned, a different counsel than the medicine usually given for such natural diseases. It must be a special medicine, outside of all other common recipes, of which not many have been discovered until now. Therefore, it is necessary to learn and experience more than all physicians have learned and experienced until now; otherwise, no sick person would ever be helped.

# The First Book / of the Great
<margin>A</margin>

It would be fair and right that no one be called a **wound surgeon** <term>original: "Wundartzt"; a surgeon specializing in external trauma and sores</term> unless he had seen and experienced such things many times over; and furthermore, had learned to help those complicating diseases that arise. And it should not be that he is referred to internal medicine, but since these complications take their origin from the wounds, they should rightly be treated within **surgery**. For he is not a surgeon who can only bind wounds and cut away flesh, or use corrosives and scrapers: rather, he is one who can turn away that which the wound lacks for healing.

## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the hidden, secret diseases of the body which unite with wounds, from which Cancer, Fistula, Serpiginous sores, etc., arise.

It is also to be known that within the body lie causes and origins from which, in the meantime, **Fistula**, **Cancer**, holes, open sores, cold or hot **gangrene** <note>original: "Brand"; can refer to gangrene or severe inflammation</note>, **Serpigo** <term>original: "Syren"; creeping skin eruptions like ringworm or shingles</term>, **Lupus** <term>original: "Wolff"; literally 'the wolf,' referring to an 'eating' or 'devouring' ulcer</term>, and other such types arise. Now, if it happens that in such a place this matter intends to "hatch" a disease as mentioned, and if into that same "nest" a puncture wound or similar is struck, then such a disease opens itself along with the wound. Out of that disease and the wound together, a great harm is made. Now follows the healing of the wound: they make themselves stubborn and refuse to go into a complete healing; they manifest themselves—let the medicine be as good as it will—so that the closure of the wound will not occur. For as long as a fistula, a cancer, etc., has fallen into it, the wound-medicine cannot be effective; these require fistula-medicines. Therefore, in the end, they reveal themselves as fistulas, cancers, or other aforementioned diseases. Although it will often happen through good medicine <margin>B</margin> that the wounds are healed quickly—especially where such matter was still in its early stages and not yet fully "hatched"—where the matter has already hatched, nothing helps; that which is present must take its course. For the medicine for wounds and the medicine for such sores are like **White** and **Black** against each other; and thus, from then on, the medicine for such bodily diseases must be undertaken, and the wound-surgery must be set aside.

A physician should also be well-versed in this, so that he is well-reputed in knowing these diseases of nature, or he will have to retreat in shame. Therefore, you should not only be able to heal wounds, but also fistula, cancer, lupus, serpigo, **phagedena** <term>original: "Fressel"; a rapidly spreading, 'eating' ulcer</term>, etc. Where such a case stands, you must know how to heal it, and not shamefully abandon and ruin the patient. Should you encounter this, you must know how to protect yourself, to stop the wound-surgery, and to attack the matter in other ways.

<margin>Origin of the species of growths grown out, see page 152. 155. X</margin>
Furthermore, you should also know that it often happens, and has happened, that **proud flesh** <term>original: "geyl fleisch"; excessive granulation tissue that grows out of a healing wound</term> has grown in the wounds, growing out like a **fungus** <note>original: "Schwamm"; refers to both sponges and mushrooms/fungal growths on trees</note> on its tree. And men have attempted to remove it with corrosives, but it grew worse; also cut it away, but worse followed. For ignorant physicians have done such things, from whom nothing good ever comes; and thus so many kinds of growths have sprouted forth that it is pitiful to write about. Know the cause of such growth thus: they are like **warts**; when they are cut off, they become even larger, and the more often they are cut, the longer and larger they grow. The same happens with corrosives if they are not suitable for warts: and also such large "sponges," like a mushroom, etc., grow out, the unpleasantness of which is indescribable. Since this manifests itself naturally, the proud flesh that <margin>C</margin> grows out of wounds into a fungus or mass also comes from the origin of warts; thus, such a "wart-nest" has been struck, and subsequently, out of its own malice, it is driven into such a growth. Although it often happens that these fungi open up and grow out through closed wounds over several years, the cause here is from warts, and the wound has awakened them into such a growth, so that they were caused to take that form. It has also happened many times that they have grown in the form of glands or lumps, which are less harmful than others. However, every surgeon should see to it that he has knowledge of these complications and knows how to instruct himself accordingly, so that he does not undertake that for which he has learned no knowledge or help, nor has experience. And I say this so that such "presumed" doctors, who want to make such diseases healthy and use nothing but pure destruction in the process, do not bring shame upon the sick. For this reason, I make mention here so that everyone may know to beware of them and may escape the greatest harm and disaster.

For such complications, which arise from innate, natural, embodied diseases joining with wounds, are so manifold and of such a wretched sight that they cannot be described. You, physician, as you boast of being a master, should know how to heal such things: but where you cannot, remain a **Bachelor**, a half-doctor, and not a whole doctor.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### Concerning poisoned wounds, which are poisoned by weapons.

There is also a great attention to be paid to the poisoning of weapons. Although it is a frivolous and dishonest way, yet it also happens that swords or sabers, **hooked arrows** <term>original: "Hackenpfeil"; specialized arrows or bolts with barbs</term>, or other...

# Wound Surgery: The First Treatise.
<meta>catchword: so must</meta>

<margin>A</margin> There are other weapons of war from which not only wounds, but also poison <note>original: "Gifft"; in this period, "poison" could mean chemical toxins, biological infections, or even the "nature" of a substance</note> brings great pain. Such poisonings are of many kinds, which are not proper to describe here. There are similar other instruments used in crafts and labor that become poisoned through daily use. For example, <margin><unclear>scythes</unclear></margin> <note>original: "Sägesen"</note> in the meadows, which, from the various grasses they mow down, receive a poison into themselves through the heat that the blade naturally acquires, becoming contaminated by the sharpness of certain herbs. Also, snakes, toads, spiders, shrews, field mice, and grasshoppers may be hacked apart by them, and their poison "eats" especially into the iron. Therefore, such weapons do not only create wounds, but also poison them. For this reason, special care must be taken with such weapons to heal the poisoned wound. Even though whetting or sharpening might remove some of it, it cannot be entirely removed in any way.

The same applies to the plowshare <note>original: "Pflugeysen"</note>, which receives poisoning from the nature of the earth; these should also be regarded as poisoned wounds. For every piece of iron takes on a foreign nature <margin>Old iron</margin> from that in which it is used. This is also true of garden shovels and the like. Sickles also take on another nature, though less so than the aforementioned instruments.

Carpentry axes and tools used for wood, such as plane irons and the like, receive no poisoning, but rather take on a healing nature <note>Likely referring to the clean, resinous nature of many woods compared to dirt or blood</note>. Glass in itself is a poison; if its pieces do not remain in the wound, it may not poison; but because it often remains, it causes a severe poisoning. 

Regarding wounds caused by wood that is handled frequently, such as spindles: these take on a "hard" poisoning, especially from women’s hands, for the "evil moisture" <note>An Early Modern reference to sweat or humoral excretions</note> of humans penetrates through the sharpness of the wood and poisons severely. 

Stone has no poison within it, nor do other metals. Nevertheless, it is true that iron is sometimes not well-cleansed of "smelter-smoke" <term>original: "Hüttrauch"; literally 'foundry smoke,' usually referring to arsenic trioxide, a byproduct of smelting metal ores</term>. Such iron is more harmful <margin>B</margin> than other iron.

How these poisons should be drawn out of the wounds requires no special recipes to be written here. For the recipes in the Second Treatise draw all poisons out by the power of their specific properties. Therefore, apply yourself to having those same recipes. If you do not know them, but instead use the medicine from the **Little Book of Knives** <note>original: "Messeren Büchslin"; likely a derogatory reference to Hieronymus Brunschwig’s popular surgical manual, which the author often critiqued</note>, then it will be necessary for you to seek other medicines, lest your ruin leads to greater offense. No better advice can be given to you than to use those [Second Treatise] medicines and throw yours away. 

You should also take good care in such wounds to know whether the "wound-sickness" comes from such poison or not. For it may well happen that a wound-sickness arises from another cause and is mistaken for poisoning, or it may spring from such poisoning but be attributed to another cause, for the signs are nearly identical. Although with weapons that are poisoned with intent, clearly recognizable signs appear, such as burning heat, a hot swelling, discoloration of the flesh, and stinging in the tendons—especially with barbed arrows <term>original: "Hackenpfeilen"; arrows with hooks designed to tear flesh upon removal</term>. If the pain presses in so violently, pour a cold mouth-oil <note>original: "Mund öl"; a soothing, refined medicinal oil</note> into the wound and proceed with "puncture plasters" <note>original: "Stichpffastern"; plasters meant to draw out toxins from deep wounds</note>, and it will be mastered. Other weapons, however, do not cause such violent distress, unless the fat of toads or spiders entered along with the weapon; in that case, apply the medicine as recorded in the Third Treatise.

You should also know regarding the deliberate poisoning of weapons that it may be done in many ways, which are not proper to describe. But you should know that it is done with the most poisonous things; therefore, apply yourself to good medicine and do not rely on your **Little Book of Knives**.

### CHAPTER IX.

### Concerning the patients' own ruin, through their lack of discipline in food, drink, exercise, unchastity, etc.

<margin>C</margin> Even if the doctor applies his best diligence and proceeds with certain, true art, and provides for and protects all things so well that no defect can be found in the medicine: the patient may still ruin all of it and throw nature backward. Thus, it happens quite often that through the patient's lack of discipline, a "lame wound" <note>A wound that refuses to heal or leads to loss of limb function</note> develops, which otherwise would not have. Additionally, a wasting disease <term>original: "Schweinsucht"; literally 'swine-sickness,' referring to atrophy or consumption</term> subsequently grows from it, which also would not have come otherwise—along with other such accidents, and sometimes death itself. This must be carefully weighed so that it may be discovered who is the cause of such ruin. 

For the "wantonness" <note>original: "mutwill"; refers to a lack of self-control or stubbornness</note> of the patient angers Nature, so that she no longer moves toward recovery as she was previously inclined. We note this especially in unchastity <note>original: "Vnkeuschheit"; sexual activity, which was believed to divert the body's "vital balsam" away from the wound</note>, for the injured limb becomes so inflamed that there is no ailment that could not possibly be born there: including bodily diseases that can never be removed, as well as wasting and other accidents difficult to describe—varying according to the nature of the wound and where it is located. 

Therefore, take heed and be diligent so that you know the distinction in such cases to prevent such harm. For it has often happened that during such "exercise" <note>A euphemism for sexual activity</note> the "wild fire" <term>original: "wilde Fewr"; Erysipelas, a painful streptococcal skin infection</term> struck into the wound, such that the limb had to be hewn off, or the patient even died; or deadly fevers fell upon them, or sometimes **Bergticht** <term>A Paracelsian term for a specific type of gout or joint pain</term>, or sometimes the **red flux** <term>original: "roht Ferich"; dysentery</term>, and many more. And you should know that if such a thing should happen, you have no power in any way to turn away such wanton accidents; rather, you must let the "exercise" run its course and subsequently take even better care with the healing. You should also know regarding the exertion of that same limb that many kinds of accidents are to be expected, though not as harmful as those from unchastity. Nevertheless...

# The First Book of the Great [Surgery].

<margin>A</margin> so must <note>continuing from previous page: "...if the patient is restless..."</note> from the exertion and too much exercise of the limb, wound-sickness <note>original: "Wundsucht"; refers to complications like infection or inflammation</note> occur, through which subsequently a gangrene <note>original: "Brandt"; literally "fire," referring to tissue death or necrosis</note> may develop, or a wound fever, paralysis of the limb, or a wasting sickness <note>original: "Schweinsucht"; a term for atrophy or consumption</note>, and many other accidents besides, which are not to be described here. Therefore, let the sick lie quietly with that same limb, so that out of disregard—which never does any good—a worse thing does not follow afterward.

Thus you should also manage him with food and drink, so that he does not take in anything against the wounds, nor overfill himself. For overfilling in the sick makes Nature <note>The author personifies "Nature" as the internal healing force of the body</note> unwilling. For when there is a defect in the body, Nature desires that her measure be kept, so that she may resist that same defect. But if she is overloaded, she falls into a rage, and according to the nature of rage, she storms through the whole body. Such raging is also a cause of wasting, of fever, of wound-sickness, and other pains that befall the wounded, which are not necessary to describe. Therefore, to avoid such heavy accidents, it is proper that the physician anticipate them and not look at the status of the patient’s person, but rather look at the heavy anxiety and distress that meets them out of disobedience. Heavy illnesses also often occur through unchastity <note>original: "Vnkeuschheit"; refers here to sexual activity during recovery</note> more than has been said, such as stroke, sudden death, the falling sickness <note>term: epilepsy</note>, also dropsy, and all these illnesses are incurable and end in death. Also, with food, no disregard should occur. Reason: if one can heal wounds through wound-drink <note>term: medicinal decoctions consumed to aid healing from within</note> and wound-diet, so can one also ruin them through food and drink; for the bad proceeds more quickly than the good.

<margin>B</margin> There are many presumed doctors who let their wounded people carry out their arrogance <note>meaning their reckless behavior or lack of discipline</note>, and even help them in it. Such people deserve a broom across their backs, because they drive lightheartedness out of the wounds <note>meaning they treat the serious nature of the wound too lightly</note>, which have no day of freedom from evil. It requires earnestness, diligence, and all care: the hour and the day bring much upon such arrogance.

## CHAPTER X.

->On the accidents, nature, and essence which arise from the patient's own nature and complexion.<-

It is also no less true that one human is healthier than another, faster, slower, more favorable, and more unfavorable. This is a thing for a physician to consider deeply, so that he does not attempt anything further than what Nature herself is capable of. For as this example shows, so also know it to be of the human being.

<margin>C</margin> One wood is better for carving than another; one more knotty than another; one harder than another; one stubborn and cross-grained, however one handles it; yet in the end, it will all be planed. It is the same with the various kinds of stones. Just as there are many differences in such things, so also know it of the human. For we all come from the earth and grow out of it, and in it there is that which is coarse, rough, unrefined, refined, and mild also. And as it is in the earth, so it comes out of it. Therefore, where such a nature and property is found to be more unrefined or milder, the physician should yield to such nature and consider that a linden wood is planed sooner than a crusty fir. Furthermore, it also happens that sometimes the sick are of such a subtle nature that specifically with them, wounds sometimes become fatal that would not even affect another person to that extent. For the nature in man is so miraculously different in the body that it is well worth great consideration; where such special bodies are, they should also be treated specially. It is a great reason why I reject the medicine of the "presumed doctors," because their medicine sometimes serves one body and thereafter will never help in ten others. For this reason, I direct you to the recipes of the second treatise. When you use those, you have a plane that planes all woods. And even if it goes faster with one than with the other, it will still be planed in the end. And although they are often cross-grained, it is not necessary to change the medicine, but rather to wait for the time. Thus every wound-surgeon <note>term: "Wundarzet"; a practitioner specializing in external injuries as opposed to internal medicine</note> should be diligent to have such medicine that is not only good for one flesh, but for all flesh. For such articles of belief have made a great mess in medicine and introduced much ruin, so that they have switched back and forth with the medicine and yet never found the wellspring of medicine. From this it follows that some of my adversaries say with their "little measured book" <note>original: "Messtnen Büchlin"; likely a rival's manual or a book of standard dosages he finds ineffective</note> whether any wound was ever healed without a sticking-plaster <note>term: "Stichpflaster"; an external adhesive dressing</note> or without my recipes. That is as much as to say they have no need of my recipes; and they do not consider that through my recipes many thousands have been healed in battles and storms, and never one ruined, Nature having always restored her capability. And that through their medicine, not even every twentieth man has escaped unruined and undamaged (I will be silent about the other mess they have committed, even when things went well). I reckon that he who heals the twentieth and the nineteen correctly is better than this one who ruins the nineteen. I also reckon that if I put the better medicine in its place and reject the worse, no wise man will hold it against me. And I point out such chapters so that one may learn to recognize the medicine and see its foundation. For good medicine was worth just as much a thousand years ago as it is now, and bad medicine just as worthless as now. And although it is as old as the good, and comes from just as far back as the good, it is still no better for all that, even though evil is as old as good. The rat [dropping] in the grain is as old as the grain, but it is not used in place of the grain. I intended such understanding to come into the world, since the good arrives more easily than the other: to leave the worse, and to look upon nothing with mercy whereby the evil might be preserved.

Wound Medicine: The First Treatise.

<margin>A</margin>

# CHAPTER XI.
## Concerning the wounds that might befall women while they are experiencing their natural monthly flow.

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, there is a special point to be noted: namely, when women receive wounds at the same time their common flow <note>original: "gemeiner Fluß"; referring to menstruation</note> is occurring. It is necessary that such a section be mentioned for many reasons, because of the accidents and complications that occur so frequently in these cases, some of which are known to me. Specifically, I have seen that the menstrual flow itself exited through the wounds. At such times, powerful complications occurred, such as the falling sickness <note>original: "Fallendsucht"; epilepsy</note> and also gouty fits <note>original: "Bergicht"; likely referring to paralytic or arthritic contractions</note>. These did not stop until the menstruation was brought back to its proper path and the womb <note>original: "Mutter"; the uterus</note> was stilled in its rising or sinking <note>The "rising of the womb" was a common historical diagnosis for various physical and emotional symptoms in women</note>. 

There will also be much wound-fever <note>original: "Wundsucht"</note>, great heat, and many headaches, as well as shortness of breath and a distaste for food. This results in a dangerous and miserable healing of the wound. If one wishes to still such complications, the menstruation must have its exit through its rightful place; only then can other medicines be applied and perform what medicine is commanded to do.

You should also know that in women there is a particular natural anger <note>original: "angeborner Zorn"; referring to a constitutional temperament or "humor"</note>; where it happens that such anger strikes, it is more dangerous than the natural flow. For out of this anger, gouty fits <note>original: "Gegicht"</note> move through the whole body. Once these are awakened, they also move the womb, and then two illnesses come together, each of which creates its own special complications. From the gout comes lameness in the hands and feet, and from the rising of the womb comes a condition like the falling sickness.

Regarding this, it must be known that these illnesses all move toward the wound first and desire to make an exit at that same <margin>B</margin> place. Therefore, the first counsel must be how to settle the womb and remove the gouty fits, and only then heal the wounds. Seek such counsel from the physicians who have experience in such illnesses. Do not regard the titles they hold, for such names are often bought for mockery-money <note>meaning titles bought through fees rather than earned through skill</note>, but the Art <note>the "Art" of medicine/surgery</note> cannot be given with a title. Therefore, seek Art where it truly is, and take counsel from those who are experienced. Although it would be proper for me to show the way here, because such things are difficult to translate into German and would require too much writing, it is better left out, as it might not be understood by the common German doctor. 

It should be noted here that if a complication should break out during such illnesses as mentioned above, they are difficult to drive away. For instance, if a wasting sickness <note>original: "Schweinsucht"; atrophy or consumption of the flesh</note> or a persistent discharge <note>original: "Wundfluß"</note> occurs, they tend to persist until death. Even if they can be helped, it happens only with much delayed time. Therefore, see that you prevent such things in the beginning. Where such dangerous illnesses are to be expected in the future, be diligent to act more skillfully at the start. For where a heavy end and lingering aftereffects are feared, strive at the beginning to act and apply your remedies with greater certainty and foresight.

# CHAPTER XII.
## Concerning the signs that appear in wounds, what they signify, and what follows from them.

<margin>C</margin> In every wound where a misfortune <note>original: "Unfall"; a medical complication or setback</note> is about to arise, it begins with signs. Therefore, it is necessary that every surgeon knows and recognizes the signs when a misfortune happens to a wound and what it signifies, so that every wound may be healed gently, mildly, without pain, and without any adversity. But where this does not happen—where it falls against the custom of medicine, showing inflammation <note>original: "entbörung"</note> or other such accidents—it is to be suspected that a misfortune or something worse is about to happen, and that the order of medicine is about to fail in that place. 

Therefore, in this chapter, I will treat only what is to be recognized and understood from those signs that appear. I consider this to be the greatest secret for any doctor. What I show you hereafter, I speak from my experience, which will in no way fail you. Although no mention of this has ever been made by all the other doctors of surgery or even internal medicine, it is proper not to withhold what someone else has experienced. For the ancient writings do not see things the same way as the current self-proclaimed doctors might write—as if every case were the same—in which no perfection nor grounded understanding can grow.

First: every wound that creates a swelling out of pain (I mean wounds on the four limbs), if they cause pain and a growth <note>original: "Gesücht"; an abscess or internal collection of fluid</note> in the joints of the shoulders (if the wound is on the arm) or in the hips (if the wound is on the legs), which improves or worsens according to the weather, or according to the full or new moon, and is felt with pain especially toward the night—that is, before midnight. Such wounds are those that lead to wasting <note>original: "Schweinen"</note>; that is, they begin to waste the limb away, and only after the wound has healed do they truly begin their [destructive] operation.

Furthermore: every wound that seems to be healing well on its own, but produces a swelling near the wound—extending toward the hands or feet, or backward into the joints—and that swelling hardens and will not yield even as the wound heals, but retains its pain (that is, the pain is outside the wound itself). From this, it follows that a growth <note>original: "Gesücht"</note> is gathering near the wound, which corrupts the neighboring limbs even worse than the wound did. It rots not only the flesh and veins but also the bone, becomes a fistula <note>original: "Fistuliert"</note>, and makes many holes around itself, so that an incurable disease comes of it which is difficult to help.

<meta>This page continues the diagnostic observations of the surgeon, moving from the specific complications of wounded women to general physical signs—both fatal and manageable—that appear in various injuries. It then transitions into a new chapter regarding "corrupted" or botched wounds caused by unskilled practitioners.</meta>

The First Book of the Great [Surgery]

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, if the joint fluid <term>Glidwaſſer</term> <note>synovial fluid</note> takes its course and drains out, know that a powerful wasting <note>original: "Schweinung"</note> will settle in that place, affecting the marrow as well as the entire limb. Such a consumption will develop that no one will be able to help, unless the joint fluid is restored by proper balance; otherwise, the limb dries out like a chopped-down tree. This wasting is called a withered limb <note>original: "Aridum membrum"</note>.

Furthermore, any wound that begins to take away sleep, makes the patient restless, and prevents them from lying still—likewise if stitches in the side <note>likely pleurisy or sharp internal pain</note> occur—wherever this happens, it is a cause that leads toward death, especially where great thirst accompanies it. However, take heed that this does not come from bad medicine, for I speak here only of the natural course of the body.

Furthermore, if a twitching <note>or cramp</note> appears in the eyes, or if there is stammering in speech, or a failure to notice when questioned, it is also a sign of approaching death, especially if they become hard of hearing.

Furthermore, if they look at people with stormy and fierce eyes, speak with defiant words and a strong voice, act bold toward people, and are hot-tempered and hot-headed: this is a sign of a frenzied stupor <note>original: "Taubſucht"; referring here to a state of delirium or madness</note> or a similar insanity, depending on the circumstances at hand.

Furthermore, if wounds finally begin to leak watery fluid and no longer produce the proper pus of the waste matter <note>original: "Eyter des Excrements"</note>, and healing stands still: these will turn into either cancer, a fistula, or ulceration. Or, if this is accompanied by forgetfulness, weakness in the limbs, or heart palpitations, it indicates death.

Furthermore, should it happen that the wound appears to be healing well, but the body refuses to be cheerful—where the better the wound looks, the sicker the body becomes—that would be a sign of death.

Furthermore, where the wounded bite their teeth together and grind them, and do not recognize themselves: this is a sign that a fatal omen is about to strike. Unless, however, worms are found within them, in which case the symptoms would follow from that cause.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if it happens that they foam at the mouth and draw their breath with difficulty, and also snore through the nose, with twitching eyes and cramps in the hands and legs: this is a herald of paralysis <note>original: "Gegicht"</note>, or the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, or a sudden death—especially if they twist and bend their bodies.

Furthermore, if a twitching comes into the wound, during sleep or otherwise: it is a sign that some trouble will follow, unless it specifically happens due to a fright or heavy dreams.

Furthermore, when a swelling occurs that allows itself to be pitted <note>original: "grüblen laſſet"; referring to edema where a finger press leaves an indentation</note>, accompanied by a delicate healing in the flesh and a long delay in closing: it is a sign that the limb intends to "fall asleep" and will henceforth become insensitive.

Furthermore, if the stomach becomes unable to digest and will not keep food down, accompanied by a great thirst: it is a sign that the veins have been severed and the nerves shattered, and they no longer stand in their rightful power.

Although many more such signs could be written, these greatest ones are enough. I place them here in this chapter so that they may be more diligently considered at the beginning, and that one might prevent what they signify. For every sign is placed before our eyes so that what it portends may be properly forestalled. And even though specific recipes are not shown here for how to handle each case, it is only because such recipes cannot be mastered without great experience and understanding. Therefore, my advice is to learn well and experience what necessity requires, knowing it with a good foundation. Such things cannot be laid out in writing for everyone, but will be completed in other books.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->How to treat corrupted wounds which are considered hopeless.<-

<margin>C</margin> **A**lthough I began this book with fresh wounds, since there are more corrupted ones, it is necessary to write more about them. For they are all still wounds, even if they have been botched by ignorant barber-surgeons <note>original: "Scherern"</note>. Indeed, if one looks at the skill of the barber-surgeons and bath-keepers <note>original: "Badern"</note> among the general lot of them, it is a miracle that they can even heal boils <note>original: "Eyſſlen"</note>, let alone proper wounds. Therefore, a special chapter should rightly be dedicated to their botching. To this end, the shortest foundation is this: that you recognize what it is that has corrupted the wound—whether an incoming disease or the corruption of the doctor. Thus, in these two ways, learn to recognize all corrupted wounds. For if an incoming disease is present and the barber-surgeon knows nothing of it, the wound is corrupted through his ignorance. If that is not the case, but he corrupts it through his lack of fundamental skill, then observe how that corruption occurred.

Should an incoming disease be present, it is no less important; you will find much written about these, and how each is to be healed, in the other books of my *Great Surgery*, in which the healing of such things is taught; it is not necessary to present them here. You may also learn from other writers and self-proclaimed doctors.

But since they do not provide "signs" <note>proof of efficacy or diagnostic markers</note>, no faith should be placed in them. For the body must trust in the works: that is, the medicine should show signs and reveal its works. Where that does not happen, the medicine is not truly there, for God embodied medicine to perform signs and works.

One thing I will present to you which has been left out of all the recipes of other doctors, but is accepted in my school, and which also prompts me to write this chapter: there is a principal substance <note>original: "Hauptſtück"</note> available that resists and heals all corrupted wounds caused by the nature of incoming diseases—such as cancer, fistula, and the like. This is a compound of Realgar <note>an arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, like an Alkali, which I do not teach here, but suggest you seek in its proper place and in its own book. With it, you may heal all fistulas, cancers, etc., in front of wounds and within wounds <note><margin>* for wounds.</margin></note>.

Since this was never before revealed, but remained in ignorance, I have discovered it now in my own time.

# Surgery: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> It is only right that this topic should have its own chapter, for it heals all fistulas, cancers, the "wolf" <note>original: "Wolff"; refers to lupus or similar "eating" skin sores</note>, scurf, fungal growths, and the like. Once these are healed, the healing of the wound itself follows—that is, once the complicating illness has first been removed. Afterward, as I teach in the Second Treatise, the wounds should also be healed. It is not necessary to reveal that entire process and order here. I may well say that I have the right and reason to reveal many secrets of Nature, since I have experienced, learned, and seen more than the others. My experience especially compels me to boast when I see that the Doctors, Barber-surgeons, Bath-masters, etc., are so utterly inexperienced and skilled in no arts; they perform signs, they are esteemed, yet through their "art" they bring ruin, and they carry nothing through according to the right order of Nature. This makes me bold, for they have many hammers but do not know how to strike with them, nor do they know what the hammer can achieve. For what is a pearl <note>original: "Berlin"; a diminutive of pearl</note> to a sow, since she knows nothing but how to eat? <margin><gloss>Alchemy, figure 4 H</gloss></margin> I praise the art of **ALCHEMY**, for it provides the secrets of medicine and offers help in all desperate illnesses. But why should I praise the practitioners themselves, since they do not know the secrets of Nature that are in their hands? I also greatly praise the art of medicine. But why should I praise those who are physicians but not alchemists? That is: if the art lies with the alchemists, the physicians do not understand it, for they do not hold the secrets in their hands. I must, however, praise the one who can lead Nature so that she may be helpful: that is, the one who draws out the good and casts away the bad, and who also recognizes what is within her. For Preparation and Knowledge—that is, Alchemy and Medicine—can never be separated from one another. Where the two were separated, there arose a "simplicity" <note>original: "Einfalt"; implying a naive or foolish ignorance</note> which should be called a folly, affecting both alchemists and physicians, such that neither has any true foundation in the things they deal with. But so that you may see what a great secret it is to heal corrupted wounds, look at how miserably the sick must consume their lives, and how much varied advice is given <margin>B</margin> to them, and how much is attempted on them. Yet in the end, it is all for nothing, for the longer it lasts, the worse it gets. They fall from one practitioner to another, and each one demonstrates his own lack of understanding, but the patient is not helped by it. Furthermore, know that this corruption comes from the physician himself, through etching <note>cauterizing with chemicals</note>, cutting, burning, baths, ointments, and sulfur-cloths, as they are done through many ungrounded arts. Cast all such maneuvers away and hold yourself only to healing through cleansing and closing, as contained in the other treatise. For according to the manner of the barber-surgeons and their kind, it becomes worse the longer it goes on. Therefore, I praise God that I have discovered a medicine through Him, in whatever way it reached me. However, because I am both the Alchemist and the Physician, and I know both, it is right for me to reveal such falsehood in the art, to do away with unfit medicine, and to put a better one in its place. I am also one who wishes you well, more so than a godless quack <term>Hodenschneider</term> <note>literally "testicle-cutter"; a derogatory term for unlicensed, wandering surgeons</note> who boasts about every illness with nothing but empty proverbs. I will also sufficiently explain myself to you in the other book of surgery, if God wills it, so that you shall wonderfully restore such corrupted wounds. Not only corrupted wounds, but also many more of the natural ailments that are attached and related to surgery, so that the folly of the ignorant masters, and likewise the Doctors, may suffer a decline in their own ignorant arts, and also in the ruining of good types of wounds, many of which have come to me from these people.

### CHAPTER XIV.

-> What should be stitched and what should not: how stitching is no needle, but rather the medicine is the needle. <-

<margin>C</margin> In the stitching of wounds, it is proper to expose their folly. Therefore, you should adopt a different practice, discard the needle with its patchwork, and not be ashamed to learn something better. <margin>An old custom is just as old as the witty and the wise.</margin> Stitching is an old custom, and nearly so old that no one knows its beginning; just like the age of fools, it is exactly as old as the witty and the sensible. But what of that, that the old custom should remain? Fools are also old, but what does that concern the wise man? Even if your father did it, and your grandfather too, why do you want to deceive and trouble the people, since so many are ruined and there is no profit in patching, when it can be done better and more bravely without it? What does the father’s foolishness concern the son? Take this instruction from me: even if you stitch a wound together, think to yourself that it will not last long anyway. It rots away and does not stay; afterward, it is just as it was before. What was wide before is wide afterward. What good is the result that you pay so dearly for in the beginning, if in the end it must be open just as it was at first? What is this flow of folly? Therefore, do not surrender yourself to foolishness. Furthermore, much evil and harm arises from it, which I will omit here for the sake of brevity. You cause great pain and draw inflammation <note>original: "Fluß vnd Sucht"</note> to it that would otherwise not come, through your shameful sewing.
So that you may know a better way of joining than you currently do, learn this foundation which I present to you: that Nature draws things together as much as she heals on that day. That is: however wide the wound may be at the top, Nature draws it together where it is best, both "lips" <note>the edges of the wound</note>, in the same way that a cabinetmaker joins two boards, and so on and so forth until the very top. It reaches the narrow measure just as well as if you had pulled it together with shoemaker's thread. I have often stood by while the barber-surgeons, fearing the threads would rot too soon, thought to use fine shoemaker's thread with pig bristles just to pull it through and tie it. Now see what understanding is in those "scabby" folk: for no wound heals any sooner or any finer because of it, but rather more unhappily and worse.
Therefore, you should now apply yourself to good medicine according to the contents of the true foundation. And when you have that, then stitch the wounds through medicine, so that everything is done well and skillfully, without any cause for reproach.

<margin>A</margin> ...is completed—whether it be vessels, nerves, ligaments, skin, or flesh—everything that is there is commanded by Nature to be sewn together. If you choose not to follow this practice <note>referring to following Nature's own healing power</note>, no one can consider you a true surgeon, but rather one who works against Nature. And if God grants no more health to the sick than what you can provide, no one would ever recover because of you. For Nature's desire is to be healed without pain and agony; she knows what is best for herself, and therefore she pursues it, and she is filled with dread when such "Torture-Jacks" <note>original: "Folterhansen"; a derogatory term for surgeons who cause unnecessary pain</note> arrive with their "art." I am not against stitching solely because of its coarseness, but because of the pain and misfortune it introduces or brings about. Truly, it is a pity that something requiring no skill is called an "art." But it is the same with stitching as it is with inspecting urine: it is all about the money. One stitch costs a guilden; one urine inspection <note>original: "Seich"; literally "piss"</note> costs a batzen <note>a small silver coin</note>. This practice would soon be discarded, were it not for the profit it brings to the one who performs it, even if it causes much suffering. It is also true that there are certain "stitching powders" and "stitching waters" that draw a wound together and glue it as if one were joining two boards: I call that use an "art," and it is no small thing. For in this way, miraculous things are healed, as the recipes will be listed in the second treatise. It is also true that they heal and join together things much more difficult than simple wounds. If that art had remained in use instead of needle-stitching, many wounds would have been healed that otherwise remain unhealed. But there are always more destroyers than healers, and wherever there is empty chatter, the common man seeks his "art." Thus, the true foundation is lost, and abuse takes its place.

## CHAPTER XV.
<note>original: "CAPVT XV"</note>

->Concerning the Instruction of the First, Middle, and Last Bandages, along with<-
->other necessities.<-

<margin>g</margin> In the order of medicine until the end of healing, there are several points that are well worth noting and considering. Although every medicine—as written and found in the second treatise—contains within itself its own beginning, middle, and end, and completes the work sufficiently, certain practices are best to ensure wounds are healed more skillfully and protected from misfortune. The most convenient method is this: at the beginning, when you wish to dress the wound, you should fill it with wound oil, wound balsam, or wound ointments, along with the flowers and medicines that lie within them, having first warmed them. Then, place the wound-plaster or <term>sticking-plaster</term><note>original: "Stichpflaster"; an adhesive dressing</note> over it. Also, the area around the wound should be bound with warm wound oil and the medicine contained therein; or at the very least, apply a warm compress of rose vinegar outside of the plaster or wound medicine. This should be renewed every twelve hours and continued until the eighth or ninth day, depending on whether the wound is large or small. Now, whether to be very concerned or not depends on your own skill. I advise this procedure only for large, dangerous wounds where tendons <note>original: "Flachß"</note> and other critical parts are damaged, where many evil accidents might occur, or where lameness or other complications are expected. All of this is avoided if such a beginning is maintained in the First Bandage. And where there are dangerous puncture wounds, such wound oils should be injected into them, so that other accidents in punctures are also avoided. For in the beginning, one cannot be too careful; everything is necessary. And if there are head wounds, take a linen or silk cloth and pull it through the warm wound oil or ointment. However, do not use wound balsam—meaning nothing that is <term>distilled</term>—and lay it over the wound so that it reaches nearly to the bottom. Yet, spare the skull <note>original: "Hirnschall"</note>, and fill it with medicine made from the herbs and flowers that lie in the wound oil, well-pressed, and place the sticking-plaster over the top. However, do not use sticking-plasters made from <term>litharge</term><note>original: "Glette"; lead oxide</note>. That is to say, only those sticking-plasters are most suitable for the head which are cooked with pure gums and prepared without <margin>C</margin> resin, colophony <note>original: "Colofonia"; pine resin</note>, or camphor. Bind it in every way like other wounds. And persist with this until you see the patient is healthy and strong, which usually happens in eight or nine days. After that, when you see the patient is doing well, dress him with the balsam oil, simply brushed into the wound with a small feather, and the plaster over it, until you no longer see the nerves or joints or the like. Now the Middle Bandage will be finished, and then the Last Bandage begins; this is done with simple sticking-plasters until the end of the wound’s healing. This is my advice for dangerous, prominent wounds that are cut through bone, vessels, arteries, and the like, where despair might set in. Where such dangerous wounds are not present, you may proceed with a single medicine and heal the wounds without any worry.

It is a great thing in the beginning to treat wounds very mildly and gently with applied medicine that is made from the right foundation and protected with the right medicine on top. Although other medicines are also available, such as wound-drinks, wound-powders, <term>sublimates</term>, and <term>distillates</term>, etc., their proper use will be shown in their respective chapters.

<summary>Paracelsus argues against painful surgical stitching in favor of natural healing and provides a three-stage bandaging protocol (First, Middle, and Last) using herbal oils and plasters. He emphasizes gentle treatment and warns against using distilled balsams or lead-based plasters on head wounds.</summary>

# Wound-Surgery: The First Treatise.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->Concerning various bodily diseases that are caused to grow following the healing of wounds<-

<margin>A</margin> It is also necessary to know that even though a wound may be healed, certain subsequent diseases are to be expected. Therefore, healing a wound is not the only art; one must also anticipate and turn away future damages through proper order and a healthy regimen. For example: a person who performs cupping <term>Cupping: An ancient medical practice where glass cups are used to create suction on the skin to draw out "bad" humors.</term> or bloodletting assists Nature in finding an exit through which she wishes to be furthered. If this does not happen, other diseases will follow. Now, if this is found to be true in such minor matters <note>original: "spöttigen Handel"; referring to routine procedures</note>, how much more is a "way out" necessary when many veins and other parts are cut off (which is a greater matter than cupping or ordinary bloodletting)? Nature should be assisted toward an exit through her appropriate veins or cupping, so that an evacuation occurs at that same place at a convenient time, location, and order. This you may recognize according to your own skill, so that internal diseases or ulcers—which need not be listed here—do not grow afterward. You must recognize this through your own skill and understand how an exit should be given to Nature at that place, at its appointed time.

Regarding this, you should also know that massive blood loss often leaves a mark on the lungs, or sometimes causes dropsy <term>Dropsy: An old term for edema, or the painful swelling of the body caused by excess fluid.</term>, or other swellings. Sometimes it draws the wounded person’s natural constitution and quality into an unnatural constitution <term>Constitution: Original: "Complexion," referring to the balance of the four bodily humors.</term>, so that they can never return to their old way of life and being. Along with this, one may also observe dizziness, a sour stomach, and similar ailments in other limbs, which are to be considered further than can be described here. You must prevent all of this through regimen and order as the patient recovers from you, so that future damage is avoided; do not neglect to advise on all things diligently.

<margin>B</margin> Although such help belongs to the province of the physician, none of their books say anything about it; therefore, nothing is to be sought from them. You, however, should be diligent in preventing all their ailments with bloodletting and cupping according to the nature of the wound. Use chicory water <note>original: "Cicoreen Wasser"</note>, germander water <note>original: "Gamandrenwasser"</note>, and the like to purify the blood, according to your own judgment and experience, so that no harm may grow from blood that goes astray.

Furthermore, it is also to be known that great diseases are often cured by such wounds. For just as bloodletting is useful, it cannot be denied that it is similarly useful when such veins are cut. For if blood-diseases are present and the veins are opened, it brings about great health. I knew a peasant lad who had been hard of hearing for many years; in a tavern brawl, one of his ears was cut off along with a wide flap of skin. He healed so well at that same ear that he now hears better than he did before he was injured. There have also been times when fevers <note>original: "Febres"</note> were driven away in such a manner; through such blood loss, two-year-old quartan fevers <term>Quartan fever: A form of malaria where the fever returns every four days.</term> were healed that could be cured by no other medicine. The eyesight of the eyes was also greatly improved. Thus, it is well understood that in other diseases where the blood is the cause, similar benefits may spring forth. I have also seen that after great battles, pestilence, croup <note>original: "Breune"; an inflammatory throat condition</note>, and stitches in the side <note>likely pleurisy</note> came among the soldiers; but those who had bled heavily and were badly cut were not affected, and they were a large group. I have also often seen those who were afflicted many times a year by "red gwilch" <note>original: "rothen Gwilch"; likely Erysipelas, a painful skin infection also known as St. Anthony’s Fire</note> who were freed from it for many years following wounds or stabs. Even in cases of gout <note>original: "Podagran"</note>, wounds have sometimes held the gout back for several years. Therefore, it is necessary that the doctor consider, recognize, and know more than one thing: the benefit of wounds as well as their harm. For <margin>C</margin> although a thing may be harmful in one respect, it is found to be useful in another.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->Concerning certain observations that are necessary to recognize in other wounds and stings because of their location.<-

Regarding certain secret places <note>referring to the genitals</note> that must be written about specifically, it is as follows: in the private parts, if stings or wounds occur, something more must be recognized than what was mentioned for other wounds. Namely, that in those places, the greatest pains and aches occur, exceeding all other wounds. Now, the bandaging in such wounds is such that you bind it just like other wounds, with a beginning, middle, and end. But beyond that, to mitigate the pain and the great inflammation <note>original: "Inflation"</note> that strikes there, a medicine should be made of bean-meal <note>original: "Bonenmel"</note> boiled in wine and vinegar, applied as a warm poultice. When it cools, apply a new warm one until the pain passes. Or, instead of beans, take burnt oven-clay <note>original: "gebrennten Ofenleim"</note> and prepare it in the same manner as described above, also until the pain passes. This is not only for the sake of the pain, but also as a defensive measure <note>original: "Defensiff"</note> which the genitals require. For they have more to lose in their obstruction than other limbs, and thus they must be defended and protected. But if the pain will not fundamentally go away from these, take a handful of chamomile flowers and a handful of mullein <note>original: "Wollenblumen"</note>, boil them with tree-oil <note>olive oil</note> into the form of a plaster that you may apply warm. If no help comes from these either, take the stinking dwarf elder <note>original: "Attich"</note>, boil it with wine, and apply it warm...

However, as far as I have seen through experience, such arts are not even worth thinking about. Thus, for head wounds, Basilicon <term>Basilicon: A "royal" ointment usually made of pitch, resin, and wax, used to draw out infection and promote healing.</term> boiled in wine and applied warm is an excellent medicine against many damages. Likewise, lavender, marjoram, and sage are good for the sake of the reason <note>the cognitive faculties</note>, dizziness, and other fainting spells.

So too, concerning the lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys, it is to be known that they should be sustained and nourished with Potable Gold <term>Auro potabili: "Drinkable gold," an alchemical preparation believed to be a universal life-extending elixir.</term>. Now, there are many who chatter about Potable Gold—who can take the "cuckoo" <margin>B</margin> out of the fool? Potable Gold should be in the possession of every physician: if he knows nothing of it, what is he worth? I know it well; the time, I hope, will bring it to light. It is clearly evident: it is a medicine about which all the ancient writers were silent, as are you young "cuckoos" <note>original: "Gugger"; a derogatory term for someone who repeats things they don't understand.</note>.

### The Conclusion of the First Treatise.

N<image-desc>Decorative drop cap N with vine and leaf motifs</image-desc>ow that I have presented the most necessary points and articles that a wound-surgeon should know and understand apart from the recipes: for if he does not understand and know these things, the recipes that follow in the second and third treatises will be of little use to him. Yet I must still be mindful, as I mentioned in the first preface, that I have often distanced myself from medicine and was terrified to burden myself with its cares. The reason, as stated in the first preface, was because I considered the foundation held by the self-proclaimed physicians to be the entirety of the art. But when I found their foolishness, I knew nothing more lovely than the true art of medicine. Upon this, I may rightly write and teach, so that the righteous and certain foundation of medicine might achieve progress and advancement. When I consider this, the foundation must not be revealed by the self-proclaimed physicians, nor formed within them: therefore, they are not to be heeded, and no single comfort should be built upon them. It is no less true that in the German nation there are mighty and excellently learned fellows and men who would be useful and profitable to such a foundation: but it is a pity that (they) do not weigh the great utility that can come from medicine. For since we should love our neighbors, we must fulfill that love in what is dear to the other; yet such learned men burden themselves with such useless tasks and labor in writings that give neither fruit nor profit, which are useful neither to them nor to humanity. I must lament that they are so blinded, for learned, pious, righteous, and brave physicians could become of them, and through them the incompetent barbers, bathers, and Doctors (I mean fools) would be driven out, and <margin>C</margin> they could give aid to medicine and tear it from the wolves and their maws. But they value their own teaching higher than all the treasures of men, though it is nothing but air, giving neither cold nor warmth, neither to the soul nor the body. That same honor passes like the sound of a bell, just like a <margin><unclear>Luſſ... in Teu... Phien</unclear> just like a bagpipe</margin> bagpipe; while it hums, one is merry, and when it is over, there is misery and need. Thus I thought that they should learn more useful things that are more in accordance with Christian love, rather than wasting away in things commanded neither by God nor by Nature. I can also well observe that man is more inclined toward aggravation than toward improvement. Although their honor has a great appearance, it lasts only fourteen days: for this reason, medicine has hitherto lain in great contempt and has been brought to such mockery that whoever used it was said to act against God. And these same despisers and mockers have not only touched upon the wonders of God in medicine, despising His works and creatures, but they have blasphemed, annihilated, and mocked Him Himself in His saints. Not only did they despise His word where He says: "The sick have need of the physician," but they have accepted the entire Gospel in nothing that they have not defiled. From this I can well perceive that the foundation of medicine cannot be placed upon the "learned" men: for the reason that they are too defiled and too firmly led into those [seats] upon the "chair of pestilence" <note>A biblical reference to Psalm 1, implying a seat of corruption.</note>. But what the flying air has born will meet its end, of this I am comforted: The physician is created by God. When I think of that, I desire none of them near me; they are called to their "buffalo-driving" <note>original: "Buffelfuhr"; crude or mindless labor</note>, not to medicine. Medicine requires honest men who are for deeds, not for chatter.

I can well understand that everyone wants to speak of God: but it is not commanded of everyone. Those appointed must work in the vineyard: and where they let the wild sows break down the fence, and let every wild beast run into the vineyard to devastate and tear it <meta>catchword: apart, so</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...break out <note>original: "reissen"; referring to the uncontrolled spread of corruption or bad practice</note> [until such time as the arrogance reaches its limit, then it will come to an end. Then, I hope, every person will come into the stall where they belong and perform the work commanded of them there. It is no less true that there are now a great number of physicians, but few who are proven. For there is no sow that has not run into this vineyard and rooted around in this medicine. Such as the **Apostates** <note>original: "Apostatæ"; here referring to those who have abandoned their religious orders or proper vocations to pursue medicine for easy money</note> who have been gluttonous, greedy, lustful, and lazy all their lives. To continue the lifestyle in which they were raised, they have taken up medicine: for the reason that, according to the supposed rules and skills of physicians, neither skill, proof, nor truth is required, but only chattering and gossiping. However it goes, it always pays off. The Count has much money; likewise, the Merchant—one must "comb" <note>original: "strälen"; a metaphor for fleecing or swindling money from someone</note> them. Thus, medicine has become a field for all those who desired to nourish themselves with dishonor.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>It lies with God for both</margin>
So it is that not only have such **Apostates** rushed in, but also many frivolous people, such that a pious man must be ashamed to be counted among them. Such as executioners, dog-catchers <term>Dog-catchers: In this era, certain professions were considered "dishonorable" and socially excluded; Paracelsus complains that these marginalized figures were practicing medicine without proper knowledge.</term>, and other frivolous, lazy folk who could not maintain themselves with honor. If the prophets could not remain untainted, but false prophets had to stand beside them, and the Apostles had to allow false apostles to remain: how then can the physician not endure having false physicians stand beside him? For the false patients seek their own kind of doctor, and the righteous seek the righteous: thus God joins together those who belong together. Therefore, good and evil must live with one another, for as no wheat has ever grown without weeds <note>original: "Ratten"; likely referring to tares or darnel</note>, one must let it be so. And even if I wished with all my heart and labored day and night so that every person might be as I would most wish them to be: if it is not pleasing to God, and he shall be nothing, then it will never happen. Therefore, what is destined for a man, that shall be his: everyone receives, but not everyone for salvation—that is, for the benefit of their neighbor. This is a great thing for a physician to consider, as Christ says: "No one comes to me unless my Heavenly Father draws him to me." So too with medicine, every person is drawn to where they belong: one to the righteous, the other to the destroyer. Nevertheless, there follows here the Second Treatise; read it for the benefit of the sick.

# The Preface of Dr. Paracelsus to the Second
## Treatise of his Surgery.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'I' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>C</margin>
Everyone who wishes to write for the common good and fulfill the commandment "You shall love your neighbor," should above all things take care that they leave their writing unblemished by things that have not been thoroughly investigated. For just as a field gives little fruit unless it is cultivated according to its actual needs—neither too much nor too little—so too does a writing give little fruit if it is written outside of such order. He who now wishes to write and takes a work upon himself should remember only to look at what the work actually is, and neither subtract from it nor add to it. The reason I introduce such a thing in this preface is this: where this is not observed, and there is too little, the work is without fruit; if it is too much, it is harmful and useful to no one. So that you understand this, I will present to you several writings and books in which this has happened—those who have written of all diseases from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, leaving nothing out that does not fill a specific chapter. And yet, I can testify with the truth that they have not truly experienced a fourth part—not even a tenth part—of their writing, to know that it is as they write. Namely, there is no truth without lies; that is, truth is mixed with lies. Everyone has wanted to be seen and held in high regard by people, putting together things that fit and things that do not, and gathering lies from here and there so that they might be seen as a teacher and master. Many have taken offense that I do not test or use anything from those books, as if I should be esteemed as less of a scholar (though they all should not be fit to untie my shoelaces, whether they be German or Italian/Foreign <note>original: "Welsch"; usually referring to Romance-language speakers, particularly Italians or French.</note>), yet I devote myself to writing nothing but what I can and dare testify before God. Since I take this as my foundation, they would all like to stone me. How can I fulfill my writing if I write and collect it from other books, when I do not know what is found in them? That is: they write, and it is so interspersed with lies that I can pull no truth from them in which there is not a deception. And if I must speak upon my conscience: these are only suggestions that have been neither proven nor tested. For even a blind man could grasp that the writings of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicennæ"; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose texts dominated medieval European medicine.</note> cannot be a truth, and yet they are regarded as if there were no lies in them. Not only his book, but also **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), another foundational medical authority of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> and other writers who have made great books and cannot testify to a tenth part of what they have written as truth. And many a man writes of a hundred diseases who in all his life has never been able to heal—or even seen healed—more than six diseases. Why then should I rely on such writings, since I know fundamentally and truly, and can also prove it, that those who are their students and followers destroy a hundred before they make ten healthy, and give a hundred pieces of advice where, in truth, only five...

# The First Book of the Great [Surgery]

<margin>A</margin> [...might] not be able to prove? So if such a thing is found, that one dares to undertake it—someone who can describe a disease with such useless chatter and does not consider: *Of every useless word you must give an account* <note>A reference to Matthew 12:36; the author emphasizes that medical writers will be judged by God for misleading patients with flowery language.</note>. Instead, they write like "Fantasy-Doctors," born of the **Arrogance** of which Italy is the mother <note>The author frequently criticized the Italian universities of his time for what he saw as theoretical vanity over practical healing.</note>.

Therefore, their followers also believe they have the power to write in such a way that they climb higher than they are meant to fly. Why should I be troubled by such excessive writings, when I can clearly feel and sense the falsehood within them, and I know that they only seek fame? And so that they may keep that fame, they devise all sorts of things to give their writings an appearance of authority. And since the Devil is the father of such deceit and, moreover, a fine **rhetorician** <note>original: "Rhetoricus"; a master of persuasive but potentially deceptive speech</note>, how could these books *not* be produced? Woe to the fool who holds them equal to the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>.

<margin>The Letter Kills</margin> One should write and establish the truth; and where one is in doubt, or does not know the foundation, one should refrain from writing. This should happen not only in medicine, but also in chronicles, in histories, and in all other books—even in the Holy Scriptures—where everyone wants to be seen. Thus, lies come among the people, who then love the darkness more than the light. Therefore, I want to give a report to you who write: The Scripture says, *The letter kills, but the spirit gives life* <note>2 Corinthians 3:6. The author uses this famous theological phrase to argue that "the letter" represents false, superficial writing, while "the spirit" represents the underlying truth of nature.</note>. Now note the difference between the two—what the letter and the spirit are. The **Spirit** is that which alone has the truth within it. As one who writes only what is true, he does not write a "letter," but rather the truth, which is the spirit; yet it is not visible in itself, but must reach us through writing or a voice. But the **Letter** is that which is written when it is not the truth. So, if one writes what is not true, he writes lies. From this it follows that the letter kills—that is, the lied-about letter. Therefore, anyone who wishes to write should strive to remain in the truth, so that he **kills** no one: for killing is forbidden upon pain of losing Eternal Life. Take as your example how briefly the Prophets wrote: the reason is that they wrote the truth. Look at the Evangelists, how briefly they wrote: they wrote only the truth—what they had seen and heard from the mouth of Truth—and they left out their own additions, writing not a single "letter" of their own, but only what was commanded of them.

Therefore, since we see this among the greatest writers, who have written of the highest good: how much more should we, who write of lesser things, not stray from those same footsteps? We must not let ourselves be led astray by temporal fame, for it cannot be achieved without these "letters." It is also good for me to know what Christ said: that when He is taken up from this world, He would send us the **Holy Spirit**, who would teach us all things. Therefore, mark my words: He will teach us nothing more than what is the truth. Now, the truth can be grasped with very little; but the world's pleasure must carry a long, wide magnificence. Look at a **pearl**; it is quite small. Yet it is of much more use than many wagonloads of rotten wood, which only adds to the bulk. Therefore, even if it might be said that the Holy Spirit teaches such long-winded chatter, do not believe it.

->For if the truth lay in such length, then<-
->**CHRIST** would have spoken too little.<-

I point this out because medicine has fallen into chatter and into the "letter," so much so that there is almost no foundation in medicine anymore, except what happens by mere chance. If I now try to separate such "letters" from the **Spirit of Truth**, people will take me for a fool. I cannot blame them for that, but must let it be: it is a great sea that no one can wade through; rather, whatever enters it must drown. They say: *One should not cast pearls before swine*, and *that which is holy should not be given to dogs*. By this, they want to prove that the truth should not be written. And they are right, for the reason that *they* are the swine. 

<margin>Truth should not be written</margin><margin>C</margin> Therefore, the pearl does not suit them, for their foundation and their "letter" follow only from the idea that one should write lies. Oh, woe to such a twisted understanding! Does Christ allow the pearl and the holy word to be written for everyone through his Evangelists, and command His Apostles to announce it to all creatures? Why then should a man not follow Christ his Creator, especially since it is written: *He who believes and is baptized shall be saved*? So, if the swine are separated from those who are not swine, and the swine do not accept it: why should I then not write the truth, and not let the swine turn me away, since God blinds the liars in the face of the truth?

It is just like a beautiful maiden: many look at her, but only one takes her as his own. Therefore, there follows hereafter the **Second Treatise** of my First Book, in which I include all the **recipes** <note>original: "Recept"; in this context, specific medical formulas and instructions</note> and medicines through which, truly and certainly according to the Order of Nature, every wound or stab is healed and brought to the state where it should be, and as far as it can be brought, regardless of what others write.

Sometimes it might happen that old arts agree in some parts with my own. Understand it thus: that medicine has always been a truthful foundation, but it was corrupted by supposed doctors who put falsehood in its place, with perhaps a little truth added. My experience has been to root out the falsehood or the "hair mixed into the wool." Thus, when I do this, some recipes might match mine. Furthermore, I can certainly prove through **experience** <note>original: "Erfarnuß"</note> that I know more to teach you—to what end and how the medicine is good—because much has come to my hands in many ways. Additionally, I can well reveal to you where I have experienced it better, and how it was to be improved for this present time. Therefore, read and learn the following recipes, so that you may act as faithfully toward your neighbor as you would want done to yourself. And remember: that arrogance, splendor, pomp, and chatter cannot heal; only the **Art** can, and only the Art within you pleases God. Therefore, leave behind what is contrary to the Art, so that you may be a true physician.

He then introduces his second treatise, which provides practical, experience-based recipes for healing wounds.</summary>
