<meta>Following the previous page's critique of theoretical "Fantasy-Doctors," the author now transitions into the practical "First Treatise" of his work on surgery. This page focuses on the "regimen"—the diet and lifestyle rules essential for recovery.</meta>

Wound Medicine: The First Treatise.

<margin>A</margin>
## Of Abstinence / Regimen and Order / How the 
## Wounded Should Conduct Themselves.

Since disorder ruins a healthy body, how much more must it be considered in a sick person, and especially in the wounded? Particularly when we see that through food, drink, and good order, wounds may be healed, just as they may also be ruined. Therefore, in all things, an order should be maintained that serves health and does not act against it. For bad order and good medicine cannot perform a good work; likewise, bad medicine and good order can do just as little.

I must first report the order of the alleged doctors <note>original: "vermeinten Artzet"; the author is likely referring to university-trained physicians whom he frequently criticized for being out of touch with practical healing</note>, who have prescribed water-soups, burnt mush <note>original: "brente Müßlein"; a common early modern dish made of roasted flour or grains cooked into a thick porridge</note>, barley water, and the like for the wounded, all of which is contrary to the natural order. For a healthy body dreads such food and drink—how much more the wounded? Regarding this, one should consider that the wounded person should be kept on good food and drink, according to the suitability of his <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Deuwung"; refers to the process by which the body breaks down and "cooks" food into nutrients and blood</note>.

You should keep this practice for yourself: if a drunkard or a glutton is struck, let him sober up well until the second, third, or fourth day. In such a case, you have full permission to give water-soup and oatmeal pap, along with barley water. But if a sober person is wounded, you should keep him on the best food and drink. For his nature has not been disrupted in its digestion like that of the drunkard. For the drunkard has two wounds: one being the internal destruction of the body, and the other being the wound on the skin.

<margin>B</margin>
You should strive to vary the food for the wounded, satisfying various cravings and not cutting off their desire—unless it concerns those foods and drinks that are forbidden in all illnesses, such as pork, goose, and whatever are waterfowl. Such forbidden foods do not need to be listed here, as they are well enough known.

This is the most important thing to measure: give often, and always a little; by no means overfill him, nor let him suffer long hunger, nor forced thirst. For the reason thirst is present is because it comes from the liver, and the liver is forced by the wound to give it nourishment. Therefore, thirst in wounded people should be addressed. For there is more medicine than a thirst <note>meaning the medicine or treatment itself creates the thirst, or the thirst is a sign that the body needs the "medicine" of hydration</note>, and it is because of the medicine that the thirst exists. Therefore, drinking is a sharing and an enlivening joy in the wound. So it is also with food; no one should be forced beyond necessity, neither to drink nor to eat, whether he be severely or lightly wounded. It would only be if the stomach had grown cold, and through that same coldness did not desire digestion nor food. In that case, for the sake of warmth, a warm and strengthening food should be given often, and always a little—such as burnt mush with meat broth.

There is not much more to write regarding food and drink, other than to look at the person and provide light and harmless food at appropriate times, as nature requires. Much depends on the drink, which should be emphasized because they have more thirst than hunger. The reason for this, as was mentioned, is that they almost bleed to death; and after such blood loss, more thirst than hunger follows. For in the loss of blood, the liver loses its nourishment, but the stomach does not. Therefore, the liver desires through its thirst that this same loss be restored. What the stomach lacks is not to be considered as highly as the liver. The stomach recovers more easily than the liver. And although every stomach becomes "undigested" <note>fails to process food</note>, so that it cannot send satisfaction to the liver from the food, the drink does not rely so much on the stomach's digestion. Therefore, you should consider the liver more than the stomach, for it is the liver that sends nourishment to the wound. If the drink is "blood-rich" <note>nutritious or restorative liquids believed to assist in making new blood</note>, the wound will be promoted all the more powerfully. Therefore, provide yourself with good drinks that you may learn according to the custom of that land.

<margin>C</margin>
Furthermore, you should leave the sick person unburdened—that is, he should not work, not make the limb restless, and in all things, the more he restrains himself, the better. You should also know that if certain complications arise for the sick person (as mentioned in the first treatise), you must know how to give or take, or add or subtract, according to those illnesses. Namely: if <term>gout</term>, <term>colic</term>, <term>epilepsy</term> <note>original: "Fallendsucht"</note>, or <term>cramps</term> should occur, let no goat meat be given. Likewise, if fever occurs, give nothing of the same from eggs. Thus it is also with other illnesses; you must know how to direct yourself according to their nature.

For if other illnesses should strike, strive to set a different order, as is practiced and should be in those same illnesses. Furthermore, there is not much to write of food; it would be superfluous.

You may certainly have the food seasoned with spices, and also use distilled waters of cinnamon, cloves, and the like, mixing them with the food and letting it cook.

Also, meat broths made in a pot without water are very good. Even if you pour water or wine into it and boil it closed for its proper time, and mix the juice with the aforementioned cinnamon and cloves, it gives the liver and stomach great strength.

And in the beginning, keep him more with moist food than with dry, and this for the sake of the liver, which has more need of nourishment than the stomach.

You should also know for yourself that in head wounds, strong drinks are never good, including burnt wine <note>distilled spirits or brandy</note>. In these large and heavy wounds, the best thing is "bread water" <note>a decoction made by soaking or boiling toasted bread in water</note>, which is more useful than barley water, when mixed with cinnamon juice.

The First Book of the Great [Surgery]
<margin>A</margin>

## Concerning Constipation of the Bowels, and of Vomiting in the Sick, as well as Afflictions of the Urine, as they may occur to them.

It often happens that the sick experience a stoppage of the bowels. This occurs for several reasons: first, because nature becomes too weak from the loss of blood and cannot expel waste. Second, the act of lying still in bed itself causes constipation. Third, hunger fades and <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Dewung"; the alchemical process by which the body "cooks" food</note> fails, meaning there is simply less to expel. Fourth, a fever sets in, as is the nature of wounds, and this heat consumes such materials. Fifth, where there is great thirst, it is natural for there to be few bowel movements.

Regarding this, you should know that it is not necessary to force a bowel movement unless three days have passed, or slightly longer, or if the patient feels a tightness in the chest. In such cases, use a suppository <note>original: "Zapflin"; a small plug of medicine inserted into the rectum</note> at first. If these do not help, then give <term>Cassia fistula</term> <note>a tropical pod used as a mild laxative</note>, or an electuary of rose juice, or <term>Diassincon</term> <note>original: "Diassincon"; a traditional purgative compound</note>, or the "Blessed Laxative" <note>original: "Benedicta laxativa"; a famous medieval purgative formula</note>, according to common practice; it is not necessary to describe them here.

Although various drinks may be brewed from senna leaves, <term>polypody fern</term> <note>original: "Engel süß"; literally "sweet angel," a common name for the licorice-flavored fern root</note>, and the like, and these should not be despised, they are so common that they need no description.

You must never force anything or act with violence—that is, with <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "Cristier"</note>—for the body does not have enough strength within it to be pressured. When the time of strength returns, the bowels will move easily. If you act with violence, you cause many accidents and other evils; therefore, do not be too eager to purge or too hasty.

<margin>B</margin>
In the same way, you should know that it often happens that the sick are prone to vomiting. If this occurs, take a handful of sourdough or yeast, and mint juice boiled with vinegar; simmer everything together with the dough until it becomes like a plaster. Then lay it warm over the stomach in the manner of a patch. When it cools, warm it again with the mentioned juice, and let it lie over the pit of the stomach as often as the patient eats and for two or three hours afterward. However, there is no need for great concern regarding such vomiting; it does not lead to a bad end but disappears as nature’s strength increases.

So too regarding the urine: if it should stop, give crushed <term>crab stones</term> <note>original: "Krebsstein"; these are calcium deposits (gastroliths) found in the stomachs of crayfish, highly prized in early medicine for treating stones and stomach acid</note> to drink in radish juice or water. If that does not work, bind saffron in a small pouch and place it externally between the genitals, or give dry acorns to eat. There is not much more to write of these things, for they vanish on their own as the healing progresses.

<margin>Water of <unclear>mint</unclear></margin>
Now that all the necessities have been completed in the First Treatise—concerning what a wound surgeon must know beyond the art of healing, and how the regimen of food and drink, as well as the three natural complications, should be managed—it is further necessary to report and present the art by which wounds are to be healed. Now, for a general instruction useful for all arts of medicine, besides the specific instructions for each individual art, you shall understand the preparation thus: No one can see the medicine itself, for it is an invisible thing; but one sees the *body* of the medicine. In the same way, in a human being, only the body is seen, not the soul. Now, I say this because the medicine is something different from its physical body, and the medicine can exist without that body. The preparation is therefore the process by which the two are separated from one another, so that the good is used and the rest is discarded. Nevertheless, the medicine cannot exist without a body; for that which is intangible and invisible, like a stone, must yet perform an action, and so it must accomplish its work through a physical form. From this it follows that there are two bodies in which the medicine dwells: one of which it can do without—that is, the coarser body that lies before our eyes—but the other, which is seen hereafter, it cannot do without. Upon this, the instruction is now given: that the preparation must take place so that the useless body is separated from the useful one.

# Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.

<margin>Not all are prepared in this way</margin>
<margin>Others still for that reason</margin>

**A** certain remedies are found that should not lose their physical substance <note>original: "Leib"; literally "body," referring to the material essence of the plant or mineral</note>, but are meant to be used within that substance. It follows that because of their nature and properties, they must be prepared according to those same properties. Furthermore, it should be known that some medicines are transferred from their own substance into another substance, and are more effective in a "foreign body" than in their own; these are also kept and prepared according to their specific properties. There are also other items which, in their raw state, have no power and do nothing; however, when they are raised higher and "sharpened" through the <term>Art of Preparation</term> <note>the alchemical process of refining raw materials into potent medicine</note>, they then become powerful and miraculous. Those that possess such properties are prepared and refined according to their kind. Thus, there are four types of preparation.

Although until now no such order has been maintained—but rather everything has been muddled through—it is no honor, but rather a disgrace, that a physician should not know that which is his duty. This has been held in low regard by many, and consequently, matters have been handled all the more shamefully. Therefore, it is better to act according to the natural order of preparation than to follow those ignorant, self-proclaimed doctors who mix two, three, four, or more things together under a single method of preparation. They wish to bring into another body that which will not separate from its own; they wish to use in its own body that which only shows its effect in a foreign one, and so it goes with all the rest. Now, it should be a matter of common knowledge for every physician to know in what preparation each thing reveals its power. He who has not "worn out his shoes" <note>an idiom meaning he hasn't put in the hard work or experience</note> in this study is ill-suited for medicine. He would be better equipped to tend to pigs, for that does not require much learning. There is also a great difference in the heat that "cooks" <note>original: "kochet"; in alchemy, heat "cooks" or ripens a substance into its medicinal form</note>: for heat is that which prepares all things. Now, four types of heat are found: Fire, the Sun, Dung <note>original: "Mist"; rotting manure provided a gentle, steady heat for long-term alchemical digestion</note>, and that heat which is innate within itself. Understand the difference between such heats in this way: when you place a medicine in a glass and set it in the sun, a different power results than if it were heated by wood-**B**fire or dung. In dung, it is different than in the sun or by fire. There is also a difference in the heat of sand and the heat of water <note>referring to sand-baths and water-baths (bain-marie) used to regulate temperature</note>, even if both have received the same external heat. Therefore, you must be diligent to recognize the nature of the heat and what heat the medicine requires, so that like is joined with like.

Since it is necessary to consider this—so that each thing is prepared in its ordained heat—it is vital to explain it. Although ignorant doctors do not see it this way and value one heat the same as another, it should by no means be so. What belongs in the sun should be placed in the sun; what belongs in the <term>Reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto a substance</note> should be committed to it; what prepares itself (like wine that ferments) should be kept in its own vessel; what requires preparation in dung should be completed in the same. As such, in the following recipes, each thing is ordained for itself, according to where it belongs. Therefore, learn and experience what the order of Nature is, and in what form she wishes to be prepared. Where this does not happen, Nature cannot accomplish what is within her. Some such preparations were briefly mentioned by the ancient physicians—as they drew from the <term>Alchemists</term>—but without their fundamental knowledge, they assigned things here and there, revealing great lack of understanding. But you, be diligent so that you do not deal in such folly. As much as is necessary here for the healing of wounds—to prepare, to separate—will be sufficiently shown; more instruction than this is not needed here. And abandon the old apothecary custom, that muddled work, that "hodgepodge" <note>original: "Rips vnd Raps"; a chaotic mixing of ingredients</note>, whether it rhymes or not. It is a great shame that an old woman should be able to cook an oat porridge <note>original: "Habermuß"</note> better than a physician can prepare his medicine—and yet they are called "Doctor" and "Master," which the old woman is not.

**K**nowing the nature of wound drinks: they have such power and might that they heal every stab and wound through the internal help of Nature. For since Nature is the physician in itself, and only desires external help from the "outer Nature"—by virtue of the alliance that both Natures have together—this same outer Nature must be presented to the inner. Therefore, Nature has certain plants within her which should be brought into another substance and applied to the body within that substance. And that substance should be the drink, which Nature accepts as a food. For when joined through food, the medicine becomes one with the body, and in such a form, it heals the wounds. Therefore, it is right that wound drinks be presented according to their proper order, as they are proven and certain medicines for healing every wound and stab. Although wound drinks have always been in use, they have been approached with the wrong ingredients and preparations through the lack of understanding of those ignorant doctors who set them up according to their folly. In such matters, one must know that wound drinks are not only a medicine but also a nourishment. In this way, a "wound food" can be just as effective as a wound drink, provided that the same ingredients used in the drinks are cooked and consumed with the food. However, because food is digested slowly and cannot provide help to the wound as quickly as a wound drink—and because the stomach does not bring food to <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Dewung"; refers both to biological digestion and the alchemical ripening of nutrients</note> as efficiently for this purpose—such [solid] medicine has been omitted so that Nature is not hindered. But where it could be properly digested, it would be useful and good for it to be given along with the drink.

potions are made, perhaps a hundred in total. From these, five or six—more or less—are taken and subsequently placed into another "body," which is to say, into wine. However things may be, some items are better, some worse, some faster, and some slower; these differences are understood by physicians, and the medicine is prescribed accordingly. Therefore, it is most necessary from the beginning to recognize the true primary ingredients and wound-drinks, specifically those that possess the greatest power, and to prepare them according to the contents of their natural order. In this way, any wound or stab may be confidently expected to reach a certain state of health. I also say this: that wound-drinks, together with the <term>wound-diet</term> <note>original: "Wundspeiß"; a specific nutritional regimen intended to support healing from within</note>, prevent many future complications. This cannot be achieved as easily through other medicines used externally as it can through those used internally. Therefore, everyone should strive to devote themselves to wound-drinks and to make them according to the correct order; for nothing better can be found, as they prevent many more complications than other medicines.

<margin>B</margin>
Outside of the order following hereafter, I have seen remarkable wound-drinks which, through a particularly great natural power, have healed miraculous wounds. Although these were natural, they were so effective against other "arts" of Nature <note>referring to the natural processes of disease or decay</note> that one could only wonder at them. In Greek Weissenburg <note>Alba Iulia in modern-day Romania</note>, I saw a Wallachian who gave nothing more than a single drink to consume, and with it, he healed every stab and wound. However, it is true that this same art was not certain in every person, in every place, or in all wounds. Nevertheless, from what I learned of his patients and the locations of the wounds, all such wounds can easily be healed in that manner. But whatever did not fit that specific form resisted the cure. Still, there is a great power in Nature.

In Croatia, I also saw a Gypsy who took the juice of a herb and gave it to a patient to drink just once. Whatever stabs to the body went deep were healed by that one drink. But whatever was prone to complications, the drink had no power over it. I also saw in Stockholm <note>original: "Stockhalma in Dennemarck"; Paracelsus frequently grouped Scandinavian regions together</note>, a wound-drink held by a noblewoman; whatever bone-shinters or joint-wounds there were, they were healed with three drinks. However, since it is rare for only the flesh to be cut, one should not rely on such things alone. I once also saw a <term>conjurer of spirits</term> <note>original: "Teuffelsbeschwerer"; an exorcist or folk-healer who used incantations</note> who had a wound-drink that healed wounds, bone-shinters, and even severed limbs with three drinks. But when I discovered the truth, it was not the drink that healed, but rather what he placed over the wounds, which is mentioned in his other chapters.

Certain items which I consider to be the "main sum" and the best for serving as wound-drinks, I will list hereafter. You may safely trust in these to heal every stab and wound, regardless of how they occurred, with no exceptions. How they should be put together and prepared follows later; the number of these herbs are as follows:

Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A</margin>
[wound-]drinks should be provided according to custom and the proper order, which you should strive to ensure are complete and good. Then you may confidently and joyfully be a physician, serving the common good with praise and honor, praising God in His works, and enlightening the art.

## On the Old Preparation, and Subsequently on the New.

It is an old custom to boil wound-drinks in wine, as is fitting, and to let them simmer down to a third or a half of their volume. Such a preparation is a misunderstanding and is contrary to the order of Nature. The reason is this: take a measure of wine and let it boil down by itself as described above; then let it cool, and it will become a tasteless, stale, and unpleasant drink that is entirely contrary to Nature. For the wine boils away, and a stinking, sour liquid remains in its place, from which nothing good can be given to Nature. Therefore, if you wish to keep the wine agreeable to Nature and pleasant, you must put it into a <term>jug</term> <note>original: "Kante"; a vessel or container for liquids</note> and seal it well with <term>luting paste</term> <note>original: "Wälbappen"; a sealant often made of flour and water to airtight a vessel during heating</note>. Place it thus into boiling water and let it simmer for an hour or an hour and a half, etc. In this way, nothing is lost from the wine; it remains entirely in its essence, and the power of the herbs enters into it more completely and strongly, without evaporating, unlike the old custom used until now. Therefore, strive to boil the wound-drinks according to the method I show you, and do not make an unpleasant, tasteless drink from which the wine has evaporated, leaving a tasteless, sour drink in its place. Understand also that the reason it becomes so tasteless is that it stirs up griping pains, <term>cramps</term> <note>original: "Vnndtwung"; a term for stomach constriction or spasms</note> in the stomach, and other miseries—especially the wines from Keltern, Zurich, and certain "Lake-wines" from Bregenz <note>original: "Pregag"</note>, which are good for nothing at all. All wines are also better the older, whiter, clearer, and more aged they are. Red wines are not good; they do not readily absorb "foreign virtues" <note>the medicinal properties of the herbs</note> into themselves.

<margin>B</margin><margin>In change.</margin> <note>original: "In muta"; likely referring to an alternative or "changed" method</note> It is also a useful practice to take wine in the autumn, when it comes from the wine-press, and pour it into a barrel that has been filled with wound-herbs. Let it age there for three months, and then strain it. Such wine provides useful wound-drinks and requires no boiling or other preparation; it is a complete wound-drink in itself. Or let the herbs lie in it longer, or <insert>add</insert> fresh ones throughout the entire year, filled like a <term>Rappes</term> <note>a historic type of thin wine or grape-stalk infusion</note>.

It has also been my common practice, when wine is not available, to take wound-herbs and chop them well, put them in a jug, seal the jug, and place it in boiling water. If you boil them for six or eight hours, a "water" <note>an essence or decoction</note> is produced; give this water to be drunk in place of the wound-drink. This is a useful and convenient practice, even for those who do not drink wine, or for those with head wounds to whom wine easily brings harm. It is good to add <term>cinnamon juice</term> <note>original: "Zimmersafft"; cinnamon was highly valued for its warming properties and flavor</note> or similar spices for better taste and for the sake of their strength.

You should also know that when you take a recipe for yourself, according to its weight and <term>proportion</term> <note>original: "Concordantz"; the harmonious balance of ingredients</note>, you may prepare it in any of these three ways as you wish, and give it as a wound-drink. For whichever way you choose to prepare it, it will be useful.

This practice is also fine and good: take the juice of wound-herbs and put it in a jug; let it boil well-sealed in a kettle of water, and a clear, beautiful drink will result. You may add appropriate spices for strengthening and good flavor, so that it becomes more pleasant to Nature.

<margin>C</margin><margin>Wound-herbs in meat broth</margin> Understand also regarding <term>wound-diet</term> <note>original: "Wundspeiß"; food specifically prepared to aid healing</note> that whatever meat or chicken you wish to give the patient to eat should be placed in a jug. Add as much water as you desire for broth, and add the following wound-herbs as much as you deem necessary. Let them boil together in a covered jug in boiling water for the usual amount of time. This is a useful food for a patient and is very helpful for healing. You may also take wine instead of water and boil it as one prepares a <term>brine</term> <note>original: "Salß"; likely a savory sauce or seasoned broth</note> in a closed jug; this sustains and nourishes the wounds above all other food.

## Presentation of Several Composed Recipes.

Take Sanicle, Wintergreen, Centaury, and Betony, a handful of each; Larkspur, half a handful; Agrimony, two handfuls. Boil them according to the aforementioned instructions.

Another recipe: Take Adder's Tongue, three handfuls; Lady's Mantle <note>original: "Sinaw"</note>, two handfuls; Small Wintergreen, one handful; Woodruff, one and a half handfuls; Rhubarb, two <term>Loth</term> <note>approximately 1 ounce or 30 grams total</note>; <term>Rhapontic rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Reupontica"</note>, six Loth. Let it also boil as described above.

Another: Take Angelica, one Loth; <term>Mumia</term> <note>original: "Mummia"; a substance used in historical medicine, often bitumen or ground remains, believed to stop bleeding</note>, two Loth; <term>Spermaceti</term> <note>original: "Sperma ceti"; a waxy substance from the head of a sperm whale, used for internal cooling</note>, half a Loth; Acorns, four Loth; <term>Goldenrod</term> <note>original: "Heydnisch wundkraut"; literally "heathen's wound-wort"</note>, two handfuls; Cyclamen, four Loth; Small and Great Wintergreen, three handfuls of each; wine as much as is enough. That is, you should take wine according to your judgment; you may also add a third part of water at the beginning if you choose.

You should also know that there are several more preparations besides those mentioned above: namely, if you take the wound-herbs out of <term>distilled water</term> <note>original: "gebrennem wasser"; alcohol or aqua vitae</note> and fill them again with the same herbs, and then let them boil in the jug as described above, they become very excellent wound-drinks, as this example shows.

# The First Book of the Great [Surgery]

<margin>A</margin>Take one <term>measure</term> <note>Approximately 1 liter</note> of small wintergreen water; place into it a handful of wintergreen, half a handful of sanicle, and half a handful of periwinkle; let it boil as described above in the jug, etc.

There is also another process for making the most noble wound-drinks, following the same method and order used to make white juniper oil from juniper berries. In this case, the wound-healing herbs are added and prepared together, a process that is particularly skillful and subtle, and to be preferred above all others. For within juniper berries lies a special, secret wound-healing virtue that serves healing more than other preparations. I strongly advise learning this method, even though I do not set it down here, for the reason that it is done through distillation—an art that is not strictly necessary to learn at this point. Thus, here follows an example of how each recipe should be added to the juniper berries.

Take two pounds of crushed juniper berries, half a handful each of both wintergreen and woodruff, and white sanicle roots; one and a half handfuls of adder’s tongue; and ten <term>lot</term> <note>A "lot" is a historical unit of weight, roughly 15-18 grams</note> each of comfrey and birthwort, prepared according to the art of this distillation.

You may also take the same waters produced in such a distillation and fill them with wound-herbs, preparing them in the jug as described above—not only from juniper berries, but also from cinnamon and similar substances.

There is also a subtle preparation where wound-flowers are combined with <term>spica</term> <note>original: "Spica"; likely spike lavender or spikenard</note>, in the same way that "Oil of Spica" is made into a fat. However, the <term>dosage</term> <note>original: "dosis"</note> to be given in food or drink is small; to better understand this, take note of this recipe.

Take one handful of lavender flowers, four handfuls of St. John's wort flowers, two handfuls of mullein flowers, and half a handful each of betony, centaury, and self-heal flowers, prepared as is custom.

<margin>B</margin>A recipe for all wound-drinks, regardless of how they may be prepared: Take four lot of comfrey, six lot of birthwort, two lot of calamus, one lot of orris root, five handfuls of periwinkle herb, and half a handful of white sanicle. Also include two <term>quintlin</term> <note>A "quintlin" or "quinte" is about 4 grams</note> of peacock feathers (taken from the "eye" or mirror of the feather), and one lot each of myrrh, mastic, frankincense, and <term>mummy</term> <note>original: "Mumia"; historically, this referred to bitumen or ground remains used as a medicine to stop bleeding and heal wounds</note>. Add one and a half lot of rhubarb. Let this boil in wine, or in distilled water, or in wintergreen juice, or in common water, as may be appropriate.

Thus, enough has been said regarding wound-drinks, both in terms of recipes and preparation. There are many who possess good recipes, and if they were to prepare them as described above, they would achieve much more. It is no less true that among all wound-remedies, wound-drinks are currently the least utilized—sometimes due to laziness, sometimes due to a lack of skill, and sometimes due to faults in the preparation. But whoever applies themselves to this, as described above, is well to be trusted; even a deep stab wound may be safely entrusted to them.

The management of the wound-drink—how much or how little to use—depends on your own skill and the strength of the preparation, which you must know and recognize for yourself. With that, enough has been said about the matters belonging to this chapter, for your own experience must also play its part; not everything can be laid right under your nose.

### C A P V T III.

->On the Consideration of Wound Salves, and how they may best be<-
->made into a perfect medicine.<-

<margin>C</margin>Concerning the writing of wound salves, take note that, according to all experience, this is the oldest art of healing wounds. It is found that salves for wounds have been used for ages, even when other medicines were not yet thought of. Furthermore, it is a skill that was once common in every household and devised by the common man—that is, by the heads of households, where each person provided for themselves in their own home with wound salves made from things they had grown on their own property and raised themselves.

Now, the foundation of wound salves is such that the "body" or base—into which the medicine is drawn from one substance and brought into this body—consisted of only two things: namely, honey and butter. The common man chose these two bases because bees suck many kinds of power from flowers and herbs. And since there are many virtues in herbs, there must also be many virtues in the honey. Likewise, cows eat many good herbs and flowers, therefore much of that same virtue must also be in the butter. Thus, honey and butter were taken as the vehicle into which the medicine should be delivered.

From this, it followed that the medicine grown on the land was united with this honey or butter; this union was subsequently preserved, and wounds were dressed and healed with it. Now, it is no less true: this is a perfect, certain, and true art, and the right way to use salves. But it happened that when the <term>sophistical physicians</term> <note>A term often used by Paracelsus and his followers to describe academic doctors who relied on theory rather than practical experience</note> arose, they destroyed this art for the common man, calling it "peasant's art." They devised other things—useless things—and rejected the better ways. But I say this: if the common man today sticks to the recipes invented by common folk and avoids the arts of these so-called "day-doctors," their wounds will be usefully and perfectly healed.

I will set down several recipes for such wound salves hereafter, so that they may come back into use and memory, and so that this process may move forward. These recipes are as follows.

### Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> There follows: And although it is true that I do not take the ingredients used and chosen by the Greeks, Arabs, Chaldeans, or Egyptians, but rather take the ingredients that grow in anyone’s garden, it is not exactly the same thing—yet it is equal to it. So you may well understand that you may use honey and butter; that is, where honey is listed, you may take just as much butter, and where butter is listed, just as much honey, and they shall be prepared as follows.

Take one pound of May butter <note>Butter made from the milk of cows grazing on fresh spring grass, traditionally highly valued for its medicinal purity</note> that is still raw and unboiled, and crush into it these ingredients: broad and pointed plantain, small and large wintergreen, mangel-root and its roots, a handful of each; and three handfuls of small adder’s tongue with the single leaf; crush and mash them all together so that it all becomes one and turns into an ointment. You may set the ointment in the sun for several months, and then strain out the dregs; it will become so much the nobler for it.

Another wound-ointment: Take three pounds of May lard <note>Schmalz; clarified animal fat</note>, one pound of green comfrey, one and a half pounds of adder’s herb with the single leaf, half a pound of cleaned earthworms, and a <term>quarter-measure</term> <note>Vierting; a historical unit of weight</note> of green birthwort. Crush all of this together so that it becomes a pulp, and then keep it in the cold. If it releases moisture, you may pour it off. You may also set it in the sun, or bury it in manure and let it <term>digest</term> <note>A process of gentle, sustained heating used in alchemy and pharmacy to extract the "essence" of ingredients</note>, and then keep it.

In this way, you may make wound-ointments in many ways, in the manner indicated, and they are sufficient to heal any wound. You may also add a little salt for the sake of cleansing, or wash the wound with salt water.

<margin>B</margin> You may also take only a single ingredient, such as honey and adder’s tongue; honey and St. John’s-wort; butter and comfrey; butter and birthwort, etc., taking more or less together, or other ingredients from those that are wound-herbs. And note also that one herb is nobler than another, and also possesses more power; therefore, strive to take the best that each land provides.

As has been mentioned, the old custom is in the preparation; but you shall prepare these same ointments according to the **New Practice**. Although it is mine alone, it is nevertheless the primary method, and it is as follows:

Take the roots and herbs that please you and crush them while green into the finest pulp; thereafter, add a little wine so that it floats slightly on top, and put it in a jug; let it boil well-sealed for ten hours in a boiler. Then take it out and crush everything well together and strain it through a cloth. Then, whatever has passed through, mix with honeycomb (separated) or with butter, and put it back into a jug as before, so that it mixes well together. Then, while it is warm, strain it again through a cloth with a press; then set it with an <term>alembic</term> <note>A distillation apparatus; here used to allow moisture to evaporate under solar heat</note> in the sun so that the moisture evaporates. Then seal it well and let it stand in the sun; keep it thereafter. Thus the juice and power come out perfectly into the honey and butter, and you may certainly expect a proper healing in all wounds, as these are agreeable to nature and do not provoke complications. For such ointments, comfrey, birthwort, the simple adder’s tongues, earthworms, and wintergreen are the best ingredients above all others.

<margin>C</margin> Beyond what the common man has discovered in using honey and butter, other types of wound-ointments have been discovered by those who see resin flowing out of trees, taking the resin for the body. Now, there are many kinds of resin, such as resin of the fir and resin of the larch; likewise, there are gums, and according to what each land could provide, it prepared its own wound-ointments, which are perfect and certain arts. And it is a great wonder that people at that time were so ingenious and sensible that they pursued such arts so that they might maintain a healthy body. Now it is necessary that I show you several of these recipes, so that subsequently everyone may take that which grows in his own land and arrange it into an ointment.

<margin>X</margin> Such recipes are as follows: In German lands, there are only two excellent resins: one from the fir trees, and the other from the larch trees. For the one from the larch trees, a recipe follows:
Take one pound of larch resin, twenty egg yolks, beat and whip them well together until a yellow ointment is made; into this, place one <term>lot</term> <note>Approx. 15-18 grams</note> of finely crushed comfrey, two lots of crushed birthwort, and one and a half lots of barley meal; whip it all together and make it into an ointment. With this ointment, you heal every wound, even without the powders.

Another recipe for fir resin: Take half a pound of fir resin that is pure and clear, let it melt gently over a coal, and put into it a little beef marrow, stirred vigorously together; thereafter, crush it in a warm mortar with enough comfrey so that it becomes one; bind the wounds with this, or use earthworms and the like.

After these arts, the wax-ointment arose, in which wax and resin were mixed together and tempered with oil into an ointment, and into these were also put the wound-herbs and roots, as often mentioned above. However, the art of fir resin is the least suited for wounds, being more useful for open sores <note>Refers to ulcers or chronic skin lesions rather than fresh trauma</note>; therefore, I do not mention such ointments much here.

You should also know that it is not necessary to set down many kinds of recipes, since it is sufficient for everyone to understand that the trick lies solely in this: that the wound-herbs and wound-roots should be united with honey and butter, and subsequently increased in their powers in the sun, so that the <term>feces</term> <note>The solid waste or dregs left over after extraction</note> are separated from the good. In this, everyone should strive to take the best wound-herbs he can find.

### C A P V T  IV.

->On the Preparation of Wound Oils and Wound Balms.<-

Thus, among the ancients, wound oils were commonly found, apart from the invented medicines; and subsequently, through the alchemists, the wound balms were found. For when the ancients saw the wound-salves, they took those same ingredients that they had put into honey or butter and placed them into oil, making a trial to see if the medicine would unite with the oil, as indeed happened. Then the common practice spread, so that wound oils were used generally and the other aforementioned medicines fell out of use. And their practice with the wound oil was such that they first washed the wounds with wine, and afterwards smeared them with the oil, and thus healed the wounds. Christ also spoke of this art when he mentioned the Samaritan in Jericho <note>The biblical Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:34), who poured oil and wine on the traveler's wounds</note>, how he served that same wounded man: Therefore, this same art of oils is an ancient, inherited art that was held in great honor for a long time. After this, the alchemists arose and wondered whether distilled oils would be better than raw ones, and mixed those same ingredients into distilled oil. Subsequently, they used these instead of wound oils and changed the name because of the distillation, calling them "Balm." Now, it is no less true that there is some difference between distilled and raw oil: However, I find through experience that distilled oil should not be "brick oil" <note>Oleum lateritium; a traditional distilled oil made by heating bricks soaked in oil</note>—that is, according to the practice of the alchemists—but should be according to the practice where the oil is distilled without any additives, through a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass or ceramic vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>. And as soon as it begins to change color, from the oil-color into a redder one, and as soon as the <term>spirits</term> <note>The volatile vapors</note> begin to emerge, one should stop; thus the taste and color of the true oil remain nearly intact. This oil you shall take if you wish to make balm for wounds. Know also that the alchemists have similarly distilled turpentine and placed herbs into it: There is also a <margin>C</margin> fault in that place, namely this: that turpentine, when it is distilled, is too hot and "subtle" <note>In this context, too volatile or sharp</note> to encourage flesh to grow in wounds. Therefore, it should also be distilled like the oil, so that it remains in its color and also in its natural taste: Now you may make a wound balm from it, and it is more useful for wounds of the veins and tendons than the other oils or balms.

Furthermore, many things have been tried: Gums have been distilled, also resins, also wax: But in none has usefulness been found. Therefore, the practice remains only in oil and distilled oil, and also in turpentine and distilled turpentine, of which several recipes follow hereafter.

A recipe that serves for the oil and turpentine, raw or distilled: Take one pound of the <term>Corpus</term> [the base oil], chamomile flowers, red roses, self-heal flowers <note>Prunella vulgaris</note>, a handful of each; three handfuls of <term>Hippericon</term> <note>St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum)</note> flowers; flowers of centaury, flowers of celandine, half a handful of each. Mix it together and let it stand in the sun until two months have passed. With this oil or balm, you heal wonderful things without pain or any aching. You may also well press out such oil the following year and fill it with a new composition, and deal with it as stands above. For its virtue is not enough to be praised, whether you take oil or turpentine, distilled or raw.

Another composition: Take simple adder's tongue, the small wintergreen, agrimony, sanicle, a handful of each; two handfuls of <term>Hippericon</term> flowers; half a handful of boiled comfrey; one hundred cleaned earthworms: Pour the <term>Corpus</term> [the base] over it, let it stand in the sun so that it digests until its time; then use it in wounds; it heals all wounds without pain and aching.

You may also well put into such oils <term>Mummia</term> <note>Bitumen or a medicinal preparation made from ancient remains, thought to have great healing powers</note>, mastic, myrrh, and frankincense, though not too much. For the wound oils and balms have their joy only in herbs and flowers, and most of all in flowers: And the noblest flower is <term>Yppericon</term> [St. John's Wort]. Often gum is also put into it; it is

## Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.
<sig>C ii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> It is a folly to use things like <term>verdigris</term><note>original: "Spangrün"; a green pigment/poison formed on copper</note>, copper ash, or iron filings; such things are not to be praised, for those self-invented doctors only cause pain with such items.

Furthermore, it is a point well worth noting: from the same herbs whose flowers you use in your oil, you may also take the seeds. Crush them and add them to the oil after the herbs and flowers have finished their <term>digestion</term><note>A process of steeping ingredients in gentle heat to extract their properties</note>. If you keep this mixture warm throughout the winter, it produces a much stronger and better oil.

A recipe for a wound oil or balm is made as follows: Take half a pound of olive oil, a <term>quarter-measure</term><note>original: "Vierling"</note> of turpentine, and as many St. John’s wort flowers as will fill the vessel. Add a third part of mullein flowers and pour over this one and a half measures of good white wine. Let it boil until the wine has evaporated, then place it in the sun for the required time. You can speak highly of this oil; wherever you use it, you will no longer be shamed by failure.

Likewise, the recipes written for turpentine may also be used in oil, or the two can be mixed together or boiled with wine, as stated above.

Furthermore, as one art follows another, the art of making <term>varnish</term><note>In this context, a resinous protective coating for wounds</note> was discovered, made with yellow <term>amber</term><note>original: "Augstein"</note>. Those who first made this varnish tested it on various injuries, specifically on women's breasts and various types of holes or deep wounds, which were healed by it. When this was seen, they took the varnish and infused it with the aforementioned flowers and herbs, letting it digest in the sun for the proper time. Although it takes longer to prepare, it is remarkably praiseworthy and has a great effect—not only on wounds and stabs but also on open sores. Following this, an addition is made to the varnish if it is to be used as medicine: three times as much <term>mastic</term><note>A resin from the mastic tree</note> as there is varnish should be added, and half as much myrrh and frankincense.

<margin>B</margin> Also, while the varnish is in the process of digestion, <term>mummy</term><note>original: "Mumia"; refers to preparations made from mummified or preserved human remains, believed to have potent healing powers in early modern medicine</note> should be added to it, according to the requirements of the composition.

You should know that when varnish is boiled out of wound oil—as described above—boiled down with wine and then prepared with amber, mastic, etc., its power to heal is great and extremely potent.

Similarly, common folk later made attempts using marrow from bones and animal fats instead of oils and turpentine. They searched through various marrows until they found that deer marrow was the best. They took this—or used children's marrow in its place—and mixed it with the flowers and herbs mentioned before, letting it stand in the sun. These also became wound oils, and they eventually found that human marrow was the most useful of all.

They also tested animal fats, taking them along with those same flowers and herbs to make wound oils, with which they certainly and perfectly healed all wounds. Among animal fats, hen fat and capon fat were judged to be the best; but above all, human fat is the best. Among the fish in the water, no useful fat was found except for <term>grayling fat</term><note>original: "Eschenschmaltz"; fat from the grayling fish</note>, which also yields a noble wound oil.

A varnish may also be made from distilled oil or turpentine, in the same way the addition was shown before; this is a subtle varnish that is more capable and effective than the raw varnish.

And although there are many recipes for balms and oils of which I show few, you should know that I have provided the best recipes, with which I can reassure and comfort you. Thus, you may arrange and make recipes yourself according to the nature of your own land, following the order shown in this chapter.

---

### C A P V T  V.

->On the healing of wounds through things that keep a wound clean and pure, and are thus healed thereby.<-

<margin>C</margin> Since nature itself carries a balm within it by which it heals wounds, and henceforth it is only necessary to keep the wounds clean and pure, it is right that I also show this method. Take this example: a dog that is struck may lick itself, and the wound heals because the dog cleanses it, and thereafter nature heals it herself. Since this example is seen in the dog, it has also been applied to humans, who have licked wounds on their hands just as dogs do, and thus they were healed. But as humanity became increasingly "unclean," they began washing wounds with spring water, and many were healed through this, especially flesh wounds. However, because spring water easily caused the wounds to smell and required frequent washing, the people grew weary of it and thought further on such cleansing. They took wine, but it was not effective enough for large wounds. Next, they came to use salt, so that they salted the water well and washed the wounds with it; this practice became common. They also healed all the wounds of injured cattle with it. But in time, this practice was also abandoned, and other cleansers were made, some of which I will list hereafter.

They took wound-herbs and boiled them in wine or water, added salt, and washed the wounds often, laying crushed honeycombs over the wounds instead of a plaster.

Likewise, they took <term>elecampane</term><note>original: "Alant"; a medicinal plant often used for respiratory and skin issues</note> and dissolved it in water, adding a little <term>white vitriol</term><note>original: "Galtzenstein"; zinc sulfate, used as an astringent and antiseptic</note>, and healed wounds in that manner.

Such an art was much dearer to them than the invented medicines of the sophist doctors, with which they have ruined people. This should not be omitted from being shown. But I wish to instruct you further on one thing that necessity requires: to adopt a different order for yourself, as shown in other chapters, because so many complications befall mankind. These cannot be prevented through this simple order.
<margin>B</margin>
Where, however, complications are not to be feared, you may well use the order of this chapter: so that you do not fall into the "over-art" of the fictitious masters. Better to be healed slowly and well <term>closed</term><note>original: "erschossen"; literally "shot through," referring to the successful granulation or knitting together of the wound.</note>, than to be slowly ruined with "over-arts." Furthermore, these simple methods cannot help in great wounds, unless the person had a completely healthy <term>complexion</term><note>original: "Complex"; the constitutional balance of the body's humors or elements.</note>, such as existed at the beginning of the world; it is no longer so now, but henceforth necessity requires one to act more earnestly.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the preparation of stitch and wound plasters, how they are wonderfully discovered in their effect.

Although this chapter is made with foreign items and not from those that grow in this land and are well-known—nevertheless, since one land may be helpful and useful to another, and since an innate friendship has been ordained by God, it is proper that the benefits of other foreign lands, which may come to us through them, be described. Following this is the foundation and essence of the experienced and proven art and virtue of <term>plasters</term><note>Medicinal bandages or dressings.</note>, and how they should be made: and you should know that great complications are driven away by them. And since so much befalls mankind, it is proper that one also has greater diligence to establish the medicine more thoroughly and provenly. Although it is no less true that a wound is easy and slight to heal, and for the sake of healing alone it would not be necessary to reveal these plasters to you: yet because no misfortune comes alone, but falls together in heaps, I wish to show such things for that reason. Although it is also true that with other items that grow in our lands, complications may be prevented:
<margin>C</margin>
I place those in the "small wound-medicine," and here I shall only present the <term>stitch plasters</term><note>original: "Stichpflaster"; specifically for puncture wounds, such as those from swords or thorns.</note>. As the origins of several medicines are recounted, many kinds of arts have been found by craftsmen who made trials with their tools and the materials they handle. For example, the <term>tinkers</term><note>original: "Keßler"; itinerant menders of kettles and metalware.</note> have stopped blood with <term>copper scale</term><note>original: "Kupfferschlag"; the flakes that fly off copper when it is hammered.</note>, and also dried out weeping wounds with it. Likewise, the smiths handled wounds similarly with burnt iron (which is called <term>Crocus Martis</term><note>original: "Crocus Martis"; literally "Saffron of Mars," an alchemical term for iron oxide or rust.</note>). Likewise, the potters also had experience in this way with <term>litharge of silver or gold</term><note>original: "Silber oder Goldglett"; lead oxide produced during the refining of precious metals, used as a drying agent in plasters.</note>. There are many such items that man has wonderfully discovered, and thus it was called an <term>experiment</term>. Many kinds of experiments were also experienced through the alchemists, who try many things and many things come to their hands, which are not necessary to describe here, such as <term>minium</term><note>original: "Myni"; red lead.</note>, <term>white lead</term><note>original: "Bleyweiß".</note>, and the like. In such times, the philosophers also intervened and described such power and nature. In their writings, it happened that all kinds of medicinal powers were described and brought to the point that they put several items together so that many pieces came together into one body. Thus it happened that they took wax and oil together and boiled them, and thus made plasters out of them. But when it did not have excellent utility in itself, they added sometimes <term>minium</term>, sometimes <term>white lead</term>, sometimes <term>calamine</term><note>original: "Galmey"; a zinc ore.</note>, sometimes <term>iron rust</term><note>original: "Eisenrost".</note>, sometimes <term>copper ash</term><note>original: "Kupfferaschen"; copper oxide.</note>, sometimes <term>litharge</term>, etc., and boiled them together, from which a <term>cerate</term><note>original: "Cerot"; a stiff ointment or plaster made primarily of wax.</note> was made, which they allowed to be spread on cloths. And they saw that it <term>healed well</term>. They also further learned the property of gums, that they draw to themselves, and also of the <term>magnet</term>, and thus they added those items to the cerates, subsequently finding them better than before. Furthermore, they had a wound powder, such as <term>mastic</term><note>original: "Mastix"; a resin from the mastic tree.</note>, <term>frankincense</term><note>original: "Weyrauch".</note>, <term>myrrh</term>, etc.; they also added these, and they became better than before. And thus they thought of improvement further and further, until the stitch plasters were brought into a certain order,

<margin>A</margin>[These remedies] are <note>OCR text reads "Amen," likely a transcription error for "Arzneyen" (medicines) or "Namen" (names/ingredients).</note> those through which wonders are worked. Now, how these should be prepared according to the proper order, I set forth in the following, regardless of the false recipes of the <term>fictitious doctors</term><note>original: "erdichten Artzt"; Paracelsus's derogatory term for university-trained physicians who relied on ancient texts rather than practical experience.</note> who could not bear that the common people should know so much. They have despised these methods and judged them useless, replacing them with other recipes through which they have acted wickedly. Yet they have so cloaked their own failures that people have always preferred their destruction over the true art of the non-fictitious doctors. Since such recipes are now rightfully coming to light, it is only proper that they should not be kept secret: for medicine should not belong only to the fictitious doctors but should be known to all who are outside of their deceit. For medicine was not created by God for the purpose of hoarding great treasures, but for the sake of helping the sick. For they heal wounds that are often too difficult for other medicines. Therefore, read the order that follows for making <term>puncture plasters</term><note>original: "Stichpflaster"; plasters specifically designed for deep, narrow wounds like those from stabs or arrows.</note>, and the same in more than one way, and yet all are useful and proven.

It has been a common practice to make the first plasters in this manner: Take one pound of wax, a <term>quarter-pound</term><note>original: "Vierling"</note> of <term>Greek pitch</term><note>original: "Griechisch Bech"; also known as colophony or rosin.</note>, and melt the pitch and wax together. And when it has melted, put these powders into it while it is not too hot: take small pieces of <term>carnelian</term><note>original: "Carniel"</note>, red and white corals, <term>magnets</term><note>lodestones</note>, <term>calamine</term><note>original: "Galmey"; a zinc mineral used in skin treatments.</note>, one <term>loth</term><note>An old German unit of weight, roughly 1/2 ounce or 15 grams.</note> of each; yellow <term>amber</term><note>original: "Augstein"</note>, mastic, incense, one and a half loth of each; myrrh, <term>mummy</term><note>original: "Mumien"; a common but controversial medicinal ingredient of the era made from preserved remains, believed to have healing properties.</note>, three loth of each; all finely ground and well-mixed together, and stir them into the previously melted mixture. And when it is well mixed together, add three loth of turpentine and stir it until it cools. Afterward, <term>knead</term><note>original: "beeren"; to work or mold the plaster by hand.</note> it well between your hands with <term>ash-fat</term><note>original: "Eschenschmaltz"; likely a prepared animal fat or ointment base.</note>, and it will become a plaster with which you may accomplish wonderful things, not only in wounds but also in other open injuries of the body.

<margin>B</margin>Another plaster made in this fashion: Take two pounds of virgin wax, one pound of Greek pitch, a quarter-pound of turpentine. Let these pieces melt over a gentle fire, and put into it six loth of crushed mastic, three loth of yellow amber; let it stand over a gentle fire for a quarter of an hour. Then take four loth of mummy, incense and myrrh, one loth of each, three loth of <term>hepatic aloes</term><note>original: "Aloepaticum"; a medicinal aloe resin.</note>. Mix these together, finely crushed, and stir them into the aforementioned plaster; stir it until it becomes cold. Then knead it again with ash-fat and add one loth of crushed <term>camphor</term><note>original: "Gaffer"</note> until they become plasters. With this puncture plaster, you heal every stab wound.

Another description of the most powerful plaster of this kind, with which you may draw out bullets, arrows, and whatever else might be broken off or lost in stabs and the like, and which cannot be mastered by the plasters mentioned above. Take one pound of wax, <term>colophony</term><note>pine resin</note>, and <term>shoemaker's pitch</term><note>original: "Schusterschark"</note>, a quarter-pound of each; melt them together and put in four loth of <term>gum ammoniac</term><note>original: "Gummi Armoniaci"</note>, two loth of <term>bdellium</term><note>a semi-translucent oleo-gum resin</note>, ten loth of finely crushed magnet, six loth of yellow amber; mix them together and knead it with <term>egg oil</term><note>oil extracted from hard-boiled egg yolks</note>. Thus you have a plaster that is to be used only for great needs. Also for the closing of wounds. Also, when wounds are corrupted, it is a wonderful help.

Furthermore, there is another kind of which was spoken at the beginning, the order of which is in this form. Take oil, wax, and rubbed <term>litharge</term><note>original: "Goldglett"; lead monoxide, traditionally used to help dry and heal wounds.</note>, one pound of each; melt them and boil them together so that a <term>cerate</term><note>original: "Cerot"; a stiff ointment made of wax and oil.</note> is made from it. How this is done is not necessary to write; it is well enough known. Now that this is done, there follow several additives that you may add among them as you wish; each one is proper.

<margin>C</margin>The first additive is this: Take gum ammoniac and bdellium, one loth of each; <term>galbanum</term> and <term>opopanax</term><note>original: "Galbanum Oppoponacum"; two types of aromatic plant resins.</note>, one and a half loth of each; dissolve them in vinegar and boil them, strain them, boil them again into a plaster, and add that to the aforementioned cerate. When that is done and they are united, then add these powders: calamine, red and white corals, magnets, three loth of each; incense, mastic, two loth of each. When they are well mixed together, add six loth of turpentine and one loth of dill oil; knead it into a plaster, as is the custom, with ash-fat or otherwise.

The other additive: Take a quarter-pound of opopanax and purify it well as stated above, put it into the mentioned cerate until it is well united. When that is done, add six loth of mummy, four loth of <term>birthwort</term><note>original: "Holwurzen"</note>, mastic, incense, myrrh, one loth of each. Afterward, add a quarter-pound of turpentine, two loth of laurel oil, half a loth of camphor; knead it with chamomile oil.

Or add this additive: Ten loth of prepared gum ammoniac, six loth of colophony, two loth of <term>ship's pitch</term><note>original: "Schiffbech"</note>, incense, mastic, one and a half loth of each, two loth of myrrh, eight loth of turpentine; subsequently knead it with laurel oil.

Thus you have the processes and order of how the puncture plasters are made in two ways, and how they were discovered by the craftsmen, and so passed from one to another. And follow such practice, for you cannot learn anything better from the fictitious doctors, and let them scream and do as they will. You may also easily ordain your own recipes according to this kind on your own.

Furthermore, note that through experience I have encountered better puncture plasters that more powerfully prevent all complications, healing quickly and well, and the description of them is this: Take one and a half pounds of virgin wax, one and a half pounds of wound-oil, one pound of litharge, half a pound of calamine. From these, make a cerate; into this cerate put half a pound of <term>varnish</term><note>original: "Firniß"</note> tempered with herbs, a quarter-pound of turpentine prepared according to the type of wound, but let it boil into a cerate. Afterward, put gum into it, then the powders from whichever aforementioned description you wish, and make it into a plaster, kneading it with wound-balsam for as long as it takes to achieve the right form.

### C H A P T E R VII.
### Concerning Puncture and Wound Powders, through which every wound may be healed.

<margin>B</margin>The <term>binding powders</term><note>original: "Hefftpulver"; from "heften," meaning to fasten or stitch. These were powders believed to chemically "stitch" a wound together.</note> received their name from snakes, and in this manner: it once happened that snakes, which had been cut in two, used certain herbs to bind the pieces back together. These same herbs were called <term>Adder’s Tongue</term><note>original: "Naterzungen"; the plant Ophioglossum, named for its appearance and its legendary healing properties.</note>, with which they made themselves whole again. Because two pieces were thus fastened together, the powders took the name "binding powders." Furthermore, it was understood that severed hands, arms, and legs could be put back together just like the snake. They did not consider that there is a different essence in a snake than in a human. For that which falls from a human has no more life; but that which is cut from a snake still has a long life thereafter—it cannot be denied whether both pieces might be healed together during such life. There is also a common understanding that snakes fasten and heal themselves through their own licking; it is also quite believable that they chew the juice of herbs and thus bind themselves. For God has given nature a wonderful knowledge that one must allow to exist.

When this knowledge came among the <term>artists</term><note>original: "Künstler"; here meaning skilled surgeons or medical practitioners.</note>, they attempted to do many things in this manner for human needs. But what had been cut off could never be put back: for the dead and the living accept no union. No one should even think of attempting such a thing. However, while the artists pursued such "snake-herbs" but could not reach the root of the matter, it was discovered that the skins that snakes shed are very healing, provided both parts of the wound are alive. From this, it can be gathered that the snake heals itself through its own skin, if it were time to shed it. It is further to be thought that where they heal together, it happens more without herbs than with herbs, for nature has the <term>balsam</term><note>original: "Balsam"; in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to the body's internal, innate healing power.</note> within itself. But from such an essence, the artists first held snake skins to be a binding powder <margin>C</margin> for stabs and wounds, for they could find no herbs that had such an effect within them. Later, they also took up other things through which they could bind wounds and punctures. At that time, <term>suturing with needles</term><note>original: "Nadelhefften"; the practice of sewing a wound shut.</note> had not yet arisen. But when it did arise, such wound and puncture powders were abandoned, and faith was placed in needle-suturing.

But because suturing does not always result in good, the artists thought further on how binding powders might be made that would drive both flaps of a wound together, so that they might stand against each other, just as one might push back together two pieces that had fallen apart from a saw. Thus, over a long time, certain powders and certain juices were found, along with other things that drew the wounds together so that both parts touched one another. When such closeness is achieved, nature can act upon the whole wound. But where such closeness cannot be achieved and the wound must be healed by other medicines—such as wound-drinks, ointments, oils, or plasters—nature can work no further than at the very bottom, where she binds it together with daily labor until she reaches the top. The puncture and wound powders, however, draw the top, the middle, and the bottom together equally; thus, a uniform effect can occur above, in the middle, and below.

One should also know that where puncture and wound powders are used, there must first be no swelling, no bleeding, no heat, and no hardness; rather, a mild, delicate, and natural softness must be present, otherwise the two parts cannot pull together. Therefore, be sure that you first know how to remove those complications. Continuously, while you use the puncture and wound powders, do not allow any swelling or heat to occur: for heat and swelling will tear the parts away from each other again. Although it is a fast healing—and indeed almost the fastest of all—you must be very well-guarded against the aforementioned complications.

<margin>A</margin>Now, the nature of these powders is such that they draw things together through their inherent dryness; such is the case with **Armenian Bole**, which, because of its dryness, binds together whatever it touches. Furthermore, there are other substances that draw things together aside from dryness, such as the juice of unripe sloes <note>The small, bitter fruit of the blackthorn tree, known for its extreme astringency.</note>. Then there are also certain items that glue things together, such as <term>Tragacanth</term><note>original: "Tragantum"; a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of legumes, used as a binding agent.</note>. According to these three types, all binding powders are made. It should also be noted that one should not only consider the ingredients that perform the binding, but also ensure that a medicine is added which provides nourishment to the body’s own <term>natural balsam</term><note>In Paracelsian medicine, "balsam" refers to an internal healing fluid or life force that naturally repairs the body.</note>. Thus are binding powders made and used, for which I set down three types of recipes here, following the three ways mentioned.

Take one quarter-pound of true <term>Armenian Bole</term><note>original: "Bolum Armenum"; a red medicinal clay used since antiquity as an astringent.</note>; dissolve it in <term>alum water</term><note>Water containing alum, a mineral salt used to shrink tissues and stop bleeding.</note> and distill the liquid away from it; pour fresh water over it and distill it away again. Do this as often as necessary until the Bole becomes an oil; then dry it in the sun. To this powder, add two <term>Loth</term><note>An old Germanic unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of Frankincense, one Loth of Carnelian, and half a Loth of **Mummy** <note>original: "Mumia"; in historical medicine, this referred to powdered remains of mummies or bitumen, believed to have potent healing powers.</note>. Mix this into a powder and sprinkle it into the wounds twice every day, and bind it as is the custom. A <term>puncture plaster</term><note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a plaster designed to seal deep, narrow wounds.</note> placed over it is good, for it protects the wound from "accidents" <note>original: "Zufall"; in this context, medical complications like infection or swelling.</note> such as swelling, heat, or hardening.

Regarding this oil, when it dries into a powder, know that it binds things together miraculously like a glue. The same is true for the <term>Oil of Saturn</term><note>original: "Oel vom Saturno"; a preparation made from lead.</note>, and the <term>Oil of Crocus of Mars</term><note>original: "Oel vom Croco Martis"; a reddish powder or oil derived from iron oxide (rust).</note>, as well as from copper rust. No faster healing has ever been discovered, and they are to be greatly praised, for complications do not have time to arise.

<margin>B</margin>Furthermore, take the juice of unripe sloes and boil it until it appears as a thick <term>electuary</term><note>original: "Latwerg"; a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note>. Likewise, boil unripe gallnuts, an equal amount of each, and then add an eighth part of finely crushed <term>comfrey</term><note>original: "Walwurz"; a herb famous for its ability to "knit" bones and flesh back together.</note>. Take a distilled water of <term>elecampane</term><note>original: "Alandwasser"; a medicinal root used for various ailments.</note> and boil them all together. Then take it and set it in the sun; let it dry into a powder, and use it as is the custom.

When sloe juice is taken, dissolved in elecampane, and <term>coagulated</term><note>Thickened or solidified from a liquid state.</note> and subsequently powdered, it becomes a binding powder that cements things together like glue. But you should not use this without a puncture plaster, in order to prevent complications.

I have spoken of Tragacanth as an example, yet I do not know how to make a binding powder from it alone. However, I have taken the <term>cement</term><note>original: "kütt"; a strong adhesive or putty.</note> of stonemasons and also that of carpenters, with which they glue things even under water, and I have bound wounds with it. Although not in the form of a powder, but in the form of an ointment, and with a puncture plaster placed on top, it has healed wounds miraculously. But instead of the glue-oil, I used a wound oil made from linseed oil; and instead of lime, I used burnt <term>white coral</term>; I also used <term>casein glue</term><note>original: "Keßleyn"; a strong adhesive made from cheese curds and lime.</note> in the same manner, which does not allow the wound to pull apart. Yet, do not use it without the puncture plasters. These must be "water-cements" that harden and bind in water, in the **Egyptian manner** <note>A reference to ancient builders or embalmers known for creating permanent, waterproof bonds.</note>. Since wounds are moist, the cement must be of a kind that works in moisture.

Although there are still many kinds of wound and puncture plasters made in various ways, there is no special art in them, which is why I have no desire to describe them. Yet I will add a few, which you may use in times of need: Take Frankincense, Myrrh, and Mastic, one Loth of each; half a Loth of Red Coral; four Loth of **Aloe** <note>original: "Aloepaticum"; a bitter plant resin used for cleansing and healing.</note>. Mix these and make a powder, and add it to half the portion of whichever of the two aforementioned binding powders you prefer.

<margin>C</margin>Another binding powder: Take the juice of unripe sloes, unripe gallnut juice, sanicle juice, wintergreen juice, and the juice of common viper's bugloss, ten Loth of each. Let these items dry in the sun, and when they are half-dried, add four Loth of prepared **Gum Ammoniac** <note>original: "Gummi Armoniaci"; a medicinal gum resin with a balsamic odor.</note> and let it dry into a powder. You should also know that you must keep the patient dry and sustain them with less food and moisture.

There are also several other substances that bind things together; but since they arise from **Alchemy**, they will follow later in their own chapter.

### *CHAPTER VIII.*
#### On the Healing of Wounds through Heavenly Influence, which is related to us in both good and evil ways.

Certain arts have also been discovered by the first **Astronomers**, who demonstrated miraculous effects through the heavenly power of the firmament. Now, however, this same art has declined since the passing of the first **Magi** and has fallen into such ignorance that nothing of this art is known anymore. The art is one of heavenly <term>impression</term><note>The process by which celestial or spiritual qualities are "impressed" or stamped into physical matter.</note>, such that the heavenly influence was brought into a physical body, through which body the influence of the stars was accomplished. Just as in the seed of a rose, there is the power and property of the rose, and yet the rose is not there, and the effect is similar. But when it is sown in the earth by man, or planted, then the rose grows forth along with its powers and properties. In the same way, there are also heavenly seeds, which through the **Magical** art were planted and sown into the stones that people call <term>Gamahé</term><note>Stones believed to be naturally marked with images of the stars or to have fallen from heaven, possessing occult powers.</note>. There is no other way to naturally understand it than this: just as a seed falls from a tree into the earth and becomes a tree through natural action, so the ancient Egyptians and Persians first recognized such power of the heavens and treated its **Influence** <note>original: "Influenz"; the flowing down of "ethereal fluid" or power from the stars to the earth.</note> like a seed in the bodies of the earth, such as in stones. For if the heavens can send down a pestilence and kill a person or cause other such sicknesses, it can also do good just as well. If it can strike a person, it can also strike a stone. He who has knowledge of where its arrow goes, he can...
