...also well escape: For many more [arrows] are shot than are revealed. <margin>A</margin> He who recognizes the nature of the firmament as a <term>Magus</term><note>A practitioner of "natural magic," which in this context means understanding the hidden physical and astrological laws of the universe rather than sorcery.</note>, he may well join and prepare a *Body* into which the <term>Influence</term><note>The invisible "flowing in" of power from the stars and planets believed to affect earthly events and health.</note> shoots, and is thus characterized according to the content of that same arrow. From this, it followed that there were stones among the Egyptians which, when carried, caused those same illnesses of the influence to come upon the person. Likewise, there were also stones which, when carried, protected the person from such illnesses.

In the same way, <term>Gamahi</term><note>original: "Gamahi"; also known as camaieus or chemeia, these were naturally occurring or engraved stones believed to possess talismanic or curative powers due to their celestial signatures.</note> were made, which, marked with crossbows, were good against shooting; some marked with swords were for hacking and stabbing; and many of such kinds, not necessary to recount here.

But the reason I mention it is that stones and the like were also prepared by the <term>Magi</term> so that whoever carried them was cured of fever; others for other illnesses: and not only for bodily diseases, but also wonderfully for wounds, for staunching blood, for <term>limb-water</term><note>likely "Glidwasser," referring to joint fluid or edema/swelling.</note>, gout, for the <term>falling sickness</term><note>original: "Fallen"; a historical term for epilepsy.</note>, and whatever else is necessary for wounds. And in their times, such arts were held in great esteem. However, because all arts have been <term>sophisticated</term><note>Corrupted or made overly complex and false by "sophists"—scholars who value rhetoric over true natural knowledge.</note> by the invented and presumed learned ones, the knowledge of the true foundation has been forgotten, and patchwork has taken its place. Those same stones, however, which still reach us from the ancients, are never again in such power as they were initially. For the heavens are now in a different characteristic than at that time; therefore, they should be made anew.

It is no less true that many books have been written with useless things in medicine, astronomy, and other natural matters, and provided with neither foundation nor wisdom. It would be proper, however, that such arts be considered more than other chatter. This art is called <term>Magia</term><note>Natural Magic.</note>, and because the "naturals" <note>Those who only look at the surface of physical nature.</note> have not understood it, it has been called sorcery. For they brought such power not only into the stones <margin>B</margin> but also into the words, in which words the effect of such power was completed. But because the human being who knows nothing and yet wants to know something always fakes such things, adding crosses and blessings to them, and other such patchwork, it has come to the point that those who did not understand Magic gave their faith to the crosses, conjurations, and blessings, as if it were worked through them, which is not the case. Rather, if the stone or the word was itself rightly <term>constellated</term><note>Created or spoken at a specific time when the alignment of the stars was favorable for that specific purpose.</note> and the Influence imprinted according to its art, then the power was there without any blessing, conjuration, or cross. But with these same things, the witches and hags have let themselves be led astray, and attributed the art to that in which there was nothing.

I must present an example to you, that God gives effects naturally in many ways: through the plants of the earth, one may prepare medicine for all illnesses inside and outside the body, and apply this through the earthly bodies. Likewise, such power of medicine is also in heaven as in the earth, and takes its body in three ways: it works through earthly <term>Corpora</term><note>Physical bodies or substances.</note>, such as through <term>Persicaria</term><note>original: "Persicaream"; a plant also known as smart-weed or water-pepper, used in Paracelsian medicine for its stinging, "fiery" properties.</note>; through stones, such as <term>Gamahi</term>. Secondly, in words, spoken and written, and yet not so that the writing serves above the word; thus also the Persicaria does not serve, but the Influence. Thirdly, the <term>Sidus</term><note>original: "Sidus"; Latin for a star or constellation.</note> also works through faith when it unites with another: and there is no incantation at all, but a natural effect from heaven, only in a different form than the earth has its effect. All of this I will explain more understandably in the *Magica*.

Thus you should also know that no one should wonder at such arts: for the reason is not only that such things may happen with art, but also naturally. For it is then manifest that the <term>Carnelian</term><note>original: "Carniol"; a reddish-orange gemstone.</note> does not have its power from the earth, nor does the <term>Sapphire</term>, likewise other stones, also the <term>Elk</term><note>original: "Ellend"; specifically referring to the elk's hoof, a traditional remedy for epilepsy.</note>. The <term>Unicorn</term><note>Likely referring to the narwhal tusk or "alicorn," highly prized as a detoxicant.</note> does not have its power from itself, but it is poured into it from heaven. Thus there are many such <margin>C</margin> pieces which, when they are carried, show great effects: and all that is outside of earthly powers, solely from above out of the celestial power. From this then arises that such powers are not helpful to every person, but only where the "comparison" <note>The resonance or correspondence between the medicine and the patient's internal state.</note> is found and joined. For not every illness is from heaven, but some are earthly. Where there are now earthly illnesses, they must have earthly medicine. Likewise also the heavenly medicine: from which it then follows that there are many "mis-arts" in medicine, such as for the plague, where the medicine does not always want to help, for the reason that the heaven drives so vehemently, and moreover the medicine is not set against it: therefore it works as much as is possible for the earthly.

You should strive in wound-surgery so that you well recognize such power of the noble stones, also such celestial powers in the herbs, roots, seeds, also in other creatures, and likewise in the words where such effects may happen. For through such pieces, the <term>hooked arrows</term><note>original: "Hackenpfeil"; arrows with barbs that make them difficult to extract.</note> are drawn out, the <term>lodged bullets</term><note>original: "verfallenen Büchsenkugeln".</note>, and other things where the nature of the earth is driven off and can do nothing. And do not let yourself be turned away by the ignorant who say it is a superstition, sorcery, witchcraft, and carry on such vain contempt. Although no less, the cross, conjuration, etc., do not belong to it, therefore one should remove them from it; the power remains. For take an example from the radish: even if the conjuration is not used, it still accomplishes its effect. I did not want to withhold such things from you in the need of wounded people, so that you might strive in such powers. For every perfect gift is from God, and all things are created through him, and without him is nothing; therefore it is wonderful before our eyes. For man has neither advised nor helped in such creation and gifts; therefore it is beyond his understanding.

## CHAPTER IX.
### How certain sublimates and distillates wonderfully heal wounds.

<margin>A</margin>
Although not all things are sufficiently prepared by Nature—and therefore cannot sufficiently demonstrate the power they possess within themselves—the art of **Alchemy** was discovered. Through this art, natural things are prepared and separated so that great virtue and power are brought forth from them. It is now necessary for the surgeon to be as experienced in alchemy as a shoemaker is in his blacking. If he lacks this, he cannot be a perfect physician. Much depends on the preparation: that the bad be separated from the good, and that each thing reaches its highest degree through its preparation. For a thing will not remain exactly as it is, but must be brought higher; one must not act so sluggishly in medicine. For God created medicine, and also the arts of its preparation, so that we should work and not go idle: for in labor we shall nourish ourselves by the sweat of our faces <note>A reference to the biblical labor of humanity in Genesis 3:19</note>. Therefore, we must not abandon the art of **Alchemy**, for eventually, it must be earned through toil.

Since the preparation must now take place, note that there are two kinds: namely, one in <term>sublimation</term><note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid, used to purify substances.</note> and one in <term>distillation</term><note>The process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling that vapor to collect a purified liquid.</note>. Although there are other preparations, for the sake of the items I use for healing wounds, only sublimation and distillation are necessary. I do not set down many such items; not many are in common use, and not many are experienced with them. For as long as doctors defile themselves with "apothecary cooks" <note>A derogatory term for those who follow recipes blindly without understanding the chemical principles.</note> and wish to learn no further foundations, nothing useful has been discovered or brought forth by them. But those who give themselves to Alchemy find many kinds of utility far beyond the recipes of the medical writers. However, because they do not know the properties and nature <margin>B</margin> of diseases, they cannot bring forth much usefulness: for Medicine and Alchemy should always stand together. Therefore, pay further attention to the recipes that are brought to the highest degree and perform wonderful works in the healing of wounds.

It is no less true that in <term>reverberation</term><note>Heating a substance in a furnace where the flame is deflected downward onto the material.</note>, <term>calcination</term><note>Reducing a metal or mineral to powder by heating it.</note>, and <term>dissolution</term>, many virtues and great secrets are found. Those same **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcana"; referring to the hidden "essences" or powerful medicinal spirits within a substance.</note> that come from such preparation are demonstrated in other ways; therefore, here only distillation and sublimation are mentioned.

<term>Antimony</term><note>original: "Antimonium"; a metallic element used in alchemical medicine, often toxic if not prepared correctly.</note> has within it a great and wonderful healing for wounds that are joined with bodily damage, such as <term>fistulas</term>, <term>cancer</term>, <term>the wolf</term><note>original: "Wolff"; a term for gnawing ulcers or lupus.</note>, <term>shingles</term><note>original: "Sirey"; likely referring to sycosis or similar ulcerative skin conditions.</note>, etc. Where such things do not occur, it is not necessary to use it. Since it is, for me, the highest and most proven art for such wounds, and I well believe that no greater, higher, or better item may be found (though everyone's own experience is reserved for them), I judge it to be of great necessity to reveal the art. However, the preparation can hardly be presented—that is, learned through writing—but you must experience it and learn from the alchemists how to bring this Antimony into a blood-red oil, yielding three or four <term>ounces</term><note>original: "Loth"; a historical German unit of weight, roughly half an ounce.</note> from a pound; and its recipe is as follows:

Take three pounds of Antimony, add as much <term>rock salt</term><note>original: "Sal gemmæ"</note> as is pure, and distill it through a retort at the strongest <term>athanor furnace</term><note>original: "Athanar"; a furnace used in alchemy designed to maintain a uniform heat over a long period.</note> for three days and three nights. After that, you will have the red oil, the virtue of which in the aforementioned desperate, incurable wounds cannot be praised enough.

You must go to school for such distillation and learn to distill as a furrier learns his tanning. For it would be a sin, shame, and mockery to smear the porridge into a raven’s mouth and not let him go after it himself. It must be learned from the ground up, and not gained by sitting fat on a cushion.

Furthermore, know also of the <term>sublimates</term>: if you bring <term>copper</term><note>original: "Kupffer"</note> into sublimation, there are no greater virtues in Antimony than are in Copper. But so that you know how to bring it into sublimation, <margin>C</margin> first prepare it through calcination with sulfur, and after that through <term>nitric acid</term><note>original: "Aquafort" (Aqua fortis)</note>, so that it is "eaten up" <note>dissolved</note> and dried out again. Then add twice as much molten salt as there is copper, and sublimate it through the <term>reverberatory furnace</term><note>original: "Reverber"</note>. A green powder will rise, subtle and light. If you wish to heal wounds with it, sow it into the wound and place a plaster upon it; it heals every wound that has been corrupted by bodily damage. These are the main pillars of medicine.

Now, it is no less true that there are many more such virtues which may be prepared from metals and also from ores; only the art of preparation is lacking. Therefore, it is a great grievance that one wants to be a doctor and cannot do what belongs to him. This has brought medicine into contempt, so that I have seen in many places that doctors are held to be the most frivolous of people, and are regarded as if they only deal in deceit. This does not seem unlike them, since they undertake what they neither know nor can do, and have not learned nor wish to learn what they should know by nature—which is innate to a doctor and should be so—excepting the "sophistic Pharisaic" <note>A critique of university-educated doctors who rely on ancient texts rather than hands-on alchemical experience.</note> kind. But my meaning was that everyone should learn so that they become perfect in their art, and undertake nothing before then. For every doctor may become perfect in his gift; therefore, no one should despair of the art. No one should enter it without the art, but should be able to perfectly recognize Nature, and have upright and proven experience in all things belonging to the art. Where this is lacking, no honor is gained, and both the art and the man are despised. You should finally consider being proven in all cases of wounds; do not deal with anything frivolous or with "rag-arts" <note>original: "Lappenkünsten"; refers to makeshift, unscientific, or amateurish patchwork methods.</note>, but with the righteous art, as was mentioned regarding Antimony and <term>Copper</term><note>original: "Venere" (Venus)</note> for the wounds of fistulas, cancer, etc. Likewise in other things. For it is a very great mockery when medicine is available and at hand that could take away an illness, and you know it not and cannot do it; see how mockingly you stand there.

## CHAPTER X.

### On the stanching of blood and what is required for it.

To stop the flow of blood, several points must first be noted: namely, the nature of the veins, the <term>complexion</term> <note>In historical medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person’s health and temperament.</note> of the body, the character of the person, their anger, the time, the hour of the accident, and the specific quality of the wounds. For since even a healthy person encounters accidents and adverse conditions, how much more so a wound that is in distress? For both health and sickness are surrounded by many necessities. If such a complication should occur within the veins, you should know that it is difficult to treat. In such accidents, it often happens that it is impossible to stop the bleeding with any medicines; instead, the area must waste away and drown in its own fluids. Although there are many who think they can master this and drive it away by force, if that happens, another complication arises that is even worse. Therefore, one must consider what is possible for Nature, so that she is not pressured further than is proper.

Regarding this, you should note—as must be known by all doctors—that no disease passes away unless the cause is first removed, along with everything that is not useful to the patient.

If it happens that the bleeding arises from anger, then the anger must first pass away; for Nature accepts no medicine while in a state of anger. If it is caused by unchastity <note>Likely referring to sexual excess or venereal excitement which was thought to "heat" the blood.</note>, it also accepts no medicine until that fire is entirely extinguished. If "fullness" <note>Gluttony or being over-sated with food and drink.</note> is the cause, the patient must become sober. If it results from the overworking of a limb, it must return to rest. There are many such points, and it is not necessary to recount them all; but note where they exist, for that very cause must be removed first of all, and then the stanching of blood will have its power. Likewise, if it were a matter of an astrological constellation driving the blood, it must be allowed to run its course. <margin>B</margin> And where such things are not resolved, it is possible for the wounded person to bleed to death. For who can help one who does not wish it himself? Who can turn away the affairs of anger if the person will not let it go? That which drives the cause must be removed, otherwise no blood can be stopped. For a man who is drunk has his drunken ways strike into his head and rage within it; should it happen that such a person is wounded, that same raging nature would fall into the head following the veins, and it would then rage in the blood just as it does in the head. Now, who can take away a drunken man’s drunken ways? No one. Likewise, there is no one who could stop "drunken blood." The same is to be understood regarding the other points mentioned above. I point this out so that a surgeon knows how to conduct himself in such matters, and does not undertake to do impossible things, but rather acts as an understanding doctor—as one who has knowledge of what is possible for Nature and what is not.

Now, if these conditions exert their power, the surgeon should hold back his arts of stopping blood. He should only stop the blood that flows without the aforementioned causes; for against those causes, no medicine helps—neither burning <note>Cauterization.</note>, nor binding, nor charms hung around the neck, nor <term>characters</term> <note>Magical signs or sigils written on parchment and worn as amulets to stop bleeding.</note>. And even if a stanching were to occur, another complication would arise from it. And where such causes are present, there usually follows the destruction of the limb through <term>wasting</term> <note>Original: "Schweinen," referring to atrophy or the shriveling of the limb.</note>, lameness, and so on. Take this as an example: often veins are struck in the arms, through which the arm becomes lame, wastes away, or sometimes the person even dies. If such a thing happens during a healthy <term>bloodletting</term> <note>Original: "Lässin," referring to the practice of phlebotomy.</note>, how much more so in such a condition? But where such complications do not appear, know that you may well let the blood run according to your judgment. For once a vein is opened, it must lose its "weight" of blood, and it is not useful to stop it until that same weight has flowed out. You must recognize this from your own experience and yield or attend to it accordingly.

However, to give you brief instruction on how the stanching of blood should fundamentally and properly take place—neither too early nor too late—the entire basis is this: the medicine with which you intend to heal the wound should also stop the blood, and you should use no other stanching method. <margin>C</margin> <insert>For that same medicine, if it is of the right foundation—such as wound oil, wound balsam, wound ointments, etc.—stops all blood according to its proper weight, neither too early nor too late. For the greatest secret lies in the medicine knowing how to hit the right measure.</insert> That is to say, a righteous wound medicine, out of its own power, stops all blood once its proper measure has flowed out. And whatever is started in this way is successful. But whatever is forced to stop by methods other than proper wound medicine, many complications follow afterward; therefore, take heed.

It is also no less true that it often happens that a disease lies in the blood; when this disease wants to stir and purge itself through the blood, do not stop it until it is purged—that is, until it lets its blood out. Or perhaps a "hot complexion" is present, raging in a similar way. Such things may indeed be stopped—apart from <term>stanching plasters</term> <note>Original: "Stichpflaster," specialized bandages or medical applications intended to seal a wound and stop hemorrhaging.</note> and similar medicines—through art or others, as some will follow hereafter. Yet the judgment remains with you: whether to stop it or not, according to how the case is shaped. For it is better to stop it if death is expected, even if the alternative is worse; the stanching follows better than death itself, if perhaps a means can be found within it to turn away such complications when they lead toward death. And in all things, see to it that the limbs are kept warm and not in the cold, and that they do not lie without stanching plasters. For through these, the complications are stilled so that they accept the stanching all the sooner. It also happens sometimes that certain veins are particularly more full of blood than others, perhaps swollen like <term>varices</term> <note>Original: "Varices"; Latin for varicose veins.</note> <margin>Varices</margin>. If you encounter such veins, you must let them bleed and have no fear of it; for the reason is that much filth is cleaned away with it.

Therefore, let the stanching plasters for stopping the blood be recommended to you. And even if you have other ways of stopping blood and wish to use them, see that you do not come too late or too early. But where there is a healthy nature—the mild and the pure—it stops itself, and that is the best stanching of all.

Diligently apply good medicine for healing, and the blood will be best stanched according to Nature's will and pleasure.

# Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> It is of great importance to recognize whether the medicine being used is useful and proper; I have organized this chapter based on such knowledge. Although I have often made mention of this before, I have not used it with the same understanding as I do now.

The distinction of this chapter is this: you must take note of the properties of whatever medicine you use. If pain or a "happening" <note>original: "Zufall" — refers to a clinical complication or secondary symptom</note> arises beneath it that is outside the natural, innate manner of healing, you should be careful not to leave that medicine on. For any medicine that permits or causes pain is ripe to be removed. Although the hour and time of the binding <note>the application of bandages and dressings</note> should be maintained according to how the wound digests its nourishment—some early, others late—the common practice is twelve hours. If more or less is required, one must adjust accordingly. I say this because pain can grow out of the disorder of the binding. But if the medicine is not to blame for such pain, you may more easily prevent such harm through diligence. The main thing to consider is that you prevent pain and aching in every way when they are outside the innate nature of the wound; for no matter how they appear, they signify nothing good. As I have often mentioned, no pus <note>original: "Eyter"</note> should grow in the wound, nor any stench. If such things occur, they must be turned away by the medicine. The reason is that the "evil" is overcoming the medicine, and the medicine is not strong enough; therefore, strive for even stronger and better medicine. For if such signs appear at the site, your folly will be recognized. It is also a good practice, as often happens, that wounds change and tend toward worsening; unless the medicine is frequently changed, there will be little rest. Where this worsening occurs, it is an indication of many complications and that another misfortune will follow—unless the medicine departs with goodness and leaves a good end. Otherwise, it will not turn out well if the end is not friendly and successful.

<margin>B</margin> You should also note that you need not wait for many complications with wounds, but rather they should proceed fortunately for you. The same applies to wound drinks <note>original: "Wundtränck" — medicinal potions taken orally to aid healing from the inside</note>, especially when they are made from ingredients that bring peace and rest to all the limbs that make the body restless. Wound salves also have their nature in the binding, in that they wait for the twelfth hour; however, they do not always require exactly twelve hours, but sometimes need to be renewed in the eighth. You should note this with all medicines: whatever seems to you to be adverse or failing, change it and bind with another. Keep watch in case a "filling" <note>likely referring to "filling" a deep wound with tissue</note> or similar necessary help is required, and let that be pursued. This is to say: although the recipes in this treatise contain the best and most proven recipes in all of Europe, it may be that something adverse to the recipes is present that requires necessity—perhaps to provide assistance, but with no great art other than cooling. For I confess that one wounded person is naturally inclined toward wound drinks, another toward wound salves, another toward wound oils and balms, another toward stitch-plasters <note>original: "Stichpflastern" — adhesive plasters used to pull wound edges together</note>, another toward heavenly impressions <note>astrological influences or alchemical signatures</note>, and another toward sublimates and distillates. How each person is naturally inclined should be specifically considered, and one should wonder at it accordingly. Do not think: "Many became healthy with this medicine, therefore this person must also become healthy." For God has created many kinds of medicine because there are also many kinds of people; one should and must yield to such nature.

Thus, understand which medicine is to be given and not given, and how it should be administered. No one should trust solely in the belief that they have hit upon the right hour and time, nor should they fail to consider the properties of the patient and the medicine against each other. Everyone should take care to see how the patient and the medicine unite, and how the nourishment of the wound and the medicine harmonize, so that 
<margin>C</margin> pus, stench, worms, etc., are not encountered at the site. He who binds and acts in this way may peacefully carry out his business there. What further necessity is required will be told in other chapters; experience also provides this, so it is not necessary to write of it. Only these three points—finding the comparison between the patient and the medicine, the binding according to the discharge, and first, according to the presence of pus, stench, and pain—comprehend all things, and further instruction is not needed.

However, if there are stabs or deep wounds in cavities, or if deep pus collects, prevent this with renewal and washing <note>original: "Lavation"</note> in this manner: boil wine, myrrh, and salt together, and spray it into the wound to clean it to the very bottom. Afterward, lay the patient so that the cavity is at the top and not at the bottom, so the pus can sink downward <note>likely meaning to drain out</note> and not be hindered by its own weight and eat into the depths. What else is necessary to know will be provided by experience and the frequently mentioned practice in this writing.

If it happens that a person is wounded and "bad luck" <note>This refers to unfavorable timing or celestial influence.</note> falls upon him, his wound will become all the more unfortunate. For in the same way that a wind blows and we are all within that same wind, it follows that the same wind does more harm to the injured person than to others. Therefore, this is called luck or ill-fortune, an accident or a mishap, etc. It is not that it *must* be so, but rather it happened by chance that good met with good, or two evils met, or evil and good met. To understand this: know that whatever wounds are struck while the moon is in Gemini, Virgo, or Capricorn are the worst when calculating by "luck" <note>Astrological positioning was considered a vital part of "luck" or timing in 16th-century surgery.</note>. ->On the closing of wounds, so that no evil follows hereafter, but they remain<-

It is no less true that every wound is closed, and it is a small art to heal flesh. And yet they all wish to write and set down great books, which are seen in the letters, but not in the art itself.

# Wound Medicine: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> It is only right that such things be mentioned. Now, the most important part of ensuring wounds heal correctly is that a <term>wash</term><note>original: "Lavament"; a medicinal liquid used for cleansing a wound.</note> be prepared, and that the wound be washed with it during the first dressing. That is to say, if any "roots of warts" or similar growths are found, they should be removed and driven away with this wash. These are easily recognized. Thus, with this same wash, pieces of lint should be soaked and laid over the area as far as the "wart" extends until it is consumed. This wash is made of <term>Sal ammoniac</term><note>original: "Sal Armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, often used in alchemy and early medicine for its cleansing properties.</note> which has been <term>sublimated</term><note>A process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then collecting the purified solid that forms upon cooling.</note> with <term>Tartar</term><note>original: "Tartaro"; the potassium bitartrate sediment from wine barrels, used as a chemical reagent.</note> several times and then dissolved into a water on a marble stone. Wherever this water is used, it results in a good closure of the wound, so that such growths never return. To prevent such damage is, in my view, a great matter. Do not think that this sublimated Sal ammoniac is too harsh or intended to destroy in a harmful way; rather, it is mild and the most essential component. I also say this: every practitioner should immediately and as often as possible consider and examine what might be found in a wound that could cause future harm, so that it may be prevented. For merely "healing" is not the whole of medicine; the true art is healing well while guarding against present and future complications.

Furthermore, it is possible that a wound might break open again later and turn into a <term>cancer</term>, <term>fistula</term>, or <term>sirey</term><note>An old term for a corrosive or spreading ulcer.</note>, which can also be prevented while the wound is fresh. The reason is that the "origin" of these diseases is still young and weak; otherwise, it would have broken out in the wound before it was even healed. Therefore, such an origin is easily and effectively removed. This must be done using **green Oil of Vitriol** <note>original: "Oleum Vitrioli"; a form of sulfuric acid, which in early medicine was used in various dilutions to cauterize or "kill" diseased tissue.</note>. When the wound is bathed and washed with this during the first dressings, the origin of the disease is killed and exits the body along with the wound's discharge. You should not be frightened by this <term>pus</term><note>original: "Eyter".</note>. In this way, fistulas, all kinds of cancers, the <term>Wolf</term><note>original: "Wolff"; a term for lupus or any "eating" ulcer that consumes the flesh.</note>, and other types of spreading sores—whether deep or wide—are removed. You should

<margin>B</margin> also strive to have good knowledge of whether such signs lie within the wound or not, so that you overlook nothing. For this reason, you must learn and gain experience; since you do not wish to be a doctor like a "peasant" but rather a Doctor or a Master, you must know these things, or you will accomplish less than the peasant does.

You should have no fear of the green Oil of Vitriol, for it is the fundamental basis that takes away all cancers, fistulas, the "Wolf," etc. He who does not know this, cannot do this, and does not understand this, should not call himself a doctor, for he is not one.

It also frequently happens that after a wound has healed, a <term>flux</term><note>A discharge of fluid or a shifting ailment.</note> settles in over time. This same flux moves into the <term>joints</term><note>original: "Gleichen".</note>, causing gout, limb-aches, and the like, which bring more or less pain according to the weather and the phase of the moon. Commonly, <term>scrofula</term><note>original: "Schweinsücht"; literally "pig-sickness," referring to swellings of the lymph nodes.</note> and other forms of limb paralysis follow. Preventing this can also be done during the healing of the wound, provided the signs are observed through the weather and the moon. That is to say: if during such times the wound becomes more restless than usual, it is a sign that such a complication will come with time. You should treat this with gentle purging using **arthritic pills** <note>original: "Pillulas artheticas"; pills formulated to treat joint pain and gout.</note>, depending on the person’s constitution. Additionally, depending on the circumstances, when the pain makes itself felt, **oil of bricks** <note>original: "Oleo laterino"; a traditional remedy made by distilling bricks soaked in oil, believed to have deep-penetrating warmth.</note> should be poured in warm and the area subsequently bandaged. You should also know how to recognize if other complications are occurring, and learn to prevent them. I have presented the most common complications to be expected in the future, as far as my experience up to this hour has taught me. I do not write or teach anything further than what I have discovered and proven myself. Thus, in this chapter, my concern is that you

<margin>C</margin> prevent future damage that has not yet opened or shown itself, even though the origin is already there. It has often happened that I presented these ideas to <term>barber-surgeons</term><note>original: "Scherern und Badern"; lower-tier medical practitioners who performed minor surgery, hair cutting, and baths.</note>, but being inexperienced, they despised them. Their answer was: "If it comes back later, I’ll take more money and help then." They did not know, could not do, and did not understand the matter, but instead boasted in their lies.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->How a special order and supervision is necessary for punctures or similar<-
->arrow-wounds, more so than is required for common wounds.<-

Although enough has been said regarding punctures, if they should become problematic for no other reason than the medicine being too far from the "bottom" <note>The deepest part of the wound.</note>, this must also be considered. Common wounds allow you to see the bottom, but punctures do not. Therefore, punctures are much more dangerous than open wounds, although this is rarely an issue because **puncture plasters** <note>original: "Stichpflaster".</note> can turn the tide. However, just as not everything that grows on a tree is good—there may be a deformity or a worm-eaten apple—so it is with punctures or wounds where a certain "malice" is inherent, making one more unlucky than another without an obvious cause. This must be specially considered, as it requires more medicine and counsel than others.

Since special counsel is required for such punctures, and once you recognize them, know that they are prevented through two ways: namely, providing a **wound-drink** <note>original: "Wundtranck"; a medicinal beverage intended to heal from the inside out.</note> along with the puncture plaster. Secondly, in addition to using the wound-drink and the plaster in their proper order, you must inject a wash and cleanse it until it runs out clear. This wash should be made from **honey, wine, water, alum, and salt**, etc., taking more or less of each ingredient depending on the situation. Do not worry that I do not write exactly how much of each you should take—

# The First Book of Great Surgery

...you should measure; that is, how much water, how much wine, how much honey, how much salt, how much alum. For <margin>A</margin> if you cannot put such a recipe together, you belong in a general store and are a total failure as a physician.

In addition to what has been mentioned regarding the <term>puncture-plaster</term><note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a medicinal plaster formulated specifically for deep, narrow wounds rather than wide surface wounds.</note>, <term>wound-drink</term><note>original: "Wundtranck"; a medicinal potion ingested by the patient to promote healing from within.</note>, and <term>wash</term><note>original: "Lavament"; a liquid used to irrigate or cleanse a wound.</note>, you should also use wound syringes to reach the very bottom after the wash is finished, and afterward bind the wound with the puncture-plaster. You should also know that giving <term>crab’s eyes</term><note>original: "Krebsaugen"; these are not actual eyes, but small calcium carbonate stones found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine as an antacid or to treat inflammatory conditions.</note> to drink is powerfully useful and helpful in such punctures, and they do not allow decay or other <term>inflammation</term><note>original: "Inflation"; here meaning swelling or a localized infection.</note> to increase. And you should also note that in all dangerous punctures you should act thus, whether they are in the body, in a joint, or wherever they may occur. However, it is no less true that <term>sigils</term><note>original: "Characteres"; symbolic inscriptions or charms believed to channel celestial power.</note> made according to heavenly influence are above all these things, especially in <term>deep hunting wounds</term><note>original: "Waidwunden"; likely referring to serious injuries sustained by hunters, often involving deep penetrations or animal attacks.</note>, for which the nature of the earth may not be as effective.

But if it should happen that the punctures drain downward, according to the way the patient lies, you should provide for it in another way—that is, through the skillful positioning of the patient. For otherwise, it does not require so much labor: because even if one were to use wound-drinks and washes, one cannot drive the fluid back out; it always sinks to the bottom and forms a <term>pool</term><note>original: "Gumpen"; a stagnant collection of fluid or pus inside a wound cavity.</note>, which hinders the medicine from working. Therefore, position the sick person so that the bottom of the puncture is at the top and the entrance is at the bottom. This applies unless there is no such fluid in the punctures, but only the balsam or wound oil. Also, every puncture-plaster heals more gently when draining downwards than upwards.

There is also another complication in punctures, which is that they cause more anxiety to the heart than open wounds, and by their own nature are more prone to danger than wounds. Therefore, be all the more diligent in dispersing clotted blood, as well as maintaining natural bowel movements, and attend more powerfully to the <margin>B</margin> diet, especially when the wounds begin to decay or show a stench. Just as when a <term>wildfire</term><note>original: "Wildfewer"; likely referring to erysipelas or a rapidly spreading gangrenous infection.</note> is about to set in, and the area around the top of the puncture becomes blue and red, and forms hollows as if a hole were about to collapse; then it is time for you to look to it and act as previously shown.

Whatever else happens with punctures outside of what I have mentioned here, you will find the same in the healing of wounds; that is, act with punctures as you would with wounds. For through this process you may safely and truly heal every puncture thoroughly, and have no doubt about it. For God has created the <term>degrees</term><note>In early medicine, the "degree" referred to the potency and specific quality (hot, cold, moist, dry) of a remedy.</note> of medicines as certainly as the splitting of wood, and has provided them with all necessities: therefore, you should have no worry about how they will be healed. Unless it is impossible, like wood that cannot be split because of the knots; that is the fault of a <term>malformation</term><note>original: "Mißgewechs"; a term for physical deformities or a corrupted constitution in the patient that prevents medicine from working naturally.</note>. For where there are malformations, the medicine is "frightened," so that it does not find a suitable person formed according to true nature. Therefore, malformations are a cause for concern: for since they are corrupted by their own nature, what shall the medicine accomplish in them?

### CHAPTER XVII.

->On the management of barbed arrows and other lost iron or other things in wounds or punctures.<-

Regarding barbed arrows that are forced to be pulled backward: this cannot easily happen, for the barbs catch in the flesh. Apart from this catching, many arts are found—as are also included in this treatise—by which everything may be pulled out through the wound through which it entered; only that which catches in the flesh when turning backward <margin>C</margin> remains stuck; for that, no arts have been found by which it may be brought back out. This is also the case with musket balls, which are sometimes shot with force between the <term>bones</term><note>original: "Rhor" or "Rhör"; literally "pipes" or "tubes," often referring to the long bones of the arms or legs.</note>, or into joints, or into the bones, and thus flatten themselves, through which flattening they wedge themselves and strike against the bone. To bring such things out, no art has yet been invented in natural things. Although much is written about herbs and roots that pull things out by their own power, yet that power is only effective if the object does not wedge itself; if it is thus hindered, one should stick to the common medicine, which is more useful.

It is also said that there are roots and herbs which open locks: this is quite laughable, for the reason that it has never been proven. Much is also said about noble stones that pull out whatever is stuck in a wall; it is said no nail is driven so deep that it would not be pulled out: this is also presented mockingly enough. Many such "hunters' tales" are put forward in other sections by the "Herbal Doctor." Much is also said about those things that return with the air: all their power to pull in such a way is just like the magnet, and in this form: it attracts a free and unburdened piece of iron; but if it is wedged or held fast, it will never attract it. So it is with such things, and nothing more.

That some locks have been opened, or similar nails pulled from walls, has happened through the <term>mages</term><note>original: "Magos"; wise men or practitioners of natural and celestial magic.</note>, who compared the magnet of the earth with the magnets of the firmament, and thus pulled nails out of the walls, lifted the latches on doors, and pulled the locks back, according to how the magnet was positioned. By such magnets, such barbed arrows have also been pulled out. Likewise, there are some roots and herbs that have had an attracting power of their own, and subsequently through the mages were also united with the heavenly stars, and then they also pulled things out, as mentioned above regarding the magnet.

# Surgery: The Second Treatise.

<margin>A Magnet.</margin> But it follows from this that while people say every root does this or that, it is not so; nor does every magnet perform the same way. Rather, only those that are <term>constellated</term><note>original: "Constelliert"; refers to objects prepared or harvested at a time when the stars and planets were in a specific, favorable alignment to imbue the object with celestial power.</note> perform these tasks. Furthermore, such things become perishable over time; they die off and come to nothing, just as death exists in all things.

However, regarding the extraction of arrows, bullets, or other such things that have splintered or become lodged, there is only one single counsel: there are certain <term>constellated words</term><note>original: "wörter Constelliert"; these are spoken charms or incantations believed to have physical power when uttered by a practitioner aligned with natural laws.</note> that can pull any arrow out from the <term>flesh</term><note>original: "Test"; an old term for the body or the site of an injury.</note> into which it was shot, using only two fingers. Such words must be present, for we cannot attain these results through other means. The reason for this is that such arts have been suppressed by the lousy <term>Sophists</term><note>original: "Sophisten"; a derogatory term used by the author for university-trained physicians who relied on ancient Greek and Latin texts rather than practical experience and natural philosophy.</note> and despised through their great lack of understanding. Consequently, under the threat of banishment and burning at the stake, no one has dared to use them. Yet these are natural, certain, and proven arts, without any sorcery or devilry. They are instead an art made from the things that God created for the benefit of mankind, so that His wonders might be miraculously sought out. But what He has made for man’s benefit, man rejects, and instead attributes the honor to the Devil. This is how those who know and understand nothing behave.

Where such knowledge is not present, and the cure must happen through <term>medicine</term><note>original: "Arzney"; here referring to physical remedies like ointments or surgery rather than the "constellated" arts mentioned above.</note>, it must all be managed until the wound is widened so that the object strikes nothing as it comes out. Otherwise, it must be cut out, or pushed backward, or shoved all the way through, or broken into pieces with instruments. All of this is handled without mercy. But let happen what must happen; if one is not allowed to learn the true foundation of the art, then let it go as it may. I would just as soon be ashamed to rob God of His honor as those self-proclaimed "saints" think highly of themselves. I consider within myself that I intend to follow the Divine Will more closely <margin>B</margin> than those same "saints" claim to do themselves. With this, I wish to conclude the last chapter of this treatise.

But I must say one more thing: the good medicines I have mentioned in this treatise soothe and soften the wounds, and work so much through their own power (unless the wound is entirely blocked) that they draw the object back out through the same opening by which it entered, without pain or instruments. Therefore, rely upon this, you good, gentle, and righteous physician: so that the wounds are not "angered" <note>original: "erzürnet"; an early medical term meaning the wound becomes inflamed, red, or aggravated.</note> but remain without swelling, these plasters will draw out such embedded or broken weapons of metal or otherwise. But if you choose to work with instruments, worse usually follows, and it rarely turns out well for the patient.

## Conclusion of the Second Treatise.

As I mentioned at the beginning in the preface to this treatise: no one should write unless he holds the truth in his hand and knows the righteousness and foundation of his writing for a certainty. He should not doubt, nor "ween," nor "opine," nor "suppose," nor "hope," but rather possess the truth of the art so that it truly is what he claims it to be. Now, I may well boast that in this "Great Surgery," whatever I propose, maintain, teach, and write, I can testify to by its own works—which provide me with visible evidence of the truth itself. It is a great thing, and highly to be regarded, when a thing proves and validates itself visually. And whoever would not believe me for my own sake will be compelled by the signs to believe my writings. And if you will not believe them, then the works themselves prove that such a person, and not I, is in the wrong. <margin>C</margin> And I praise God that among so many enemies who strike at my hands in the medical art, these things prove and validate themselves, surpassing both the ancient and modern "supposed" doctors who sit upon their academic chairs.

Thus, the teaching of my surgery is such that I do not have a <term>nose of wax</term><note>original: "Wachsene Nasen"; a popular 16th-century idiom meaning something that is easily manipulated or twisted to mean whatever one wants it to mean. The author argues his medicine is based on rigid truth, not flexible theory.</note> before me that I can bend this way and that, but rather a straight path forward. I am also not "sitting in a reed" <note>original: "im Rhor sitzen"; likely meaning to be in a position of ease or to speak hollow words.</note> cutting pipes as I please. Nor am I one who "lets it be" because I "know" it. For the true art of medicine does not tolerate such attitudes, nor can anyone use such excuses in medicine; for the works prove the end result, and they neither can nor will hide the truth. Everything is revealed clearly before all the world when the results come out. This is not a business like that of a man who wins something in the morning and loses it again in the afternoon to win it from another. I say that medicine is no hollow reed and has no nose of wax; it cannot be won with mere chatter, but with works and signs. Now, let us say how the physician ought to be.

Therefore, I may freely speak of my experience: what I have experienced and what the foundation of medicine is, that I have written. If I had wanted to pull the "nose" to the side, I would be found a liar, as many writers are found to be. Although one should not "cast pearls before swine," it is nonetheless to be considered that even if the art comes among many, there will be one among them who will take it up. Health is not granted to everyone, nor is skill granted to everyone. Not everyone sees who has beautiful eyes; not everyone hears who has beautiful ears. God knows where He shall draw all things. Many ore mines are found, but only the smallest part of people take the profit and treasure from them. God is the one who distributes all things, and it shall remain according to His distribution. The righteous physician will be found righteous; he to whom medicine is not given will be sensed in his falsehood. Without praying, nothing will be given to anyone; without seeking, no one will find anything; without knocking, it will be opened to no one. But what those have, who neither pray, nor seek, nor...

Therefore, I have now completed this treatise with the secrets that I have experienced and learned over a long time. And it is no less true that now there are so many frivolous people from the Pharisaic crowd <note>Paracelsus frequently uses "Pharisee" as a derogatory term for university-trained doctors who followed strict, ancient rules rather than observing nature.</note>, who are always inclined to please people and gain favor with them, hanging their cloaks according to the wind in whatever way they can. These same <term>Hypocrites</term><note>original: "Gleisner"; refers to those who put on a false, "shining" outward appearance of knowledge to hide their ignorance.</note>, whenever they get hold of a single successful experiment, they stretch it out at length and adorn their hypocrisy with it; they want to be seen as experienced in all arts and wise in all faculties, saying there is nothing under the sun in which God has not enlightened them. These Hypocrites and Pharisees have written something on medicine and made books: and I am still waiting for a book that some lowly hypocrite has not merely patched together. It is a great thing with these Hypocrites; there is nothing they do not ruin, or at least attempt to ruin, except for woodcutting, blacksmithing, carpentry, and other such labors. For the Hypocrite can perform no hypocrisy in manual works, but only in what proceeds from fantasies—that is a soft, mild labor. Since it serves their hypocrisy, it brings no blisters to their hands; with one experiment, they gain favor for themselves, and whatever they later botch is all well defended. Therefore, see to it that hypocrisy does not seduce you, for it produces no good doctors, no good lawyers, no good apostles, but only good Hypocrites. But hypocrisy is loved more than truth, just as they have always been held in higher esteem than Christ and his Apostles. And just as a whoremonger loves harlots more than wives, so too are the Hypocrites loved more by their swine and dogs—since such a pack surpasses the world, it will be difficult for anyone to become a righteous doctor.

Therefore, remember that in this place you have body and soul under your hands; see that you ruin nothing. For your name—whether you are called <term>Master Hans or Master Kunz</term><note>Generic names used here to represent any common practitioner or "everyman" surgeon.</note>—will not shield you on the Day of Reckoning. ### Preface to the Third Treatise of Doctor Paracelsus.

<margin>C</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring scrolling botanical motifs inside a square border.</image-desc>Outside of the wounds mentioned above in the Second Treatise, there are several other wounds that are not caused by weapons, yet are bound to the same medicine, so that a surgeon should also be knowledgeable in them. For although a dog bite is not a weapon, it is nonetheless a wound. The same applies to other bites and external poisoning. Likewise, there are bone fractures with wounds, which are included in surgery, for it is a wound of the bone. So also with burns, of whatever kind they may be—it is an injury to the skin. Also, clotted blood resulting from falls or blows belongs to surgery. Likewise, frostbite. And although <term>cold and warm gangrene</term><note>original: "kalt vnd warm Brand"; "warm brand" likely refers to erysipelas or acute inflammation, while "kalt brand" refers to true gangrene or necrosis.</note>, as well as anthrax, plague, and <term>apostemes</term><note>original: "Apostem"; an old term for an abscess, swelling, or tumor.</note>, are placed by some into surgery, they do not belong in this book, but in the book concerning "Blemishes and Ulcers," which is why I omit them here. For not only manual procedures, but also internal treatments must be understood and recognized with them. But what is contained in this treatise—all those things, etc.—should be mastered by a doctor along with wounds and stabs; for they are all certain and of true experience, so that every surgeon knows and grasps what he can and cannot do there, and what is and is not possible. For in these other ailments—St. Anthony’s fire, abscesses, plague—one cannot be so certain. Here in this book, only that which is certain and possible for Nature is presented, and the rest is omitted for now, except for a few exceptions. Furthermore, let every observer understand what is committed to medicine and what is not, what is fatal and what is not, and what serves life and what does not. And
<margin><unclear>Led in the manner of a lamb</unclear></margin>
even though the ignorant think that those who are mortally wounded should be kept alive through medicine—from which it follows that medicine is greatly despised by such "buffaloes" <note>A common Paracelsian insult for stubborn or stupid people.</note>—they think everything, possible and impossible, should happen through medicine. Therefore, it is necessary that the impossible be abandoned and the possible be maintained and made healthy, so that it does not also become impossible. For there is no medicine for the impossible, only for that which is possible; and death is just as present in the possible as in the impossible. In the possible, however, death is to be driven away, provided that the possible is not turned into the impossible.

Following in this treatise, I set down the diseases outside of those bound to weapons that belong to surgery, so that I may report to you the foundation from which these same arts were delivered to me; and I by no means withhold them from the common profit of the whole world. I give you the instruction that the

# Wound Surgery: The Third Treatise.

<margin>A</margin>The arts of medicine have been found by the common man, one after another, and one arising out of the other—some with diligence, others by chance. However they were revealed, the Light of Nature <note>The "Light of Nature" (*Lumen Naturae*) is a central concept for Paracelsus; it refers to the innate wisdom placed by God within the natural world, which can be perceived through observation rather than just reading books.</note> worked through them. This light even shows the dog that licking heals its wounds. Likewise, for human needs, Nature in her light has revealed much to those who have inclined themselves toward that Light of Nature. And although such arts have been brought into the hands of the Pharisaic doctors, the Scribal doctors, and the Hypocritical doctors <note>Paracelsus uses "Pharisee" and "Scribe" as derogatory terms for university-trained physicians who value tradition and status over practical results.</note>, they are of no use to the common man through them. In the same way that Christ speaks of the wounded man in Jericho, whose neighbor was the Samaritan; although the Priest and the Levite could also have shown him mercy, the grace was not given to them, which is why they left the wounded man behind, for they could not help him. But he who possessed the Light of Nature could help; to him God gave the grace. Where He gives it, there one should seek it. This is as much as to say: where the Light of Nature is not present, nothing is accomplished. Similarly, where the Spirit of God is not, nothing shall happen through the Spirit. And if wonders <note original: "Prodigia"></note> and signs occur, they must happen through the false-Christ <note original: "Pseudochristum"></note>, and likewise through the false-physician <note original: "Pseudomedicum"></note>. This means that medicine should remain within its own light and not with those supposed, invented doctors. Thus, many things have come to me from the Samaritans—that is, from those who are not counted among the number of the fictitious doctors.

<margin>B</margin>And just as some of these people do not have full skill in their arts to use a thing as it should be used, but rather have failings in that area: for medicine carries with it great practice and a long time of schooling. Each particular art should not be discovered in only one patient, but in several hundreds, with industrious diligence and good observation of how Nature is constituted and disposed. Only then does such manifold proof, practice, and observation teach one to recognize Nature and how she should be used. Now the doctor may act and recognize himself as a doctor. Thus, arts have come to me from lowly people which were used unskillfully by them. But because of long practice and testing here and there, I boast that I am a corrector and examiner of these same arts, who has brought and set them into their right use according to the content of their power. I dismiss the invented arts of the supposed doctors, who also "correct" and bring forth great prestige, yet all without fruit or use. For with them there is neither practice nor sufficient proof, as every proof requires its specific number of patients. For many are those who write and who puff themselves up as knowing great arts. And when they should use them most out of necessity, they might have helped once, but not there. The reason is they cry out too early, before they are sufficiently proven. It is a wretched writing, to write before the examination is finished. No chronicle can be written unless the stories have first happened. How would it be possible for the writers to have sufficiently proven as much as they write? Had they considered this, they would have spared many words.

<margin>C</margin>Therefore, as far as sufficient experience proves and shows, it is right to push away the unfit and inexperienced part of medicine—that is, the chatter. This means that silent arts <note>By "silent arts," Paracelsus likely means theoretical knowledge that doesn't "speak" through results.</note> help nothing, but only the proven ones in their place. It is right for me to test my art through my experience, even though I am greatly resented for not testing it through the writers; yet I have the pride to know more in that which I boast of than they all have ever understood. For I have experienced so much that speculation <note original: "Speculieren"></note> does not make a doctor, but the art does; and art is not speculation, but an experiment <note original: "Experiment"></note> discovered through the hands. Subsequently, contemplation <note original: "Contemplatio"></note>—that is, paying attention to Nature—belongs to it, to know how one should use her. Only then comes the experience of that art; she is the master, not the barbers and bath-keepers <note>Barbers and bath-keepers were low-status medical practitioners who performed minor surgeries like bloodletting.</note> nor their like. For a doctor's theory <note original: "Theorica"></note> should be: experience. Thus, what follows hereafter is the description of wounds not caused by weapons, how they should be healed and named, together with the regimen and other necessities.

## Of the Order pertaining to the Wounded who have
## been bitten by Mad Dogs and their like.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
To describe the regimen for those bitten by mad dogs—though it is just as good for other dog bites, though not as urgently necessary to maintain. Now the regimen is such that it alone overpowers the bile and choler <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, "choler" or "yellow bile" was the fluid associated with heat and aggression. Paracelsus believes the dog's bite "poisons" this humor.</note>, so that it does not get the upper hand. For as soon as a dog has bitten, this bite unites with the choler and bile, and poisons the choler to such an extent that it rages; and whatever future illnesses in a person might spring from the choler and bile are stirred up, making a small spark into a great fire.

Now it is not necessary to consider many things here as one usually does with choler and bile. Instead, let him drink cold water continuously, and so much that he vomits it back up, and further avoid wine. But beer that is not strongly hopped, he may also drink. Among all others is peas... <note>The word "Erb-" at the end is a catchword for "Erbsen" (peas) on the following page.</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...sloe-berry drink, or apple-water; these are the healthiest and best. And should you think that the drinking will cause the illness to strike the limbs, this does not happen at the beginning—unless it has already struck the limbs and you have arrived too late with the regimen.

You should also keep the patient on cold food, such that they eat pickled cabbage or sauerkraut, and in all things enough so that it causes them to vomit <note>The text suggests "widerbrech," implying a cleansing of the stomach through induced vomiting or simply eating to the point of satiety; in this context, it likely refers to purging the stomach.</note>. And if you wish to treat him particularly well with the drink, boil senna leaves and rose petals in skimmed milk, add a little *Benedicta laxativa* <note>original: "Benedicta laxativa"; a common medieval laxative electuary made of various herbs and roots.</note>, and let him drink it cold so that it breaks through thoroughly. Do not pay mind to what the self-proclaimed doctor says—that senna purges melancholy <note original: "Melancholiam"; one of the four humors, associated with black bile and sadness.</note>. It purges the correct matter in that place. You may also give him enough salad, vinegar, and oil, and also rose-vinegar and an electuary of rose-vinegar mixed into his drink if the condition persists severely.

You should also be careful not to give him any kind of spice, nor anything pleasant-tasting from hot things, nor any smoke made from any kind of thing. And if the heat becomes so great that he begins to fall into a rage <note>This refers to the onset of rabies, often called "hydrophobia" or "the rage."</note>, then give him rose-vinegar mixed with pea-water to drink, and all such things according to the condition of the sick person.

In this matter, you must also consider that such illnesses take on the nature of the dog. Therefore, no mild or gentle regimen belongs here, but rather a very strict one; as has been said, it is good to place the patient in cold water for a time at the beginning.

However, if the bite of the dog should turn into another temperament <note original: "Complexion"; the bodily balance of humors.</note>, so that the person does not have much "cholera" <note>In this context, "cholera" refers to the yellow bile humor, associated with heat and aggression, rather than the modern bacterial disease.</note>, then make his regimen milder. Not all who are bitten by dogs become rabid; rather, they fall into other harms according to each person's individual nature.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, pay attention to the signs of which sickness each person is prone to fall into, so that you may grant or withhold treatment accordingly.

## Regarding the regimen for those wounded by snakes, adders, vipers, lizards, or other venomous animals.

Regarding the poisoning from wild animals when they snap or bite a human—whether it happened by chance or was moved by anger (which is even worse), or the worst of all, which happens through sorcery—the order for these is that you give only those things to eat which protect the stomach, the liver, and the heart. For poisons press toward the heart; they do not desire only to leave their venom in the limb itself, but by the properties they possess, they seek out the noblest organ of the human being. Therefore, that organ must be protected above all things.

Now, for the protection of the heart and other vital organs, if you perceive that the poison is trying to press toward the heart with force, his drink should be olive oil <note original: "Baumöl"; literally "tree oil," commonly referring to olive oil.</note> in which steel has been quenched several times. To one pound of olive oil, mix in four ounces of crushed red coral and one ounce of the mixture of precious stones <note original: "Species de Gemmis"; a medicinal powder made from ground gems like emeralds or sapphires, believed to have heart-strengthening properties.</note>. Give this to him to drink warm for the first draft; the others he should drink cold. He should drink at least five drafts of this in a day. Following this, his drink should be "steeled" red wine <note>Wine in which hot steel was cooled to impart mineral properties.</note> mixed with a little theriac <note original: "Triacker"; a famous ancient "universal" antidote for poison.</note>. And with every drink, give half a quintlin <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1.8 grams.</note> of crushed red coral, and stay with this drink until favorable signs are found. But if the thirst becomes too great while drinking the oil, give warm milk with coral to drink. I have a secret remedy <note original: "Arcanum"></note> that I call *Laudanum* <note>While later associated with opium, Paracelsus's "Laudanum" was a complex alchemical preparation he considered a supreme curative.</note>; it is above all others when death is near, and it is described in its own chapter.

It is also no less useful—even if all other doctors would be against it—to mix *Philonium Persicum* <note>A traditional sedative and analgesic containing opium and henbane, named for Philo of Tarsus.</note> into the drink; it is very beneficial to take a good draft of it between the oil drinks to protect the vital organs.

Furthermore, if an unnatural thirst should occur, it is not necessary to grant the patient his will in this. Even though this thirst, as soon as it appears, is a sign that the poison is increasing toward the heart, it is good and useful that the heat be quenched externally by applying rose water mixed with camphor <note original: "Gaffer"></note> and sandalwood.

As for food, keep him according to the circumstances of the illness with light and easy food, and very little of it. Further instructions will depend entirely on the medicine, as is recorded in its specific chapter.

## Regarding the order of how those with bone fractures and with blood stagnating inside the body should conduct themselves.

In the order of bone fractures, it is not necessary to look specifically to food and drink, except to keep the patients cool so that they do not fall into heat or fever. Otherwise, feeding them with the most nourishing food in a moderate and reasonable amount is best.

But for those who have blood stagnating internally <note>This refers to internal bruising or hematomas from a fall or blow.</note>, their food and drink should always be mixed with purging things: such as boiled barley water with a little rhubarb <note original: "Reubarbara"></note>, or a little swallow-wort, or a little senna, or a little turpentine added to it, or lacca <note>A resin or sap used in early medicine.</note>. Likewise with the food, let them boil "mummy" <note original: "Mummiam"; ground remains of embalmed bodies or bitumen, used historically to treat bruises and stop bleeding.</note> or rhapontic rhubarb <note original: "Reuponticam"></note> in it. Keep them in such order and form, along with the medicine that belongs to them; you may decrease or increase this according to your judgment.

## On the Diet and Regimen of the "Fire" <note>original: "Brand"; likely referring to gangrene, St. Anthony's Fire (ergotism), or severe inflammation.</note>, and how Food and Drink should be given therein.

In common cases of "the fire," food and drink are not of great concern, except when the "fire" becomes life-threatening. In such cases, the best regimen is good medicine that draws the "fire" backward and out. However, it is no less important that if the heat reaches far inside, it may not be pulled back entirely by external medicine; therefore, be diligent to quench it internally as well.

The internal quenching, provided in the form of food and drink, is done by mixing houseleek juice <note>original: "Haußwurtzsaft"; traditionally used for its cooling properties.</note> and giving it to drink in water, and the like: Or crab-juice with lime-blossom water, strained through a cloth, and given in that manner. Know also that rose-vinegar is powerful and good, and food should be cooled with it; other things as mentioned above may also be mixed into the food. And yet, do this no longer than you perceive that great necessity requires.

## On the Regimen for those who are Frostbitten.

For those who are frostbitten and whose frost strikes inward, rose-vinegar together with long pepper should be given to drink in wine, and the food should also be mixed with it, more or less according to how the frost reveals itself. And those who are frostbitten unto death should be given burnt wine <note>original: "gebrannten Wein"; an early term for brandy or distilled spirits.</note> mixed with theriac <note>original: "Triackers"; an ancient herbal jam used as a universal antidote.</note>, and also the root of coltsfoot <note>original: "Roßhufft"; *Tussilago farfara*.</note> tempered together and drunk, and not in small amounts. Or, where you do not have such things, ginger, or cloves, cardamom, grains of paradise <note>original: "Partskörner"; likely *Paradieskörner*, a pungent West African spice.</note>, etc., boiled and drunk hot, and then placed into a sweat, so that the cold may be driven back out.

# The Third Treatise of the Great Surgery of Doctor Paracelsus: Teaching the removal of the poison and bites of all animals occurring from without: Also the healing of bone fractures, and also in every kind of "fire," according to the manner of craftsmen, or from the minerals of the mines, such as "weather" <note>original: "Wetter"; refers to hazardous gases or "damp" in mines.</note>, salt-boiling, vitriol pans, gunpowder, and the like, concerning congealed blood and frostbite.

## CHAPTER I.

### Concerning those Wounded by Rabid Dogs, as well as other Bites of Dogs.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' containing an illustration of a landscape with dogs or wolves, one of which appears to be attacking another animal.</image-desc>The bites of dogs are divided in three ways: into the rabid bite, the angry bite, and the common bite. Those that are rabid bites are the worst: for the nature of the madness strikes into the human along with the bite, so that the madness and the biting are joined together. Next are the angry bites; these occur when dogs are provoked to anger and then bite with that same anger, resulting in a poisonous bite: for the anger remains united with the biting in the wound. After that is the common bite—that is, when they bite in a snap or in a hurry; this is the least of them and the easiest to heal. You should also know that the bites of wolves are to be healed in the same way as those of dogs, as well as those of wild boar and similar animals. However, these are not classified under the rabid type, but rather as an angry bite.

Now, concerning the bite of the rabid dog, it is further to be noted how they also make the human rabid through their biting, so that the person falls into the dog’s madness, which happens thus: when the dog bites, all its nature and spirit <note>original: "Arth vnd Gemüth"</note> is fixed upon the human at the place where it attacks him; and in that same quick attack, the human also flinches back and sets his entire focus <note>original: "Speculation"; here meaning an intense mental or spiritual fixation.</note> upon the bite. Thus, the human with his fantasy and the dog with its own are joined together in an instant, and so the human’s focus is poisoned by the dog’s imagination, in the same way as when two kinds of smoke come together, or a stinking thing and a sweet-smelling thing. For although imaginations are not tangible, they are nonetheless bodily, in the same way that a wind has a body. And thus the mixture together is in the form of two kinds of smoke entering into one another.

Similarly, the fantasy of a human is like a magnet in its nature, such that it draws other fantasies to itself, just as when someone hears or sees something from another, now...

is drawn into them by his imagination <note>original: "Fantasey"; in Paracelsian medicine, "Fantasy" refers to a powerful creative force of the mind that can physically transform the body or attract disease.</note>, and he possesses it within himself just as much as the other.
<margin>A</margin>
So here too, in this place, the human’s imagination draws to itself the nature of the dog, which emanates from its own imagination; he forgets himself in that drawing-in and transforms into the nature of the dog, just as saffron colors water. Thus, human reason is stained and broken by the dog's rabid nature, and as the nature of the dog is, so also the human becomes.

Afterward, it happens that the human becomes rabid and falls upon people like a dog; he also acquires a stomach natured like a dog's, so that he eats like a dog, along with other traits that could not come to a human from his own nature, but solely through such imagination. Therefore, these are not natural diseases, but are contrary to nature; and if it makes him rabid, his madness is exactly like a dog’s, with all its traits and properties. Likewise, whatever heat, swelling, "wound-sickness" <note>original: "Wundtsucht"; likely referring to an infected or ulcerating condition resulting from a wound.</note>, and the like occurs, it is not like other wound-sicknesses, but is against that same nature and property; and whatever other illnesses happen to fall upon him, they differ from others. Therefore, the physician should not undertake to act only in the way one deals with common wounds, but he must know more and use something else.

Therefore, if the healing is to be undertaken, the first thing is that internally the gall and the yellow bile <note>original: "Gall vnnd Cholera"; referring to the "choleric" humor, believed to cause heat and aggression when imbalanced.</note> must be purged at the strongest, so that in no way can they gain the upper hand. And they should be purged from below and above <note>meaning through both laxatives and emetics (vomiting).</note>. For the yellow bile becomes so poisoned in a human that if it were not removed, it would kill the person. Now, the same medicine is made in such a way that it should only purge the gall and the yellow bile, whether with colocynth <note>original: "Coloquint"; a powerful purgative fruit.</note>, or with agaric <note>original: "Agarico"; a medicinal fungus used as a laxative.</note>, or with spurge <note>original: "Esula"</note>, or with the juice of elder bark, or with rhubarb, or the like: and the more strongly it drives it out from above and below, the better. For in this case, there must be no sparing, but rather the driving out by whatever way one can and may.

<margin>B</margin>
Likewise, while you are purging in this way, you should be diligent to cool the injured limb from the outside with cooling agents that they call "naming and killing the worm" <note>original: "den Wurm nennen vnd tödten"; refers to the folk belief that rabies was caused by a small "worm" (lyssa) under the tongue or in the wound.</note>, for it is one and the same healing. And these
