medicines are the numbing agents <note>original: "Stupefactiva"</note>, such as water-lily <note>original: "Fröschleich"; potentially "frog-bit" or water-lily used for cooling.</note>, oil of mandrake, and their like: and use them until the pains and aches are stilled and taken away. And your base should be made of puncture-plasters <note>original: "Stichpflastern"; plasters specifically for deep puncture wounds or bites.</note>: provided that no Greek pitch <note>original: "Griechischpech"; also known as colophony or rosin.</note> is added to it. And thus, through these three pieces—purging internally, cooling, and the puncture-plasters—you may heal every rabid dog bite. You should also know that if the madness in the human will not subside but spreads further, you must use opiates and administer them according to their form. And do not let yourself be talked out of it, but use them according to their nature. For through them, the madness is stilled. And the best among them is the sulfur taken from vitriol <note>original: "Sulphur der vom Vitriol"; refers to a preparation of "sweet vitriol" or sulfuric ether, which Paracelsus famously used as an anesthetic or sedative.</note>, in the way it is roasted and prepared; you may also take other things, as is well known. Although many types of recipes for purges, cooling agents, and opiates could be written, it is not necessary here, but only to present the components from which they are made, as noted above: such composition depends on your skill, which you should have learned and experienced over time.

Know also of other dog bites of anger <note>original: "Zorns"; bites from an angry dog that is not rabid.</note>, that they do not need the internal medicine: but externally in every form and fashion as is mentioned above.

And with common dog bites, only use the medicine that is useful for wounds, as recorded in the other treatise.

Let this be enough said about dog bites: only see that you have diligence and understanding in this. And you should also take note: where the dog bites are not treated in this manner—that is, with the medicine as indicated—a persistent disease <note>original: "Erbkranckheit"; literally "hereditary disease," but here meaning a chronic or lingering ailment.</note> follows from it, which is an internal
<margin>C</margin>
disruption or a bodily injury, carbuncles <note>original: "Delfenckel"; an old term for a deep, ulcerating sore.</note> or other similar open injuries. Therefore, you should be diligent that such things do not happen.

This you should know: that otherwise in all dog bites, whether from anger or in another way, the puncture-plasters are most useful, as with wounds: only with the attention to cooling the choleric heat and bringing rest through the opiates, as their use entails.

### CHAPTER II.

->**On the stinging and biting of snakes, vipers, lizards, and sim-**<-
->**ilar unclean animals.**<-

The snakes and similar animals, as mentioned in the title, have a particular nature in their poisoning and other types of wounds, as has been noted. Now their biting is divided into two ways: into an "angry bite" and into a "mad bite." An angry bite is when one makes them angry and they bite in retaliation. The other is when they are conjured <note>original: "beschwören"; refers to magical charming or enchanting of animals.</note>, then they become mad. Regarding this, take note of a specific point. The anger that such snakes, vipers, and the like have is natural, and just as the nature of their poison is natural in itself, so also that wound is natural. But that which is conjured has another nature about it, outside of nature and its course. In this matter, mark my words: nothing natural can be mastered by conjuring, for nature is mastered by no conjurer. But that which is conjured must be possessed; and what is not possessed is not conjured. From this it follows that some snakes are conjured and some are not. Additionally, some conjure and the conjuration has power; some conjure and their conjuration has no power. This is the cause: that which conjures,

<margin>A</margin> ...sword in the union of spirits; for these things do not leave the natural body except through fasting and prayer, that is, through Divine Power. For through faith, all things are possible. Whatever happens outside of this is called "conjuring" <note>original: "Beschwören"; refers to the ritual attempt to command spirits or animals through incantations.</note> and is a presumed power—the conjurer thinks he has commanded it and believes he has mastered it, though he is still far from doing so. Regarding this, know that when the serpent kind <note>original: "Nater geschlecht"; likely referring to vipers or adders.</note> are conjured, they become enraged, just like the swine that were possessed by the spirits which Christ drove out and permitted into the swine <note>A reference to the biblical account of the Gadarene swine in the Gospels.</note>. If such snakes are attacked by conjuring, they become furious: for the evil spirit within them makes them wild, like the swine that drowned themselves. And whatever they bite in such a raging state is the most violent bite that can exist among all others.

And you should know this in sum: that nothing is conjured unless it was already possessed by spirits, or the one who performs the conjuring is himself possessed. For vermin have evil spirits within them; they allow themselves to be handled and caught in this manner not out of the power of the conjuring, but out of a fury to cause more ruin and fulfill their malice.

Note this: where they bite a limb in such a state, that limb is transformed into the likeness of that same serpent, with its colors and every characteristic. Therefore, it is well to remember that such biting and poisoning is in no way natural, but comes solely from the spirits that dwell within the conjuring; these drive the serpent's venom so powerfully into the human that it exceeds natural strength. For if the swine that drowned in the sea had bitten someone, it would not have been a natural bite, but a supernatural one, just as has now been reported regarding snakes.

<margin>B</margin> It is also not to be denied that rabid dogs become possessed, and subsequently make the humans they bite insane and rabid through the power of evil spirits. Since dogs are treated with too much luxury and the poor are forgotten in the process, it is no wonder if a spirit—by God's permission—enters a dog because of such inhuman love shown to the animal. Although I do not mention this in the chapter on rabid dogs, but only provide the natural procedure, if that same order of treatment will not help, it is likely that such a "Fantasy" <note>original: "Fantasey"; in Paracelsian thought, a destructive force of the imagination that can physically manifest disease.</note> is at work. It also happens that wolves are sometimes found that attack livestock and people, tearing and biting them to death or otherwise mangling them; this is not according to the natural way of the wolf, but according to the way of evil spirits. And it cannot be argued otherwise than that evil spirits are present, having entered the wolves and appearing among them like a possessed person among people, so that even the other wolves flee from such a wolf. Since humans take such powerful pleasure in hunting, and set more love upon it than upon their own souls, it is not surprising if God allows such things to happen; everything should be used with moderation, and the better things should not be neglected for the sake of the lesser. Since God permits humans to be possessed by the evil ones—which lies plain before our eyes—there is no doubt it is also permitted for livestock, and even more so than for humans, since the curse fell upon the serpent because the cause was within her. And one must be very careful of such possessed animals: for the "favored ones" <note>likely referring to those in league with spirits or practitioners of folk magic.</note> do much through them, making them skilled and subject to humans—not only wolves, but also others, birds and the like.

<margin>C</margin> But now, to speak more naturally of these things: know that when the venom enters a human, the veins are opened and those same veins receive the poison. It is the nature of the poison to follow the veins back to their source. If it hits the veins related to the head and brain, then a sickness of the head follows. If it is the liver, then likewise; if the heart, likewise. As it is, so it takes its nature with it. Now it is good to remember that death is to be feared at that location. Therefore, it is necessary to use an internal medicine so that the heart and internal organs are protected, and additionally an external medicine that draws the poison back out. Alongside these, use a "Defensive" <note>original: "Defensiva"; a protective ointment applied to prevent the spread of inflammation or poison.</note> upon the limb because of the swelling and venom lying within it. But where the spirits are acting in that place, I have no medicine and no counsel; I show only as much as is natural, and as much as I have tested and proven.

The medicine to protect the inside is this: take four <term>loth</term> <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 1/2 ounce or 15-17 grams.</note> of <term>Mithridate</term> <note>original: "Methridatum"; a famous ancient "universal" semi-mythical antidote containing dozens of ingredients.</note>, and two loth of <term>Theriac</term> <note>original: "Triackers"; a complex herbal paste used as an antidote to poison and plague.</note>, and mix in three loth of crushed red <term>Coral</term>. Depending on the nature of the case, give as much of it as necessity requires. One cannot specify a fixed dose, therefore experience and learn so that you may recognize the need yourself. If this will not help, I have no further medicine to offer other than <term>Diaphoretic Gold</term> <note>original: "Aurum diaphoreticum"; a chemical gold preparation used to induce sweating to expel toxins.</note>, or <term>Laudanum</term> <note>In this context, Paracelsus's specific solid medicine, not the later liquid tincture.</note>, or <term>Pearl Essence</term> <note>original: "Materia Perlata".</note>, or <term>Dissolved Gems</term> <note>original: "Gemma dissoluta".</note>. All of these powerfully support the vital organs in such a crisis, upon which everyone may surely rely and take comfort.

The medicine for the wound is as follows: take the <term>Stitch-plaster</term> <note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a surgical plaster used to close wounds or draw out impurities.</note> made with <term>Litharge of Gold</term> <note>original: "Goldgletté"; lead monoxide used in plasters.</note>, gums, and <term>Mummy</term> <note>original: "Mumia"; a common ingredient in early modern medicine, either from actual ancient remains or a prepared medicinal equivalent.</note>, one quarter-pound, and add to it four loth of the four gums, cooked and prepared together. Melt them together and then dress the wound with it, according to the usual practice. And take care: as soon as the wound begins to improve, you should then use the stitch-plaster without the additive until the healing is complete. But you should be diligent not to delay long, but act quickly in all things because of the swiftness of the venom.

The "Defensive" with which you should rub the limb or bind it is this: take Mullein, Rue, St. John's Wort flowers <note>original: "Ypericon blumen".</note>, and Roses together, and place them in a good vinegar. Let it digest in the sun for the proper time. Apply it warm with linen cloths until the heat or swelling, etc., subsides.

### Concerning poisoned animals, such as toads, spiders, and their kind.

There are also other animals that cannot cause a wound by themselves, but only by producing a wound through their poison, which strikes there. Now know this regarding the nature of poison: that there are many kinds of poison from the earth and in animals—so many, in fact, that it is not possible to describe all their essences and properties. For even though I mention several poisoned animals here, such as spiders and toads, you should know that the other animals are not known to me in their healing; therefore, I omit describing their cure. For I can well consider within myself that there are many kinds of poison, and not just one single type. It would also be proper to indicate as many kinds of medicine as there are types of poison, but that does not belong to my experience.

<margin>B</margin>

And there are so many kinds of poison that one tortures and kills in one way, and another in a different way. Who can show so much counsel and help for so many kinds of poison? The scorpion has its own special poison and heals itself; but what else is like it? Arsenic <note>original: "Arsenicus"</note> poisons a person but does not heal itself. Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> makes many people healthy, yet it is a poison and also kills many a man. You should know that in the secrets of poison, the true foundation has never yet come to light. Wound Medicine: The Third Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> Much has been written about this, but all the doctors—both German and Italian <note>original: "Teutsch vnd Welsch"; "Welsch" traditionally referred to speakers of Romance languages, particularly Italians or French.</note>—have never understood that the "Apothecary's Earth" <note>original: "Apoteckerisch Terra"; likely referring to Terra Sigillata, a medicinal clay often sold as a universal antidote.</note> is nothing but a swindle, yet they have used it again and again.

### CHAPTER IV.

### On the Healing of Bone Fractures, and How They Occur.

Regarding the origin of bone fractures, not much needs to be written, for it is a dangerous break that happens through force. For bone and steel share a similar hardness: for this reason, when a sudden blow strikes steel, it breaks; it is the same with bones. And this breaking occurs because the bones splinter against one another, much like <term>Talc</term> or <term>Orpiment</term> <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; a deep yellow-orange arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in medicine, known for its flaky, layered structure.</note>. Yet they are bonded together so strongly that the bone is like steel itself. Therefore, when bones break, they splinter and create shards; they do not break off cleanly and evenly like steel, but because of their layered nature, they produce such shards, though sometimes they do not.

<margin>B</margin> But now we must speak of the healing. First, if the skin is not injured, a skillful joining must take place at that spot, so that every piece returns to its proper place. Once it is set and ordered according to its original form, then the medicine should be used as follows. You should also note that it sometimes happens that an open wound occurs with such a fracture. Should this happen, one must use the <term>Stitch-Plaster</term> <note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a specialized herbal plaster used to close wounds or treat punctures.</note> and wound oils, just as with other wounds; and over that, the medicine for the bone fracture. Thus, there are two types of healing in fractures: one where the skin is whole, and one where there is an open wound. Pay close attention to this distinction, as explained further below.

Furthermore, bone fractures should be bound twice every day. They should not be clamped in splints <note>original: "eingespalet"; referring to the use of rigid wooden boards or shingles to immobilize a limb.</note>, but rather held with iron rings set upon screws, as I have instructed several of my disciples—the description of which cannot be fully disclosed here. But this method should be used above all things, so that you may access any part of the fracture without disturbing the set position. For it is a great point in bone-setting to heal them without splints and without displacement, checking them twice a day; then the broken bone—whether it is wounded or not, whether it is inflamed or not—will not shift. And the braces you use can be added or removed as necessary. Indeed, binding twice a day is not to be rejected, for many reasons, including so that the air does not become stifled. For where this is not done, many complications arise—namely, where there are delicate complexions, they easily become overheated, and from this heat, rot <note>original: "Feulung"; gangrene or necrosis.</note> sets in. And as soon as they begin to rot, they lead to the destruction of the entire limb, and often to death, depending on the location and the circumstance. Therefore, guard against any heat striking it, for once that rot begins, it cannot be taken away; first, holes will appear, then fistulas, and an evil-smelling condition at that site. Therefore, guard it better, and bind it with a clean bandage, as mentioned, so that you may remove the heat every day and inspect it. In no way leave it unbandaged on the third day, but bind it twice every day; <margin>C</margin> thus you are certain that nothing will go wrong. Even if you have healed many according to your own head, know that it was not right, because of the risks you took.

Furthermore, in splints, the fracture often shifts: for the constant unbinding and rebinding cannot happen without causing displacement. For this reason: if you want to bind with splints, you must press so forcefully and smother the limb with cloths that it must swell; it is impossible otherwise, and traumatic inflammation <note>original: "Wundsucht"; an old term for inflammatory swelling or infection following an injury.</note> must strike it. Also, as often happens, such swelling subsides in the morning, and as it subsides, the bandages become loose, and in that moment, the bones shift. Before you can tighten them again, the damage is done, and you can never heal a bone fracture with certainty: either you smother it so that it goes into rot, or you let it shift so that it heals crooked, which is the fault of your skill-less way. Therefore, take care that you do not act recklessly, but apply yourself to the true art of bandaging, so that you may be free of the worries that arise from it, whether your name is Master George or Heinz.

Now, it is also true that a fracture heals readily, especially in the young. There is no great "art" in healing fractures, provided they are well-tended and not ruined by the medicine. For Comfrey <note>original: "Walwurken"; *Symphytum officinale*, historically known as "knitbone."</note>, crushed and boiled and applied over it, heals any fracture, unless it is in very old people. Likewise, Birthwort <note>original: "Holwurz"; *Aristolochia*.</note> on its own also works. Also, any kind of Adder's-tongue <note>original: "Naterkraut"; *Ophioglossum* or sometimes Bistort.</note> or Woundwort <note>original: "Wundkraut"; a general term for various healing herbs like Goldenrod.</note>, boiled in wine and applied morning and night, is sufficient for any healing.

There is an herb called <term>Flixweed</term> <note>original: "Sophienkraut"; *Descurainia sophia*, historically used for fractures and sores.</note>; applied either boiled or raw, it heals any bone fracture. Also, wound oils, stitch-plasters, or wound salves—whichever you use—will heal any fracture. Only proceed diligently with good care, for Nature does everything herself, with only a little help added.

# The First Book of the Great [Surgery]

<margin>A</margin>
Regarding the nature of bone fractures—how and in what way they occur—it is not necessary to write much, for you should know such things yourself: how to set broken fingers, etc., or whichever part of the body it may be, such as the back, ribs, head, neck, and so on. Nevertheless, make use of the medicines mentioned above, whatever the case may be.

You should also be prepared for two specific scenarios: if a wound is present, first set the bone, then dress the wound with wound-oil, <term>sticking plaster</term> <note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a medicinal plaster used to hold wound edges together or draw out toxins.</note>, etc. Following this, treat everything with <term>comfrey</term> <note>original: "Walwurz"; historically used to "knit" bones and heal tissues.</note> or <term>hollow-root</term>, and check it often, both morning and night.

Likewise, if a fall or a blow occurs that causes <term>congealed blood</term> <note>original: "gestanden Blut"; referring to internal bruising, hematomas, or blood that has settled and clotted within the body.</note> to form internally, from which stabs of pain, coughing, or sneezing arise, then give the patient something for that congealed blood as described in its own chapter, so that it may be expelled from the body—and the sooner, the better.

You should also know that Nature herself joins and orders the ribs and other broken bones as best she is able. Therefore, you should not be overly worried about the "setting" or straightening, unless the break is very badly displaced, such as in the arms or legs.

You must also know about complications, such as heat and swelling, which are dangerous; for rot can easily set in beneath them, turning into a foul condition. Therefore, cool it down with rose vinegar applied warm. Using "St. John's Oil," as I have taught in the section on wound-oils, is even better, as is mullein oil. This causes the swelling and heat to vanish; you need not take any other care than what has been mentioned.

But where it falls into such ruin—which must be the fault of the medicine alone—that <term>wildfire</term> <note>original: "Wild Feuer"; a historical term for Erysipelas or spreading gangrene.</note> breaks out, as often happens, or through careless medicine and care it turns into a fistula or another hole and injury: then you should know that it is difficult to help, and usually leads to death or the amputation of the limbs. You should prevent this through your skill and not through your inexperience.

<margin>E</margin>
You should also know that crushed bones are treated the same as bone fractures: shape them and bind them as described above, and apply what is necessary to the injured part.

### CHAPTER V.
#### On congealed blood, and how to expel the same.

Congealed blood has its origin solely through falling, pushing, or otherwise through blows. When such a thing happens, the injured blood "suffocates" and rots, creating a festering decay in the injury; all of this depends on the location where it occurred.

Regarding this, it must be known that there are two kinds of congealed blood: inside the body and outside the body. That is, inside the trunk/torso and outside in the four limbs. Thus, there are also two healings: one for internal congealed blood and one for external congealed blood.

External congealed blood is not dangerous, but internal blood can often be fatal, or turn into an <term>abscess</term> <note>original: "Apostem"; a localized collection of pus or a deep-seated swelling.</note> and a long-lasting, permanent sickness. Therefore, one must not let internal congealed blood remain, but must drive it out; no matter how slight or minor it may seem, trouble can always arise from it over time, depending on the nature of the internal organ—such as blockages, sores, and the like.

<margin>C</margin>
You should also know that in crushed limbs and extremities, you should always cleanse the internal blood, for it rarely fails that misfortune follows afterward, except perhaps in young people. And as soon as the congealed and crushed blood is driven out, the rest is easy to heal. But as long as the congealed blood is not removed, and you try to heal the fracture or the bruise, you cannot escape without harm. Therefore, the very first thing is that you melt, resolve, and drive out the congealed blood in the body or externally; after that, everything follows successfully. But if it remains there and you do not remove it, then rot, inflammation, "wildfire," and the accident of amputation will follow.

Now there are two ways to remove congealed blood, internally and externally: one is by ingestion, the other is by external application, and it is done in this way. First, for the external:

An oil, which you use to anoint the ends and places on the body where the fall, push, or blow occurred, morning and night, takes away all congealed blood, whether it be in the body or outside in the limbs; it is made thus:

Take a handful of mullein, three handfuls of St. John's wort flowers, half a handful of swallowwort root, two <term>loth</term> <note>A loth is a historical German unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams.</note> of <term>mumia</term> <note>original: "Mummien"; in this era, "mumia" referred to a medicinal substance often derived from bitumen or powdered remains, believed to stop bleeding.</note>, two pounds of fresh, young olive oil, one pound of turpentine, and two <term>mass</term> <note>A "Maß" is a historical unit of volume, roughly equivalent to a liter or quart.</note> of good red wine. Let these things boil together for seven hours, then place it in the sun in sealed vessels; afterward, press it out, boil off the wine, and keep it. You will find nothing better for external application.

For the medicine used internally, have this powder made at the apothecary, and give a <term>quintelin</term> <note>An old measurement roughly equal to 4 grams or a drachm.</note> weight of it to drink in linden blossom water, as often as the case requires.

# Surgery: The Third Treatise.

### C H A P T E R VI.

->Of the Burn caused by Wood-fire.<-

First, you should know that there is a distinction to be made regarding burns; they are of many types and cannot all be healed in the same way. For just as you see that a thing sealed and enclosed in glass takes on a different nature when placed in the sun, so too is the heat of a fire from wood different from the fire of coals. It is one thing if the fire is from sulfur, and another if it is from <term>brandy</term> <note>original: "Brentenwein"; distilled spirits, which cause a different type of chemical/flammable burn.</note>. Therefore, there is one type of burn when someone is burnt by wood-fire, and another type from milk, water, brandy, etc. Another type comes from gunpowder and sulfur; another from metals; another from "weather," thunder, or storms <note>likely referring to lightning strikes</note>, and the like. There are also other types found in mines, such as when the "weather" <note>original: "Wetter"; referring to firedamp or explosive gases in mine shafts</note> burns them, or they are burned by <gloss>*</gloss> vapors, or from salt-boiling, or from <term>vitriol water</term> <note>original: "Vitriolwasser"; a solution of metallic sulfates, often highly acidic and corrosive.</note>, or from alum water, and the like. Following this, a special chapter is dedicated to each type. First, concerning wood-fire, to treat that burn, proceed in this way:

<margin>B</margin> The very first step is to "draw out" the burn, which is done in this manner: Take butter and make it hot—as hot as possible—and pour it immediately into cold water. Beat the butter and the water together for so long that the butter becomes as white as snow. Then pour off the water and keep the butter as a salve. Bind the burn with this two or three times a day, or more. That is, take care that it is constantly greasy and moist with the salve; do not let it dry out. Keep it always damp with the ointment, reapplying it as often as it begins to dry. This will draw all the "fire" out of the burn, no matter how large it is or where it is on the whole body; it will not fail you. And if the burn is so great that you see holes or similar deep burning damage, first draw out the burn as written above, then heal it with <term>sticking plaster</term> <note>original: "Stichpflaster"; a specialized medical adhesive used to close wounds and protect regenerating skin.</note>. You will suffer no lasting harm and need not rack your brain further. This is enough said regarding common burns, and there is no need to write more.

You should also know that burns from water, milk, etc., are treated in the same way, as are those from oil, resin, lard, and similar substances. However, more diligence is required for burns caused by fatty substances than others, and more care in using the sticking plaster.

And although any wound medicine is good and sufficient for healing once the burn has been drawn out, one should not neglect to use the most certain methods where necessity demands.

### C H A P T E R VII.

->Of Burns from Metals, Salt-water, Copper-water, Rust-fire, and Slag.<-

<margin>C</margin> Regarding the nature of metals and ores, it must be known that they possess a particular poisonous quality within them, according to their own nature. First, metals themselves require a specific medicine. Although the remedy for wood-fire is also helpful, it is safest to act according to professional skill. Mercury has a special way of being "extinguished" <note>cooled or neutralized</note>; likewise, there are specific treatments for burns from salt-boiling, vitriol-boiling, and alum-boiling. Just as with the metals, there are three ways to extinguish burns from ores and metals.

You should also know that a poison accompanies these burns, much like a dog bite or a poisoned weapon. Therefore, it is necessary not only to draw out the burn but also the poison. For from this same poison—which arises from <term>copper-water</term> <note>original: "Kupfferwasser"; often referring to copper sulfate or acidic mine runoff.</note>, alum, salt, ore, etc.—there is a tendency toward <term>swollen legs</term> <note>original: "Oelschenckeln"; chronic, weeping sores or edema of the lower limbs.</note>, open sores, and sometimes even <term>leprosy</term> <note>original: "Auffatz"; historically used for various skin diseases including leprosy.</note> and its like. Even if they do not find the true origin of such diseases there, these burns produce "bastard" versions of them, and by their nature, they attract "fluids" <note>humors</note>, inflame the blood, and destroy the body's proper balance.

To extinguish and draw out the burn of metals: take bacon fat, make it hot, and pour it while at its hottest into <term>nightshade water</term> <note>distilled water of Solanum nigrum, used for its cooling and sedative properties.</note>. Beat it until it turns into a salve, and bind the wound with it until the end. It is not necessary to draw much out, but rather proceed to the end with common wound medicine. For a burn from mercury, however, hot milk should first be applied with a wet cloth, at least twenty times; as soon as it cools, apply a new one. After that, proceed with the salve made of butter or lard (as with the bacon fat) until the burn is drawn out, and then cover it with plasters made with <term>colophony</term> <note>original: "Colofonia"; pine resin used in plasters to draw out toxins and seal wounds.</note> until it is closed. Such burns occur during <term>amalgamation</term> <note>the process of mixing mercury with other metals, common in alchemy and mining.</note>, for otherwise mercury is seldom used in fire. It also often happens that from a mercury burn, toothaches or tremors occur. When this happens, remember to remove all mercury from the patient and let them heal on their own. Do nothing further than to give <term>Aqua Vitæ</term> <note>original: "Aqua Vitæ"; concentrated alcohol, literally "Water of Life."</note>, wash the limbs with it, and wash the teeth with lavender water.

...swung or rinsed <note>likely referring to a limb being washed with a medicinal liquid</note>; thus they recover without anything else being done, rather than with a great deal of medicine. This occurs often where cinnabar is made, and where mercury is distilled downward, as well as in other methods of separating metals through fire. Furthermore, concerning the burns that arise from salt-boiling—whether it occurs in the pans, in the brine, etc.—as well as those involving copper-water <note>original: "Kupfferwasser"; refers to copperas or vitriol</note> or alum: you should know that these are powerfully harmful burns. If they are not properly drawn out, they cause and bring much evil afterward. Where such burns occur, the remedy is to bind the burn twice every day with the following ointment until you have drawn out all the burning, swelling, heat, and pain; this will happen quickly. If further treatment is needed, heal it with wound balsam, wound powder, or wound ointments, as these produce the fewest scars and seal well. And the ointment is made thus: Take half a pound of nut oil, one pound of deer tallow, one and a half pounds of slaked butter <note>butter that has been washed or "extinguished" in water to remove impurities</note>, mix them together, and use it as described above. You may also use this for all burns that occur among dyers and the like.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### Concerning burns from [gun]powder, from muskets, from saltpeter, from sulfur, from Aqua Fortis <note>original: "Aquaforts"; nitric acid</note> or separating-water, or other such alchemical accidents.

<margin>B</margin>
This type of burn is a penetrating one, which in itself contains a great and noticeable heat; it is hard and does not cool quickly, but rather slowly, and where it attaches, it sticks firmly. For sulfur and nitre <note>original: "Niter"; saltpeter</note> do not let go until they are entirely consumed. Except for the fire from heaven <note>lightning</note>, there is no heat above this heat and burning. This is also true of the "strong waters" made by alchemists; these are also of the greatest malice, not only because of the heat but also because of the great corrosive nature they bring with them, as is demonstrated in "separating-water" <note>nitric acid</note>, and also in mercurial water, grading-water <note>original: "Gradierwasser"; used to purify or "grade" gold</note>, in Royal water <note>original: "Aqua regis"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acid capable of dissolving gold</note>, and the like. It is rightly necessary that a separate chapter be dedicated to these two immeasurable burns—that of powder and that of the "waters."

Firstly, regarding burns from powder, as well as from sulfur and saltpeter—each on its own—there is a remedy. Secondly, there is another remedy for alchemical waters; whatever is most severely burned in that manner should be treated under these two healings. The first is: as soon as the burn has occurred, bind it with the ointment: Take one pound of lard, half a pound of nut oil, half a pound of deer tallow, and a quarter-measure of beef marrow. Melt all these pieces together and, while at its hottest, extinguish it in water-lily water <note>original: "Seeblumenwasser"</note> or something similar; do this four times or more, then beat and whip it into an ointment to bind the wound. As soon as it warms up and melts, bind it anew until the burn is drawn out, which happens quickly; afterward, heal it with wound-healing treatments.

But for separating-waters, do likewise until you have taken away the burn; afterward, bind it only with wound oil and a sticking plaster placed upon it. In this way, its eating, gnawing, and corrosive nature will be drawn out and removed, and it will be healed well and cleanly.

I have received many types of recipes during my days for such emergencies, but among them all, there are not many that were excellent, because of slow healing and much destruction to be expected besides. For there is almost no man who does not have some advice and some medicine, but they are not good for everything. Therefore, among all of them, the one mentioned above is the best and most useful.

## CHAPTER IX.

### Concerning burns from the weather, thunder, lightning bolts, and sky-flashes <note>original: "himlitzen"; referring to the flashes of lightning in the sky</note>, as they occur from above.

<margin>C</margin>
The matter from which thunder-fire or lightning-fire is made is a firmamentary saltpeter and sulfur. For in the same way that sulfur and saltpeter grow out of the earth and are then organized together into a measure and substance, so too are there heavenly matters that are similar to them. For an example: if water can grow in the heavens and fall upon the earth, so too can fire grow within them. If snow can grow in the heavens, so too can saltpeter and other things from which fire is made grow there. Thus, we should know that the lightning-fire from heaven is solely a firmamentary composition of materials like those that spring from the earth, ordered by the stars into such a state and essence.

Therefore, you should know that this burn is the most evil and most harmful of all. For because it comes from the firmament, it surpasses all earthly powers. Therefore, great necessity must be considered in its healing. Although these burns commonly kill outright, or strike off a limb entirely, they consume whatever they seize, just as a fire turns wood into a coal or ash, from which no more wood can be made. So too, it happens that they burn the limbs so deeply that nature can do no more; for it is like a coal that is no longer wood; so here, too, it is like a coal in which there is no longer any flesh. You should recognize this yourself so that you do not attempt impossible things, but only as much as is possible.

Therefore, know that there are two remedies for lightning-fire: one for the burn that has not yet been burned into a coal, and the other for the burn that is charred, to release it and take it away.

# CHAPTER X.

->Concerning the burns from musket balls, and when other objects<-
->strike the body or limbs, how to remove that same heat.<-

Furthermore, there is another type of burn which occurs when bullets enter the flesh and lie there for a long time before they cool. And even if they do not carry or bring any gunpowder with them, the burn is still of that same nature, coming from the metals and from the hard impact; it is a severe burn. For such a burn, a cooling is required above all things, so that the bullet's heat may be extinguished. Or, if it has passed all the way through, the extinguishing and cooling are still required. Namely: that juice of nightshade, rose vinegar, houseleek, and water lilies, etc., be pounded with crayfish and frogs, and well-pressed together and injected, often and for as long as it takes until the burning stops. And then, pour in the mentioned burn salves, and subsequently draw out the burn, and finally heal it to the end with wound ointments, as with puncture wounds; especially with the wound plasters, for many reasons, including so that whatever was struck hard into the wound may be drawn out again.

There are many such coolants made from snails, earthworms, frogs, crayfish, frogspawn, etc. There are also others made with goose fat, though they are less useful in this case. Those made of houseleek, nightshade, water lilies, etc., are better. Shoemaker's black <note>original: "Schusterschwerz"; an iron-based vitriol solution used in tanning and ink-making, prized here for its astringent properties</note> is also good. However, there is no cooling like that of rose vinegar; when it is sharpened with crayfish juice, it is the best of all coolants. Also, if it happens that one must extinguish a gunpowder burn where the saltpeter and sulfur have struck in so hard, it should also be extinguished in this manner first.

<margin>C</margin>
It should also be noted that often, in great emergencies, such burns are extinguished with water, by running into it and cooling down. If such a thing occurs, then proceed with the burn salves and draw the burn out.

You should also know that such burns are often fatal for the reason that the heat damages the internal regions or the brain. Where such a legendary injury occurs, there is no recovery at that spot. But if the injury is not fatal, then extinguish it internally with water made from the small plums called *Zibarten* <note>original: "Zeparty" or "Ceparten"; a wild, tart plum variety</note>; give this to drink without ceasing. In place of all other drinks—no wine—give only what cools, such as grass-water, water, milk, beer, apple-drink, etc.

# CHAPTER XI.

->Concerning the ringing of the ears, or eye afflictions, which<-
->take their origin from artillery.<-

As it then often happens, from the noise of the muskets, ear-ringing etc. arises, with a sound like bells or the din of a mill and the like. This is possible because whatever is too strong for the hearing shatters the hearing; for the hearing is in itself a subtle thing, and what it is meant to hear should be spoken to it with a moderate voice. But if it is too loud and too coarse, and beyond the nature of the hearing, it breaks the hearing.

So it is also with the sight: whatever overcomes the sight also breaks the sight. Just as the sight requires only a day's light—that is, the light of a day under a shadow—the eyes have enough. But furthermore, if it is brighter to the eyes than a shaded light, then it damages the eyes, such as the sun, fire, and the like.

<margin>A</margin> Now it follows that from the fire of gunpowder—even though the physical powder itself may not enter—the glare is present, and it darkens the eyes and troubles them, so that they no longer have their proper brilliance, nor can they keep it. The same applies to hearing. From this follow two pieces of advice: one for hearing, the other for sight, in this manner.

For hearing, you should frequently have the earlobes <note>original: "Ohrleplin"</note> bled in a bath when the moon is in a favorable zodiac sign <note>original: "vndern guten Zeichen"; early modern medicine often synchronized treatments with astrology</note>. If this does not help, you should have cupping glasses <term>Ventosen: glass jars used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out "bad humors"</term> placed behind the ears—one behind each ear, if both are affected. If this also proves unhelpful and the condition persists stubbornly, then bloodletting <term>Lässin: the surgical opening of a vein</term> under the tongue follows, which is the final resort; beyond this, nothing more can be done for such hearing loss.

For the eyes, you should make a fomentation <note>a warm, moist medicinal compress</note> of vetch or barley flour, unsifted, boiled with water into a mash. Hold the eyes over the warmth, well-covered, and let the steam bathe the eyes until it cools. Do this every morning until they stop tearing or producing fluid on their own. Afterward, smear a drop of oil of brick <term>Ziegelöl: a traditional remedy made by heating bricks soaked in oil until the oil is distilled</term> into the corner of the eye. Do this early every morning, and the affliction will pass away.

### CHAPTER XII.

->Concerning Frostbite, and the ways in which it may occur, whether through Dryness or Moisture.<-

There are two kinds of frostbite: One that occurs over a long period, such as when one walks much in water. Though it may not seem like much at the time, eventually frostbite develops, causing pain in the face and such, which is also a form of being frozen. Many also freeze in winter such that it creates a sickness within them that breaks out after the winter has passed, and this can become fatal. Then there is also the frostbite that <margin>B</margin> shows its damage immediately, such as when a limb is frozen—a foot, a hand, etc.—or when one is frozen entirely to death, as often happens.

Now, it is no less true that such frostbite occurs frequently. First, some freeze throughout the winter or in water, but because no immediate damage is visible to the eye, they pay it no mind until the "glare" <note>the visible inflammation or reaction</note> comes, or its appointed time. Writing for those types of frostbite belongs to the study of internal medicine <note>original: "Leibartzney"</note>. Although damage in the limbs, feet, and legs may be counted toward surgery <note>original: "Wundartzney"</note>, because it distributes itself as a bodily sickness, it is not necessary to write of it here, but rather in that place where internal medicine and surgery are joined as one.

But regarding the other frostbite that is visible to the eye, you should know this: in the places and regions where such frost and freezing are common, the arts of healing should be common there too, and best known by the locals. However, there is a coarse, rough folk there who pay no heed to such things, so there is nothing to be learned from them. In Switzerland, there are great mountains, such as the Gotthard, the Gletschert, the Hocken, and others that are used daily and where much frostbite is encountered; also the Vogel, the Splügen Pass, the San Giacomo <note>original: "Sechmer"</note>, the Elbli, Vesseler, and Feldier, and the Bernina <note>original: "Perlin"</note>. But among all these people, there are no well-founded methods available, only "women’s chatter" <note>original: "Weiberräding"; a dismissive term for folk remedies not based on contemporary medical theory</note>. The same is true for those who travel over the Penffer Joch. Furthermore, the Krimmler Tauern, the Felber Tauern, the Fuscht, the Rauris Tauern, and similar places where high mines are situated, such as the Schneeberg at Sterzing, etc. Many such incidents happen there, but there is no help or final medicine to be found from anyone.

As much as experience has given me in those same regions, know this: If a limb is frozen, it is dead, and it can never be brought back. Rather, that which is <margin>C</margin> frozen rots and falls away. It is almost exactly like leprosy <note>original: "Aussätzigen"</note>. Indeed, it is nearly the same thing, and there is no denying it, except that many forms of leprosy may spring from frostbite that otherwise would not occur. Therefore, since the frozen part must go, one should not attempt to heal it, for that would be acting unwisely. Instead, one should strive to make it fall away quickly and separate from the living flesh, so that the living part may return to a state of growth and, as far as is possible, fulfill what was lost. However, if a limb, finger, or toe has frozen off, it cannot be brought back, nor can another be put in its place. Therefore, know a medicine here that shall separate the frozen from the living; it is this:

Take long pepper, small cardamoms, grains of paradise <note>original: "Pariskörnlin"</note>, three ounces <note>original: "Lot"</note> of each; four ounces of euphorbium <note>a caustic plant resin</note>; three ounces of mastic. Let these things be ground small together in a mortar; afterward, pour over them two measures of a child’s urine—or the urine of a "red man" <note>referring to a person with a ruddy complexion, often considered in alchemy to have specific humoral properties</note>—and let it boil down to an eighth part. Then strain it through a cloth, and with that which remains, anoint the frozen limb three times every day. Thus the dead separates from the living. Afterward, heal it with wound salves until it is entirely closed.

It is also the case that if you treat yourself with this juice and then find yourself near a fire while freezing, a great misfortune must occur on the day you are anointed, should you freeze or fall into harm at that spot.

Many things are also used to prevent frostbite, such as furs, leather, and such. But above all else, as much as clothing is able to prevent it, is paper, laid two-fold or more upon the limbs, in the trousers, and in front of the feet. Provided it is protected from tearing and sweating—that is, from dampness—paper lets no wind pass through it. It is superior to all leather and fur when placed under the cloth or similar materials.

But for those who freeze entirely—that is, where the frost has gone all the way through—the best thing is Theriac <note>original: "Tyriar"; a famous poly-pharmaceutical "universal antidote"</note> and

# Wound Medicine: The First Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> Distilled wine <note>original: "Brandten Wein"; brandy</note> mixed with water, administered to the patient, who is then laid down warmly, is the best remedy. And where this is not possible, the next best thing is a strong wine, boiled with ginger and sweet flag <term>Kalmus: an aromatic marsh plant used since antiquity for digestive and warming remedies</term>, and drunk; also distilled wine with spices, especially with saffron. Beyond this, I have no further knowledge of frostbite: I have labored much in this matter, but have only achieved as much as is stated above—to remove what is already frozen and to prevent further freezing. Also, as mentioned, it is good to eat many spices beforehand; this is good for general freezing of the body, but it helps nothing for the specific limbs. There is a type of freezing that does not particularly show how dangerous it is, but rather, while one thinks all is well and feels comfortable, he dies in that state, sleepy and without pain. Likewise, when limbs freeze, they become entirely insensitive, just like a leper. Also, after such freezing, scabs, the itch, mange, and similar skin conditions often follow.

### CHAPTER XIII.

### Concerning various specific manual techniques <term>Handgriffe: literally "hand-grips," referring to the practical, physical skills and manual dexterity a surgeon uses during procedures</term> that a wound surgeon should know regarding wounds and their associated diseases.

Although I have hitherto sufficiently described in these three treatises all wounds, stabs, and other such injuries belonging to wound surgery—how they should and may be healed, and that without any lingering defects.

<margin>B</margin> Now, it is no less true that others have also written much about these things, and there are many different "strange heads" <note>diverse opinions or eccentric thinkers</note>, one liking this, another liking that. However, whatever any individual may think, the foundation is sufficiently demonstrated here with every kind of medicine. Now, it is no less true that much could still be written about certain manual techniques: but they are not to be described; rather, to know them belongs to experience. You should know further that which I have not written through your own experience and practice. For practice makes a perfect man, provided he is also supplied with the correct art <note>theoretical knowledge and principles</note>, without which no practice can be useful.

Now, there are certain "grips" that belong to a wound surgeon, namely experience in the preparation of medicine, as necessity requires you to know it. For these are manual tasks that belong to you personally. Furthermore, you must recognize the treatment of complications—beyond those that have been indicated—and turn them away through your own experience and recognition. For these are not manual techniques that you are taught from books; they are not part of your experience. But these are the techniques that you find outside of all those, knowing better and differently and further than I have written: it is your duty to see if better, more useful, and more skillful ways may be found. For at this time, I only indicate what is currently the most certain in the world, among both the New and the Old schools.

You may well consider this within yourself: that not everything that happens daily can be written down. For time and the hour are so strange that they always bring forth something unheard of, so that you must know how to apply the correct medicine—as I have described it—to that thing according to its nature. These are manual skills that your own cleverness must provide. For strange wounds and stabs occur in battles, wars, and elsewhere, yet the medicine for all of them has been shown: only the application and administration cannot be sufficiently described. In this, you should use your own skill, according to the opportunity of the city, place, and other conditions, as they manifest and occur. But whatever is necessary for everything and required by need—also what is possible and what is not—that has all been sufficiently explained and opened up: only learn and practice, so that you ruin nothing through your inexperience and coarseness.

<margin>C</margin> I have also many times seen such strange stabs and wounds that, had there not been good medicine, could not have been managed by any human skill. But Nature, when she senses good medicine, is herself the one who arranges and orders what is not possible for man. Therefore, the greatest thing is that you have good medicine: for therein lies the first and greatest skill. After that, the second skill lies in you: that you do not ruin Nature’s own dexterity yourself.

Wounds are also sometimes inflicted upon those suffering from dropsy <term>Wassersucht: edema or pathological swelling caused by fluid retention</term>, fluxes, consumption, arthritis, or podagra <term>Podagra: gout, specifically affecting the foot</term>. In such a case, it is necessary that you know how to dry out the dropsy and the swelling. For where there is moisture, no wound is healed; there must be no "water" in the flesh. In other conditions—such as consumption, gout, or even paralysis—where such persons are wounded, it is sometimes good and sometimes bad, depending on the accident and the sickness. In such wounds, you should consider your own skill and ability, what is useful for it, and how you should conduct yourself—or take counsel from the physicians <note>original: "Leibartzten"; university-educated internal doctors</note>, if they otherwise know how to handle it, though I have experienced few of them who do.

Furthermore, you should know that enough has been said to you regarding every necessity, and that you lack nothing further in my writings. For I have myself experienced, investigated, and tested so much and so well, that no more may be granted to you than to Me, and even much less: therefore you can find no fault in me. Also, if there be "Doctors" who act against me in these things, they have experienced nothing at all, nor tested anything in these matters; it is a mockery for them to stand against me. And let them not excuse themselves by saying they are "Doctors" and not "Barbers" <note>original: "Scherer"; historically, barber-surgeons performed the manual tasks while doctors only diagnosed</note>. I say this: a barber is not a physician, and as long as it has stood in their hands, it has never gone well, and was quite weak. You should teach them; that is why you are a Doctor. Even if you are not a barber, you are still a physician. What do the combs <note>original: "Strälan"; likely referring to the grooming tools of a barber</note> concern you? You should be capable of the art so that people learn from you, yet you do nothing without knowledge and experience. Those are the manual techniques that belong to it: Knowing, Being Able, and Understanding.

## Concluding Remarks.

The medicine pertaining to wounds I have now, by the grace of God, completed. Although it may not suit every man’s mind: whoever can do better, I pray that he improves it. What I write has been well tested through fire <note>original: "durchs Fewr probiert"; a metaphor for rigorous practical testing, likely referencing the alchemical purification of metals</note>; I would gladly recognize another man of my kind. Boasting and self-promotion I let pass by my ears: let each man judge according to the way of Nature and through great experience, and so I will lose nothing in their eyes. I have always and ever desired from my heart to prevent the ruin of the sick; I hope no one will hold this against me. Even if much is said against me, it happens without experience: what is in such talk? Nothing. They are Pharisees, hypocrites, and scribes, who are always inclined to cause division and discord. I have satisfied the doctors in this book; for the others, I have no concern. I have used a rustic manner of speech <note>original: "Ländlichen Spruch"</note> herein, so that no one can praise me for rhetoric or subtleties, but rather according to the tongue of my birth and the country's language—for I am from Einsiedeln <note>A village in the Swiss Alps, home to a famous Benedictine monastery and Paracelsus’s birthplace</note>, a Swiss of that land—no one should hold my rustic speech against me. I do not write for the sake of language, but for the sake of the art of my experience, which is made to serve everyone in the whole world and is useful to the whole world. It should not be thought that this is the end of my arts; rather, I wish with joy to gladden many a pious doctor and help many a sick person to health, who would otherwise be brought to ruin by fictionalized doctors <note>original: "erdichten Arzt"; physicians who rely on academic theory or imagination rather than clinical observation</note>. I wish herewith to have asked all doctors not to resent me for this: that for the sake of the patients' benefit, I have practiced and worked so strictly for so long in the experience of true medicine. With this, may God give you luck and salvation, and preserve you from thoughts and intentions through which the ruin of the sick might arise, and confirm you in piety and love of the arts, toward the truth at all times.

## End of the First Book of the Great Wound Surgery by Doctor Paracelsus.

### Summary of the entire book by Dr. Paracelsus.

<sig>C</sig>

It has been written / believed / and held / that the origin of open wounds <note>The term "offne Schäden" often refers to chronic ulcers or lesions that refuse to heal, rather than fresh cuts.</note> comes from and is / out of the four <term>Humors</term> <note>original: "Humoribus"; the traditional medical theory that health is governed by four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Paracelsus famously rejected this.</note>, and according to the contents of the same / the healing was also conducted: Which then cannot be so / but rather the origin is from <term>Salt</term> <note>original: "Sal"; in Paracelsian thought, Salt is one of the three primary principles (Tria Prima) of matter, representing stability and the physical body.</note>, and through its transmuted essence into <term>Corrosive</term> / is their origin / and against such Saline <term>Corrosives</term> the healing shall be established and handled.

### Summary of the Second Part.

If there is now an error in the origin / how much more so in the healing? Upon this it is now necessary / since medicine is from God / a righteous / certain art / that <term>Opinions</term> <note>original: "Opinionibus"; academic theories or hearsay not based on direct observation.</note>, the made-up fantasies / should not be followed / but rather the Foundation / through which a physician should know how to enter through the right door / not through the roof.

### Summary of the Third Part.

Because medicine has been failing / and proves itself through its works / that it stands in doubt: Although many great and eminent persons finally believe they have the right foundation / and thus the testimony / which a physician gives / is sleeping: It is necessary to seek a better / proven foundation / so that medicine does not go so completely into ruin / torment / and contrary healing.

->End of the summaries of Dr. Paracelsus.<-

## DR. *PARACELSUS GREETS THE READER.* <note>original: "Lectori S." abbreviated from the Latin *Lectori Salutem*, a standard greeting meaning "Health/Greetings to the Reader."</note>

Because I have always considered and sought the benefit of the sick, to serve them faithfully so that they might be preserved most certainly before God and man: I have had to fundamentally abandon the idea of building strongly and firmly upon the provided books that speak of open wounds <note>The term "offne Schäden" refers to chronic ulcers or lesions.</note>, namely the writings and teachings of the physicians and surgeons of both schools. But since they were built upon sand, what could I accomplish through them? Or what was in them that was honorable and useful to us, or to the sick along with me? Finally, nothing, reader—believe that—and if I wished to burden and trouble you, I could demonstrate it to you at great length. What I write here is strange and vexing to many; but truly, reader, no doctor who wishes the sick well will find displeasure in this. 

But you should observe how the doctor today is different from what his rules ought to be. They are just like the *irregular ones* <note>original: "Irregularibus"; referring to those who do not follow the established rules of the clerical or professional order—here, "unqualified" or "unorthodox" practitioners.</note>; judge, reader, and ask: Who are those who are my enemies? If you can find one among them who seeks such enmity toward me because of the destruction of the sick caused by me, do not believe it. However, because they are recognized through such things, and because of what is within them, that is what creates the poison against me. May God turn them away: but I do not think He will do so. The reason: their hearts overflow; their bile must have vomited. 

But I want you, reader, to be exhorted and most highly reminded: the snake bends, curves, and twists itself. Let it bend, curve, and twist; if the poison is deadly, let its dust and ashes remain. If those doctors—who are not doctors but destroyers—gained as much money from my writing as they have suffered damage to their reputations, they would make a *Diana* <note>original: "Dianam"; the Roman goddess. Paracelsus suggests they would worship him as a golden idol if it were profitable for them.</note> out of me. But reader, do not let that trouble you; think only of piety, so that you maintain a good and honest reputation, protecting your honor before God and your neighbor. Therefore, I may write safely before you, and I know well that when you read it through, you will carry a judgment that will be well-received by the sick. With that, distinguish between Me and the Pretenders.

->**To the Most Illustrious and Most Powerful Prince and**<-
->**Lord, Lord Ferdinand, by God’s Grace King of the Romans,**<-
->**Bohemia, and Hungary, Archduke of Austria, etc.**<-
->**Our Most Gracious Lord.**<-

Since Almighty God has distributed illnesses equally, having no respect for the person among us mortal men—regarding one the same as another, as has been found since the beginning of the world—there has never been any regard for status concerning disease. As it is proven that *Julius I* <note>Likely referring to a historical ancestor of the Habsburgs or an early Roman ruler; Paracelsus often used historical precedents to show that even the powerful are subject to nature.</note>, your Roman Royal Majesty’s ancestor, was burdened with a severe illness; and likewise, not one of all his descendants has ever been exempted from becoming sick, as a great number thereafter died specifically of wounds to their own bodies, and suffered from a lack of medicine based on a correct foundation. Nor has anyone ever been born who was not subject to medicine. Since everyone is bound under this yoke, and yet medicine is provided for it, as is the doctor: it is right that the doctor carry his own yoke <sig>C</sig> and labor daily to turn away the illnesses of the sick, applying his highest diligence.

Now, Most Invincible King, as such is becoming of a doctor, it is never necessary for the doctor to look to follow this or that man—unless the truth is fundamentally perceived, and that the truth of medicine has a just, simple, and certain path before it, in which there can be no error, division, or <term>sectarianism</term> <note>original: "Sectierung"; the formation of medical "sects" or factions (like the followers of Galen vs. others) which Paracelsus despised.</note>. But if medicine cannot be found in such a way, neither in books nor by word of mouth, but rather one thing is contrary to another, and it is demonstrably proven through the destruction of the sick that the true foundation and understanding cannot be in that same path which is being followed: therefore I labor to write. I cast aside those same contradictions and make myself restless to describe here the Second Book of Surgery, in which I have delved so deeply that the nature and power [of healing] are clearly shown without division or error.

Now it is no less true that it will not pass without objection, namely speaking against me regarding the *Origin*: from whence open wounds take their source. Also, secondly, regarding the *Healing*, which will be strange and unknown to them. But since I consider that nothing pleases the wanderer except to wander just like they do: not one gray hair shall grow on me because of their objections. I held their *Procedures*, *Canons* <note>original: "Proceß / Canones"; refers to the established "legal" rules and formulas of traditional medieval medicine.</note>, and similar orders and writings in great worth and honor for a long time. But when I myself could accomplish nothing useful with them—nor could other colleagues of mine—I was forced to seek another foundation, which I have attained with heavy labor. I would have spared myself this labor if the *Procedures* and *Canons* of my other masters and good friends had been correct. So it is also no less true, Most Powerful Lord King, that the liberties granted by Emperors and Kings for the praise, honor, benefit, and protection of doctors have been turned toward that part which is without
<meta>catchword: error</meta>

Wound-Medicine: The Third Treatise.

<margin>A</margin> There should be no error: and yet that same error teaches the destruction of the sick, as is then clearly evident. Even if a doctor ruins someone, the <term>Aquilian Law <note>original: "Lex Aquilia"; a Roman law providing compensation for damage to property or injuries caused by negligence.</note></term> serves as a cloak for his ignorance. Such freedom should rightly and properly exist, yet not as a protection for the ignorant. Consider: it might even be right if what once happened occurred again—how a certain Roman Consul had such ignorant doctors put to death because he saw clearly that they were in error and had no experience in the foundations of medicine. If such a thing were to happen, many sick people would remain un-ruined and alive, who are otherwise treated with too much delicacy. But because this does not happen, that freedom is their hope. Now it has come to the point that no one wants to experience and learn for themselves anymore. Therefore, Most Gracious Lord, I do not write or teach out of a stubborn head, but out of my experience; and it seems right to me that I should write and teach regardless of other <term>Canons <note>Standard rules or established medical laws.</note></term>, since I must give an account for myself. I let nothing ungrounded lead me astray, and all of this is for the praise and honor of Your Roman Imperial Majesty. It is my undoubted hope that I have served Your Roman Imperial Majesty well, and have honestly considered the benefit and health of all the sick, and have been of service to everyone. I hereby submit myself to the grace and protection of Your Roman Imperial Majesty. Given at Augsburg on the eleventh of August, in the lesser number of the thirty-sixth <note>i.e., August 11, 1536.</note>.

# Preface to the Second Book of the Great Wound-Medicine
### By Doctor Paracelsus.

<margin>B</margin> As I write on wound-medicine, I am accused by all doctors of holding "contrary" views and of being "contrary"—as they call it—and of always being placed in opposition. When I measure and consider this, I find that they are right, yet with this distinction: I am contrary to them, but an <term>intimate <note>original: "Familiaris"; meaning a close friend or someone who is part of the household of Nature.</note></term> of Nature. Now judging—since I am not contrary to Nature—is it not right that I might be called "contrary" by the others? It is better that Nature leaves me un-accused than the human, who is indeed contrary. Now tell me, how can I be called contrary when I regard medicine at its highest, saying and teaching that it must flow from the highest arts? Namely: from <term>Philosophy</term>, from <term>Astronomy</term>, from <term>Alchemy</term>, and from <term>Natural Science <note>original: "Physica".</note></term>, and all of this with well-grounded knowledge. How then can Nature complain that I am her contrary? But I am a contrary to those who have not grown into being doctors in this way.

Furthermore, it is no less true that I am greatly despised because, in all my days, I have never had a fixed place to stay, and I have not sat behind the stove "turning pears" <note>A German idiom for idling or leading a sedentary, useless life while drying fruit by the fire.</note> like those who call me contrary. Therefore, sitting behind the stove and wandering over mountain and valley are unequal, and one must indeed be the contrary of the other—they of me, and I of them. But as I am instructed by the highly learned Mr. Zacharias Pirer, Doctor of Law, my dear master and good friend, that in the law a doctor is called and ought to be a <term>Wayfarer <note>original: "Perambulanus"; a traveler or one who walks through.</note></term>: I can well take and understand from this that he should not sit behind the stove or be hemmed in by the town walls. I say as much about this distinction between them and me: it is as white and black. Art does not allow itself to be inherited, nor does it allow itself to be copied out of books. Rather, it must sometimes be eaten and vomited back up; one must ruminate and masticate <note>Paracelsus uses the metaphor of a cow chewing the cud to describe the deep processing of experiential knowledge.</note> upon it, not learning in such a sleepy way as those who "turn pears." Therefore, they may well say that I am contrary. I will not appeal the judgment; I also consider that what they gain from that judgment is more of a mockery to them than a praise.

<margin>C</margin> Now tell me, have I done wrong to them by learning and experiencing how to turn away the injuries of the sick through my manifold wandering? And that I restore what my "contrarians" ruin through having experienced so much more? Should this be turned into contempt for me? I think not. But if it happens, it must happen out of envy and by those who understand nothing other than what their own "philosopher" speaks. Wisdom has no enemy but the one who does not understand it. If I now share with everyone the experience that God has granted me, should I be judged by others as being unfair, and further despised, and hindered in many ways? But since I am left untouched by those who are righteous, what does the rest matter? Whoever can do it better, let him make a better version; I teach the one who cannot do it. Now, who among those who can do it better will view this as unfair? Let him carve a more beautiful <term>Lucretia <note>A figure from Roman history, often used here as a metaphor for a perfect or beautiful piece of craftsmanship.</note></term>. I would be happy to see it, even if they were to make a <term>Helen of Troy</term>; it would remain respected by me. If the doctor cannot conclude and decide except through works and signs, I may nonetheless drink my wine with joy. Therefore, reader, do not judge according to the gossip, but

->according to the works, which make everyone manifest and give<-
->testimony of the truth.<-

## The Chapters of the First Tractate are as follows:

<margin>A</margin>The First Chapter: How, after long attempts with <term>surgery <note>original: "Wundartzney"; literally "wound-medicine," the practice of treating external injuries, often distinct from internal medicine in this era.</note></term> in open sores, no help was found, and what happened thereafter.

The Second Chapter: How the sick, suffering from open sores and great pain, turned to the <term>artists <note>Refers to skilled practitioners, often alchemists or specialized surgeons who worked outside the traditional academic medical system.</note></term>, and gave them direction toward further discovery of medicine.

The Third Chapter: How the alchemists entered into medicine, and how <term>Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimia"</note></term> reveals how to heal sores through either "wrath" or "goodness."

The Fourth Chapter: How an order was established for <term>corrosive medicines <note>Substances used to eat away dead or diseased flesh.</note></term> and surgery mixed together, and what benefit or harm resulted from it.

The Fifth Chapter: How through the ancient artists and the pursuit of health, several secret arts were discovered, through which many origins of disease were also found.

The Sixth Chapter: How the origin of open sores is found in strange ways, and how it has been proven that the origin often recedes and shifts.

The Seventh Chapter: How, during the time when various arts were discovered, changes occurred in diseases, which required the seeking of other arts.

The Eighth Chapter: Concerning the discovery of several secret main principles by the ancient, proven physicians, and how the unproven ones patched in their <term>sophistry <note>Deceptive or fallacious reasoning, often used by Paracelsus to criticize academic doctors who relied on books rather than experience.</note></term>.

The Ninth Chapter: How the origin of open sores is <term>mineral <note>original: "mineralis"</note></term> and does not come from the <term>humors <note>original: "Humoribus"; the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that traditional Galenic medicine blamed for all illness.</note></term>, and how much error has grown from this misunderstanding.

The Tenth Chapter: How a seed is placed within humans, which seed compels and forces one to reach the end of its course, and is <term>Predestination <note>original: "Prædestinatio"</note></term>, a forced future disease.

<margin>B</margin>The Eleventh Chapter: What the elements are in man, what they work within him, what their power and might are, and how they cannot be found to be "humors."

The Twelfth Chapter: How the artists were so eager to explore the secrets of nature, and experienced and sought such things through faith and the power of nature.

The Thirteenth Chapter: How the arts are found miraculously, and how the one who gives the art does not make himself known, but acts in an unknown, wonderful way.

The Fourteenth Chapter: How, first and foremost, a doctor shall know and recognize the ailments, diseases, and conditions of external creatures, and thereafter of man.

The Fifteenth Chapter: How wisdom and art flow to a man who learns nothing from others (as mentioned above), and how this befits a doctor and should be so.

The Sixteenth Chapter: How the ancient righteous doctors happened upon the righteous arts without understanding or prior knowledge of the origin.

The Seventeenth Chapter: How the newly discovered arts are now used in open sores, and how they make "doctors" of those who were not born to medicine at all.

The Eighteenth Chapter: How it is not necessary to consider "cold against warm" or "hot against cold," but rather it is necessary to consider the <term>Virtue <note>original: "Tugendt"; in this context, it refers to the inherent power or medicinal potency of a substance.</note></term>.

The Nineteenth Chapter: Indicates the further intention to describe the source and origin of open sores.

The Twentieth Chapter: How doctors should not wonder at this new proposal, but should weigh it well.
