### CHAPTER XVII.

->How the newly discovered arts are now used in open sores, and how they make doctors who are nonetheless not at all born to medicine.<-

For a long time now, the successors of the so-called doctors have regarded the recipes of their teachers as incompetent, Dilatory, and unhelpful, and have discarded them; moreover, they have engaged in foreign recipes contrary to their teachers, namely in "the wood," greasing, smoking, and washing.

<margin>B</margin>
Now, however, because an unborn doctor shall achieve nothing of the true foundation, the same has happened among these men. They first took for themselves the foundation of the <term>Four Humors</term> <note>The traditional Greek medical theory that health is governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Paracelsus famously rejected this.</note>, and thus acted upon such things with the aforementioned methods. But since the foundation does not come from the Humors, but from the <term>Salts</term> <note>original: "Salibus". Paracelsus believed the body was composed of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury; here he argues that skin diseases are rooted in the "Salt" principle.</note>, they have led so many into ruin, into further injuries and sickness. For the wood <term>Guaiacum</term> <note>A heavy wood from the Americas used at the time as a "miracle cure" for syphilis.</note> and Mercury are the main pieces they use. But now, they do not serve in the way that the Humors contain and use them, but rather against the <term>genera of Salts</term> <note>original: "genera Salium"</note>. Since it is against the genera of Salts, it is necessary to divide them into their species and to deal with them <term>specifically</term> <note>original: "Particulariter"</note>. Only then can it be found against which open sores these pieces are useful. If this is found, then one may work with the wood Guaiacum and with the metal Mercury truly and with certainty, and no one will be ruined or harmed, and no one will be promised more than the performance can achieve. Thus medicine is brought into mockery because it was founded on untruth, when more was promised than could be delivered. Such untruth arose from the idea that open sores arise and spring from the Four Humors; therefore, no <term>concordance</term> <note>Harmonious agreement or fit between the cure and the disease.</note> or joining together of the medicine and the sores can occur. But if the classification of open sores follows the content of the Salts, then it will be found which open sores belong under the wood Guaiacum, and which under Mercury. Likewise, which are treated with the wood and <term>abstinence</term> <note>Refers to the strict fasting diets often prescribed during the "wood sweat" cure.</note>, which with the wood and no abstinence, which with the wood-water, which with the wood-liquor. Similarly, which with Mercury through ointments, which with Mercury through smoking, which with Mercury in water, and the like. Thus should the medicines be used, and not like the so-called doctors, according to the foundation and classification of the Four Humors. For this is the foundation: to apply the medicine to its corresponding sickness, in the manner that has been mentioned. The reason I say this here is so that those doctors might desist from their ways and consider within themselves their daily destruction and slow torment. Even if they heal at the last, it nonetheless happens with great pain.

<margin>C</margin>
Such a foundation, to prevent further harm, happens only through this: that open sores should be classified differently than they have been since antiquity. Also, the medicine that is serviceable for open sores must be prepared and ordered differently than has been the custom among the so-called doctors until now. If the right classification occurs and the right preparation of the medicine, then truth may be spoken to every sick person, and that which is promised—or that which nature is capable of—may be upheld. For it is a truly mocking thing to act like a fool in medicine and come to no end, or not to act in the right way of nature as it was created by God. For that same order must be kept; otherwise, no medicine or art is found.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->How it is not necessary to consider Cold against Warm, or Hot against Cold, but rather it is necessary to consider the Virtue.<-

Since every sickness is now driven out not by the elemental nature, but by the <term>Virtue</term> <note>In Paracelsian terms, "Virtue" (Tugendt) refers to the specific healing power or spiritual essence of a substance, not its physical temperature.</note>: what use is it now that we want to consider whether the sickness be Hot or Cold, as a physical example? A fever is hot, but coldness cannot drive it out—only Virtue. Virtue is the medicine; the coldness is the <term>regimen</term> <note>The external management of the patient, such as blankets or room temperature.</note> and diet of the food; or warmth is a regimen in cold sicknesses. For in the same way as two people who strike one another, there neither Cold nor Warm, nor Moist nor Dry overcomes, but only the strength: so it is to be understood in all sicknesses, that the doctor should only experience the power of the Virtue; then he has learned and experienced enough. For so it is also in open sores; they have sometimes been judged hot, sometimes cold, sometimes moist or dry, and have been opposed with such medicine: but that has never been useful. For if an open sore is hot, the Salt that lies within it is hot; it burns like a nettle, or like a salt in a wound.

# Wound-Surgery: The First Treatise

A further point: a wound cannot be healed by dry things alone, but rather by those things that <term>coagulate</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "coagulate" to mean solidifying or fixing the internal "salts" of the body to stop a wound from leaking or running.</note> the Salt. **Coagulation** and **drying** are two different things. Drying only affects that which comes from the foundation and origin—much like if someone dries up the water flowing from a well, but must still let the well itself continue to flow. But if it happens that the well freezes within its own source, it no longer gives water to be dried up. Thus, the wound should be coagulated at its foundation, which is the distinction between it and simple drying. Therefore, whatever needs to be dried should instead be dissolved; this happens through the **Power** <note>original: "krafft"; refers to the innate healing virtue or spiritual energy of a substance</note> and not through moisture or wetness.

Because medicine has been brought to the point where "Cold should drive out Hot" and "Hot should drive out Cold," <note>This is a critique of the Galenic "Humoral" theory, which treated diseases with their opposites.</note> it has fallen into falsehood and error. Coldness does not extinguish fire; rather, wetness does. What is it that purges? It is neither hot nor cold, but the Power. What is it that **incarnates**? <note>original: "Incarniert"; the process of a wound healing and growing new flesh.</note> The Power alone, and otherwise neither heat nor cold. Thus, in all diseases, it must be understood that the physician should not pursue the warmth or coldness, but should seek the Power, which is the entirety of the medicine.

Therefore, I say that the useless custom in treating open sores should be abandoned. Although such treatments may mitigate or still the pain, they heal nothing. For **Camphor** is good for inflamed sores, but only for soothing them; better, however, is **shoemaker’s blacking**, **Myrrh**, or **Frankincense**, etc., because these extinguish the cause entirely. Thus, error in treating open sores is common among the bath-keepers, barbers, and also among the Doctors in their councils—but it is a wretched council. For the foundation lies first in the mastering of the **Salts**; thereafter, once the incarnation (healing of the flesh) is present, all accidents, inflammations, swellings, and the like will pass away.

<margin>Symptomatic</margin>
As for what belongs to mitigation, a cooling may well occur against heat. However, this is only if that heat comes through an inflammation and not from the disease of the matter itself. Thus, the heat that occurs in wounds, bone fractures, and the like—such heats are not the disease, but a <term>symptom</term> <note>original: "Zufall"; an accidental or secondary symptom rather than the root cause.</note>. In such heated symptoms, cooling may well be used against the heat, but not against the disease itself. For a distinction must be noted: that diseases are elements in themselves, and one must use elements against elements—such as water for fire, air for water, earth for air. For in this way, the elements overcome themselves at their source. Thus, the physician should also seek the Power and the nature of the disease at its origin, and not in that which comes from the disease, for those are merely its excrements. For we should not extinguish the smoke from a fire, but the fire itself.

<margin>Explanation 225.</margin>
If we wish for the earth to produce no good grass, then the earth itself must be disrupted, and the grass should not merely be plucked out. Thus, with open sores, the physician should only think backward to the origin, and not at what the eyes see. Those sights are signs, but not the origin—just as smoke indicates a fire, but is not the fire itself.

### CHAPTER XIX.

->Description of the Firmament, and the Source and<-
->Origin of Open Sores.<-

Therefore, because medicine has fallen so far underfoot among those who do not know it, and yet will not abandon it for the sake of profit: it is my intention, not that they should abandon medicine, but only that they should accept the *right* medicine, so that they may honestly earn the money they sometimes receive unrightfully. Although pride is great and does not willingly enter into recognition and humility—which causes me much enmity—it is nevertheless my purpose in the next treatise to describe the true foundation as it is in itself. I have already sufficiently shown the "foundation" and "earnestness" of the ancients; now I shall prove and establish the truth through the <term>Philosophers</term> and <term>Astronomers</term>.

For above all things, as I have often mentioned regarding the main schools of medicine, no one can be a physician unless he is first a **Philosopher** and knows and recognizes the nature of the elements and their fruits, in health and disease, in nature and essence. Then, once he understands such a foundation in the "sickness of nature," he shall also learn to recognize man as a **Physician** <note>original: "Phyſicus"</note>—that is, to draw and arrange his philosophy into a physical practice. And if he does not bring man into such a division, kind, property, essence, and nature, he cannot help but be in error.

<margin>Here the signature of the world in the Microcosm 4. 21. and 84.</margin>
For the outer man allows the **inner man** to be known, along with all his diseases. And thus, the medicines that are necessary for man are also found through "corresponding images and essences." In this way, not only a **Philosophy** is required, but also an **Astronomy**. For he who does not recognize Astronomy cannot be a physician, nor can he be grounded in medicine; rather, he is defective, and much is lacking in him. For just as the heaven and the earth are together, so too are the heaven and the human. And as man is of the earth, he must be understood through the earth; so too is he of the heaven, and must therefore be understood through the heaven. Thus, man, heaven, and earth are one thing—along with air and water. All this the physician should know above all things, and then he is a true Physician.

The correct main division is thus: that the physics which produces the physician stands in four things. One is in **Hydromancy** <note>original: "Ydromantia"</note>, which is the philosophy that teaches one to recognize the nature of all water within the element of water. Next is **Pyromancy** <note>original: "Pyromantia"</note>, which is Astronomy, teaching one to recognize the entire firmament. Next is **Geomancy** <note>original: "Geomantia"</note>, which teaches one to know and recognize the earth’s nature, properties, essence, and changes. Of the fourth element, **Air**, nothing has been written that has come to my hand, yet it should be recognized just as well as the other three elements. But there have come "artists" who have turned Geomancy into a craft of dots <note>referring to divination by earth</note>. Others have held divinations in water and called it Hydromancy.

# The Second Book of the Great Work

<margin>A</margin>
Others have looked for omens in the fire, calling this **Pyromancy** <note>original: "Pyromantiam"; the art of divination by fire. Paracelsus views this as a corruption of true natural philosophy.</note>. In such things, philosophy has been weakened, diminished, and has decayed, being misused outside the true laws of Nature. The physician, however, must know and recognize these laws, so that he may heal the human being—who is wonderfully made by God—in a wonderful way, recognizing him according to his true nature. He must not foolishly leave his neighbor in a state of neglect. For every man must give an account of his intentions, his claims, his trade, and his knowledge; nothing is so secret that it shall not be made manifest. God desires that we be understanding while on Earth, walking in perfection and learning the **Ground** <note>Paracelsus uses "Ground" (Grund) to refer to the fundamental, divinely-ordained reality of how a thing works.</note>, walking the right path rather than trying to climb in through the roof. He who cannot learn this from men should learn it from his own innate nature; and where that fails, he should learn from Him who gave us body and soul and created all things for us—He will teach us further.

## CHAPTER 20.

->How physicians should not be astonished by these new propositions, but<-
->rather weigh them carefully.<-

<margin>B</margin>
It is no less important to note that describing medicine requires a great turning-point. For as mentioned before, there are four parts of philosophy that are themselves not without error, and no well-grounded physician can emerge from them alone. Because the law of Nature has not often been sought according to its own justice, there must be a clarification and a clearer demonstration within it, which I will partly reveal to you with God’s help, so that the **Ground** of medicine may be laid forth. However, describing these four parts will surely provoke much impatience in many. I have also mentioned **Alchemy** several times; you should understand my meaning of it thus: it is used to demonstrate the true <term>Simplicia</term> <note>Simple, unmixed medicinal herbs or substances.</note>, <term>Magnalia</term> <note>Great or miraculous works/substances.</note>, <term>Arcana</term> <note>Secret remedies or the "inner heart" of a medicine.</note>, <term>Mysteria</term>, <term>Virtutes</term> <note>The inherent healing virtues of a substance.</note>, and <term>Vires</term> <note>The active powers or strengths.</note>, and everything necessary for healing. For what use is it to a physician to know all the origins of diseases if he cannot heal them or prove helpful? Therefore, since the true foundation of preparation does not lie within the methods of the **Apothecaries**, we must search further—that is, we must learn in Alchemy, for there we find the Foundation and everything that is required. Although Alchemy has fallen into contempt and is almost regarded as worthless, the physician should not trouble himself with that. Other arts are also held in contempt, such as Astronomy and Philosophy, and many others. I do not direct you into Alchemy for any reason other than the preparation of the *Magnalia*, the extraction of the *Mysteria*, the preparation of the *Arcana*, and the separation of the pure from the impure. This is so that you may have a clear, pure medicine—one that is perfect and certain, possessing its highest power and might as God has endowed, graded, and proven it. 

God does not intend for medicine to be served to us already cooked, prepared, and salted; rather, He intends for us to cook it ourselves, to learn how to cook it, and to exercise ourselves therein. It is His pleasure that we do not go idle upon the Earth, but labor daily. For we are those who must pray for our "daily bread," yet He gives it to us through our own labor, art, and preparation. If one calculates how much work is required before bread enters the mouth—not just labor, but the art of farming, sowing, milling, and baking—how much more of such art does God require of us in medicine? We must plant the medicines with our own hands and bring them through art to the state for which God <term>Predestined</term> them. This must and shall happen through the physician using the art of Alchemy. Such preparations are not found in the "cleverness" of the <margin>C</margin> Apothecaries; their way is but a **bungling** <note>original: "Sudlerin"; implies a messy, unscientific, or unskilled cook.</note> in medicine when one should instead be grasping the highest Foundation—to separate and prepare a thing to its highest place and degree, for which it was created. 

Let no one despise me because I lead medicine so far into other faculties, religions, arts, and sciences. A physician should be the highest, the best, and the most grounded in all parts of Philosophy, Physics, and Alchemy; he should lack nothing in any of them. Whatever he is, he should be so with Foundation, with Truth, and with the highest experience. Among all men who study Nature and its Light, the physician is the highest knower and teacher—and after that, a helper of the sick.

***

## DR. PARACELSUS’S Conclusion.

I have written this treatise according to the art of medicine, for nothing more is to be sought in it than the beginnings and the first experience of **Open Sores** up to this present time. But to describe the **Ground**—their origin and provenance—requires a longer treatise, as follows hereafter. Now, this Foundation is different from any that has ever been described before; you should not wonder at this, but rather consider that until now, the old way has introduced a harmful destruction of mankind. I write this so that we may be preserved from that. Even if a "poison" <note>Metaphorical for "venomous" criticism from his peers.</note> rises against me, it is of little concern, since the **Work** itself demonstrates the Foundation of Truth. Therefore, since medicine proves itself through works and signs, and openly and visibly shows the Foundation—showing who is righteous and who is not, where art lies and where it does not, where medicine exists and where it does not—it is easy to act and to judge, and to recognize where destruction dwells. 

Therefore, everyone who reads my work should not judge based on words, but wait for the **Works** <note>Paracelsus emphasizes "Works" (results/healing) as the only true test of a physician's theory.</note> which instruct and teach everyone. For it is not fitting to pluck roses before their time, but only when they are fully bloomed.

**Surgery: The First Treatise.**

<margin>A</margin>
**Enemies of the craft.** There are also many who hold hostility toward the arts—some out of laziness, some out of ignorance, some out of stinginess, and more of the like. That which is worthless always behaves in this way. Therefore, I speak not without reason when I say that those born into a craft should remain in that which they were born to; yet this does not happen. To the reader and the physician: read so that you may become understanding and useful to your sick. Do not occupy yourself with envy or malice, refusing to use the right path, as there are many who—out of spite for one another—destroy the sick, kill them, or let them die, even though they might well have been saved by others. But so great is the jealousy among physicians that no one will grant another honor or praise; he would rather ruin the patient and kill him entirely. From this, anyone may clearly judge why they are physicians: not out of love for the sick (which should be the first virtue of a physician), but for the sake of money. And where money is sought, there is envy, hatred, pride, and arrogance, which lead them astray. May God protect and preserve everyone from such things.

# Preface to the Second Treatise, on Open Wounds, 
# BY DOCTOR PARACELSUS.

<margin>B</margin>
While much has been written until now in medicine concerning **Open Wounds** <note>original: "Offnen Schäden"; refers to ulcers, external lesions, or wounds that refuse to heal.</note>, regarding their origin, cause, matter, essence, and cure, there are two great reasons why experience and truth have been lacking among them. The first reason is that they have known nothing certain, nor have they experienced or understood the **Ground** <note>The fundamental reality or divine foundation.</note> from which a physician should speak—namely, from **Philosophy, Alchemy, Astronomy, and Natural Science** <note>original: "Physica".</note>. Instead, they have invented a foreign cause for these wounds that goes against the established foundation of true medicine, as is proven by their writings and explanations. Secondly, there is the reason that no faith should be placed in them regarding open wounds because they hold no complete foundation; that is, they do not speak from any experience that has been **proven by the fire** <note>A reference to alchemical testing and practical laboratory experience.</note>, but only offer simple and miserable advice. For when one considers the "barber-surgeon" wisdom <note>original: "Schererische vnnd Baberische Weißheit"; Paracelsus is mocking the limited knowledge of the barbers who performed surgery, as opposed to learned physicians.</note> and cleverness of those writers, an experienced, learned physician should be ashamed to take advice from such people who understood nothing of either part. And even if they occasionally include a piece that is good, it is not their own, but borrowed from others to decorate their books.

Thus, it has been the custom among the old writers until now to make books and gain a great name for themselves, yet they possessed no foundation in medicine nor understood it, through which much harm has grown. It is even more to be lamented that for such a long time, mankind has not been able to learn to recognize those groundless books and learn something better. Instead, just as they wrote, people have staked their souls and honor upon them. They did not consider that these writers were not prophets, nor did they write the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelium".</note>, but wrote only out of their own presumed reason and understanding. Nevertheless, whatever they understood in themselves, they presented faithfully—whether it was right or wrong, they held no judgment over it.

<margin>C</margin>
Yet the most lamentable thing of all is that the great heads of the world <note>The political and academic authorities.</note> have created an order stating that those who do not act according to these books shall not be recognized as righteous physicians. Instead, they must walk, act, rule, and manage according to the order of those written books, and swear an oath to this. Furthermore, whatever is killed or crippled according to the books shall remain unpunished by the law and the physician's honor shall remain intact. This makes for bad students, for they have no desire to learn further.

So I have intended—since no "Gospel of Medicine" has been written yet—that it should not be forbidden to seek the truth further. Rather, we should take the old and new treasures together, and through them become ever better and more learned. Although a saying was given by **Christ** <note>original: "Christum".</note>, "No disciple is above his master," He also says further, "You shall not be called masters." For only One is the Master, and therefore we should not set ourselves above that Master. But this is directed against those who call themselves masters and are not. Thus, I intended to act in medicine so that one would proceed according to the intent of the Eternal Master and look upon the saying He gave when He spoke: "I have given you an example, that as I have done to him, you should also do." From this it follows that we should follow His speech and understand it in medicine: whatever Christ did, spoke, and taught, the Word and the Work were always together. So it should also be in medicine. Those who now chatter and pass their time in disputing without **Works** <note>Practical results or healing actions.</note>, those are the "idle words" for which an account must be given. Thus, we should follow the example of Christ, so that the Word and the Work are lawfully bound to one another, just as we have the example that the Apostles completed nothing without works, but confirmed their words with their deeds.

He is a **Theologian** <note>original: "Theologus".</note> who speaks of God without works; but a physician cannot be so. He must, like a saint, stand by his words and his works. For he is a saint whose words have power; likewise, he is a physician whose medicine has power. Therefore, the chattering of medicine shall be left behind, and only that which has and gives power shall be undertaken. Although every religion...

...have two ways about her: one spends her time only with chatter, the other with winning. Like the lawyers: one part wins, the other loses. He who loses is no lawyer, for he has carried out useless chatter without work. So also, further, we should know in medicine that nothing should be in it except what word and work provide together, since medicine is after all a true art, and the truth is placed in works alone, and not in chatter. If there is now a teaching in medicine and incomplete works are found, that same teaching cannot be called an art of medicine. The art is given perfectly, so we should also be perfect, as our Father in heaven is perfect. If we cannot learn such perfection from men, even in the light of nature, because of our coarseness, then we should learn from Him who has said: Learn from me, for I am gentle and of a humble heart <note>A reference to Matthew 11:29</note>. And although the supreme chief-writers of medicine, at the beginning of their books, praise and glorify God, it is not yet proven that they have been taught by God; this is revealed by their imperfect teachings and works. Therefore, reader, learn and experience so that your word and work may be one thing: where that is not the case, recognize yourself as no physician.

# The Second Treatise on Open
## Sores by DOCTOR PARACELSUS.

### On the Origin of all Open
#### Sores.

->CHAPTER I.<-

->States that there are two ways from which every physician learns. One is just,<-
->the other unjust: Thus, two kinds of physicians are<-
->to be found.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' (replacing the German 'Z') at the start of the chapter, featuring ornate scrollwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
Two ways there are from which all arts spring, though one presents the arts falsely, while the other is just. Those who present the arts falsely are the human senses and one’s own preconceived fantasy, in which a person speculates and thus brings forth a rhyme out of himself, yet in itself, it is nothing. <margin>C</margin> The other way is that a person takes his teaching from experience and the objective manifestation <term>Gegenwurff: Paracelsus’s term for how nature "throws itself against" or presents itself to the observer as objective reality</term> of nature; and from that which experience places before one's eyes, he completes his search. Thus, the one is taught out of himself, the other out of the manifestation of experience. In these two ways are written the books of the philosophers, of medicine, of astronomy, and more besides: from which it follows that the false and the just are found and read in philosophy, medicine, and astronomy.

However, since medicine must now be addressed, it is necessary that the two ways be presented at the beginning, to properly recognize their cause and origin. For medicine cannot tolerate having any kind of work introduced or mixed into it that comes from one’s own preconceived fantasy or "philosophizing"—that is, "fantasizing"—but rather it must come from the way of experience. This is the reason why the physicians, through the speculation of fantasy, have in part falsified the medicine of experience. And since man is placed before God down to the smallest hair, and is moreover His image: it is not fitting that medicine, which is created by God, should be led astray by such a stubborn fantasy, but rather that those who take pleasure in medicine should be struck down with their disputing and arguing for and against <note>original: "pro, & contra"</note>, etc. Although they thereby make their own simplicity and folly obvious, and although their followers diligently listen to their chatter, it nonetheless concludes with a poor end.

Thus there are two kinds of students: those who cling to their own fantasy, and those who cling to experience. Experience alone remains in the truth, and what one's own mind speculates cannot endure. For what nature has within her must be taught through the manifestation <note>original: "Gegenwurff"</note> that she gives, and without that same thing, nothing can be drawn from the treasury of nature. As an example <note>original: "e nExempel", likely a typo for "ein Exempel"</note>: Who can see into a mountain to know what is in the middle of it? No one. How then would it be possible to describe an invisible thing, seeing as man is commanded to do no more than to follow after that which the manifestation carves out for him. As an example: Christ has set before us the teaching of salvation; that same teaching is the experience into eternal life, and we must walk according to it, and not according to that which we ourselves fantasize.

<vocab>Paracelsus: The author, Theophrastus von Hohenheim; Artzney: Medicine or remedy; Erfahrenheit: Experience or empirical knowledge; Fantasy: Speculative imagination without basis in nature; Medicin: The practice of healing; Natur: The natural world as a divine creation; Gegenwurff: Objective manifestation or the presentation of natural phenomena; Philosophieren: To speculate (often used pejoratively by Paracelsus); Astronomy: One of the pillars of Paracelsian medicine; Offne Schäden: Open sores, ulcers, or chronic wounds.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Second Treatise, focusing on the epistemological foundations of medicine. It transitions from the theological necessity of perfection discussed on page 78 to the practical necessity of empirical experience over theoretical "fantasy."</meta>

# Surgery: The Second Treatise.
[Sig: S iiii]

<margin>A</margin> We should know that the power of the heavens <note>original: "Firmaments"; referring to the celestial influences on health</note> arises from experience, which has proven the course of the heavens. Without such experience, nothing can be described concerning the heavens. Therefore, whatever a person wishes to write or learn, they should do so out of experience, and from that same experience teach themselves and others—especially regarding life, as medicine must govern life for a time while it is being received and given. For it is Nature that teaches, and not one's own imagination <note>original: "Fantasey"; in Paracelsus’s time, this meant speculative theory or unproven ideas</note>.

I must instruct you better through examples and bring you to a greater understanding: the stubborn philosophers, whom experience blinds and brings to resentment, are led astray. Aristotle wrote a book called *On Meteors* <note>original: "Meteororum"</note>, in which he describes heavenly powers, and from the first to the last, there is almost no truth in it. Now see how subtly he brought forth this stubborn imagination and found those who support him in his error, confirming and extending it—such as Petrus Tartaretus <note>A 15th-century scholastic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle and Duns Scotus</note> and countless others not necessary to name. To describe "meteors"—that is, the meteorological powers—one must do so from Nature, proving through experience what makes the snow, what makes the rain, what makes the thunder, etc. In doing so, one finds origins different from those understood by the aforementioned Aristotle. Astronomers also have such a fabricated imagination that does not arise from natural observation but rather introduces a mental image; such are the *Geomantic Auguries* <note>original: "Auguria Geomantica"; a method of divination using markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed soil</note> and other such categories that share the same foundation as Aristotle in his description of meteors. Albertus Magnus <note>original: "Der Groß Albertus"; a 13th-century Dominican friar and influential polymath</note> described the birth of metals, also without experience, revealing his stubborn philosophy and leaving his claims unproven. So too in medicine, Avicenna <note>An 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook for centuries</note> and others described the origins of diseases which never actually occur in a human being.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, because the physician has such a subject <note>original: "subiectum"</note> beneath him—that is, the human being in whom the soul dwells—it is necessary for him to consider that God created him. If he is created by God, and God has made man subject to the physician to turn away his infirmities, the physician is not commanded to carry this out with fabricated imagination that flies out of his own head, as if medicine were a form of *Rhetoric* <note>original: "Rhetorica"; the art of persuasive speaking, here contrasted with practical science</note>. Rather, he must ensure he does not rely on such fantasy, but takes experience before him, and teaches and experiences according to it. For medicine, in its discovery, is exactly like a craft; all crafts come from experience. Therefore, they achieve the perfect end they are meant to achieve, and the end proves the truth. So too should medicine take its origin and end with the truth. Thus, the first schoolmaster of medicine is the *Body* <note>original: "Corpus"</note> and the *Matter* <note>original: "Materia"</note> of Nature. Whatever these teach and indicate, study and learn from them, and nothing from yourself; for your own imagination is nothing but a seduction away from all truth.

Great and subtle arts have been invented through experience as it is applied to Nature: namely, the invention of the art of preparing metals, which no stubborn theorist could have devised; rather, the *physical matter* <note>original: "corpus"</note> taught it through experience. Furthermore, many kinds of crafts were found in metals, from the metals themselves, for Nature reveals itself to be known.

<margin>C</margin> Since medicine alone is that which has been placed upon Nature, and Nature itself is the medicine, it must be taught and sought within Nature. As an example: the potter took his origin from clay to make vessels and containers, and perfected them through fire; thus the potter learned from clay and fire. So too from iron and fire, the smith learned through the hammer to make an axe; subsequently, from the axe and from wood, the carpenter learned his craft. Thus from ash and fire, glass arose; from wool and spinning, the weavers; from silver and fire, the goldsmiths; from the pick and stone, the stonemasons, etc. Thus all things that Nature is meant to accomplish are found through the experience of Nature, and these things cannot be invented out of one's own imagination.

I point all this out because the foreign, intrusive "sophists" <note>Paracelsus’s term for traditional academic doctors who relied on books rather than observation</note> set aside such experience and write and act based on their own imagination. Because of this, the natural light <note>A Paracelsian concept: the innate wisdom found in the world and the human mind</note> is corrupted and covered with a lantern <note>A metaphor for obscuring the sun/truth with dim, artificial human logic</note>, whereby much evil arises. The physician must be and is born out of Nature, out of the fire—that is, out of the art of the fire <note>Alchemy/Chemistry</note>—and through the fire he shall learn and experience what Nature shows and gives him. And just as the smelter brings forth gold and silver through fire, so the physician shall bring forth through fire the noble *Secret Essence* <note>original: "Arcanum"</note>, the *Mysteries* <note>original: "Mysteria"</note> of Nature, the *Great Works* <note>original: "Magnalia"</note> of medicine, the *Essences* <note>original: "Essentias"</note> of every being, and separate the impure from the pure. Furthermore, he is born from the *Microcosm* <note>original: "Microcosmo"; the "Small World," i.e., the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, meaning he should know through the fire who man is, and from what he is composed and made—namely, from Three Things <note>In Paracelsian chemistry: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>. All this is provided by the experience that springs from the fire. For from the fire, the physician discovers and learns what man and medicine are, and outside of that school, there is no teaching of the truth. Therefore, I rightly point out the two ways from which medicine has sprung—the just and the false—so that physicians may reflect on this, better examine the proof of medicine, and regenerate it so that it may be cleansed of the old filth <note>original: "Vnflat"</note>. Thus, the body, which is formed after God, may be treated in truth, and its granted, strengthened life may not be shortened, but rather sustained.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the First Origin of All Diseases, with General Instruction.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap D at the start of the chapter.</image-desc> Regarding the origin of diseases, the stubborn have devised many kinds of fantasies, especially concerning the source of open sores <note>original: "Offnen Schäden"; typically referring to ulcers, lesions, or external wounds</note>. Through this, they have introduced many errors into the art of healing, having falsely identified the primary cause of all sickness. Generally, you should understand that the true origin is known through good wisdom: that all creatures God created within the four elements, contained within the heavens <note>original: "Firmaments"</note>, were ordained and created into fragility <note>original: "zerbrüchlichkeit"; the state of being easily broken or decayed</note>. Thus, nothing is whole, but everything is so ordained that it must break, and is finally encompassed by death, which consumes all things. Therefore, all things are first led into destruction, and subsequently into death.

<margin>A</margin> Since man is thus ordained into fragility, and it is embodied and innate within him, he must wait and expect the time when decay falls upon him. This breaking, dividing, and splitting is what physicians call "disease." Regarding this, the physician should first realize that such innate adversity of the natural body is the "First Mother" of all disease; it is so embodied through creation that it can never be turned away.

We can know how such fragility comes out of the body through anatomy, for man is composed of so many various parts that they cannot all be counted. Furthermore, from the heavens come so many various "impressions" and so many influences from the elements, which, when they all come together, make a human being. Now, since man is not made from a single piece alone, no part among so many kinds can remain entirely stable; rather, one part always breaks another. As the proverb says: "Many heads rule nothing well." For there are so many things in the human being—constitution <note>original: "Complexion"; the balance of humors or qualities</note>, properties, form, and nature—that no one part matches the other. Yet they must and shall remain enclosed within one skin, each in its own quantity and quality. It is one way in the head, another in the body, and another in the limbs. There is the liver, which has its own office; there are the lungs, which have another office; there is the stomach, the gall, the intestines, the blood, the bones, the marrow, the flesh, and so on.

<margin>B</margin> There are so many of them, and none is like the other, so that it cannot be without destruction. And as many such distinct species <note>original: "Species"; here meaning types of tissue or components</note> lie within man, each with its own special condition—who can find a harmony <note>original: "Concordantz"</note> there, so that it might be said: there is unity?

In addition to all this, many enemies grow which poison these parts and species. Just as we have an innate enmity from our parents, so our descendants have it from us. For example: Adam and Eve were of a healthy nature; Cain and Abel were unhealthy, and so it continues, more and more over time. The cause is this: the unhealthy have passed on their unhealthiness in the conception of children, so that the diseases of the parents have continuously tended toward the poisoning of the seed. Thus, such poison has increased until the present time in such a way that none of the current diseases are like the old ones. And from our time until the end, many more will break in, so that future diseases—unless God shows mercy—will otherwise become incurable. Such deep-rooted poisoning is the reason why the pestilence and other "heavenly defections" <note>original: "Himmlische Defectiones"; likely referring to unfavorable astrological alignments</note> so easily ignite and move people. Now, a thousand are infected where two thousand years ago not even a hundred would have been attacked. It also returns in the third, fourth, or fifth year, which previously would not have happened in fifty. So it is with the pestilence, and with all types of disease, which is the cause of so many various and common diseases, such as open sores.

<margin>C</margin> Now, since man has come into such a state that in birth and in creation his own enemy is enclosed within his own body, he must for that reason be surrounded by disease and death. Even when he is at his healthiest, it only seems so to him, for destruction never rests for a single moment. Thus, the first origin of all diseases is an *Oportet* <note>Latin: "it is necessary"; a "must-be"</note>—that is, a thing of necessity. For he is created and born into the disunity of the limbs, and so surrounded by things and by spirits that there is nothing, either within us or outside us, that is not inclined toward destruction. Only what God has given in the treasury of the mercy of medicine, and the ordinance of our conduct and usage, provides relief; outside of these two, there is neither honey nor sugar <note>a metaphor for health or comfort</note>. To know this, such a nature of destruction should be embodied in a physician, so that he may know and recognize how these things occur. For medicine is created in such a form as to prevent such things. And since they deal with material matters, the physician should also take his teaching from them, as nature brings the same to light. And as the smith recognizes the fire and the iron in the fire, so should the physician recognize the sick person through visual evidence, without all invented and presumed natural philosophy <note>original: "Physica"</note>.

Therefore, it follows from this: since destruction is present and happens physically—so that one can see the operations of the sickness as clearly as the effect of fire—nature should be further searched to see how she makes the microcosm <note>original: "Microcosmum"; the human being viewed as a miniature version of the universe</note> known. From that, one should recognize and experience what it is that makes the disease, for medicine fights against that very thing. Likewise, many diseases are sent to us from the stars <note>original: "Gestirn"</note>, which must also take their recognition from the stars—and all of this entirely from the body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> in which they lie. Just as a fisherman who must take the fish from the water must also take the art of how they are to be caught from the water; and as a stonemason from the stone, etc. So must everyone who wishes to have knowledge of a thing take it from that in which it exists: the heavenly from the heaven, the earthly from the earth.

For speaking of God and His essence cannot be learned from the Devil; speaking of eternal life cannot be learned from Hell. Instead, each thing is learned from itself; within the thing itself lies the school, the book, and the master of that knowledge.

It follows from this that a physician is born of two things: namely, from the disease, and subsequently from the medicine. From the disease, he must learn to recognize the sickness, and from the medicine, he must learn the remedy. Outside of these two, no instruction can be given to him. However, the way he enters this "Mother" <note>Referring to the "First Mother" or origin of disease mentioned on the previous page</note> and sees the disease clearly—as a blacksmith sees iron in the fire—is not possible unless he first recognizes the anatomy of the whole world. This world provides him with an "open man" <note>The "Macrocosm," or the universe as a reflection of the human "Microcosm"</note> and sets before his eyes the physical body <note>original: "corpus Physicum"</note>, limb by limb and piece by piece. Once he has explored this open physical body, he is a Physician-Philosopher. It then follows that where the Philosopher leaves off, he begins in medicine; that is, he proceeds to the healing. For as long as a doctor merely recognizes the disease, he is a Philosopher of Medicine; but if he can heal the disease, he is a practicing physician. 

Now, a perfect physician is found in these two roles: first, to look into the "Mother" and the school and the Book of Nature—which is the open physical body—requiring the study of Anatomy of the world and Astronomy. In the second part of the physician’s work belong the natural virtues <note>original: "Naturalium virtutes"</note> and Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimia"</note>. Upon these four pillars, the physician may firmly set his foundation and be found unshakeable in his certainty. Yet, although many have written on medicine and claim great proof for themselves, they provide no other foundation for the primary medicine than the "four humors" <note>The traditional Galenic theory that health depends on the balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, and for the secondary medicine, they rely only on the *Macer* <note>original: "Macrum"; likely referring to *Macer Floridus*, a famous medieval herbal poem</note> and the *Light of the Apothecaries* <note>original: "Lumen Apothecariorum"; a common pharmaceutical reference book of the time</note>. They might well be laughed at, for medicine has a firmer, deeper, and more subtle foundation.

To naturally describe the body and the matter from which open wounds <note>original: "offnen schäden"</note> take their origin, and how this is proven and experienced in the open physical body, the general cause and explanation is this: Man is composed of three main parts: Sulfur, Liquor, and Salt <note>original: "Sulphure, Liquore vnd Sale"; these are the 'Tria Prima' or three primary substances in Paracelsian chemistry</note>. These three are the body of man, in which every limb exists. The Sulfur provides the tangible substance, the Liquor provides the juice/fluid, and the Salt coagulates the physical body together. Thus, every thing that has a body—whether sensible or insensible <note>living or inanimate</note>—is recognized and naturally formed within itself. The moisture is the Liquor; that which burns is the Sulfur; and that which remains from these two is the Salt, each according to its weight as created by the Creator. These three things are visibly proven through Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcanum"; a common alchemical term for fire or the art of the furnace</note>, who also verifies and places before one's eyes what lies within the open physical body. For through fire, all things must be experienced, verified, and discovered, whether they be in water, in the air, or from the earth. These three things are the First Matter <note>original: "Prima Materia"</note> of all creatures, and also the Ultimate Matter <note>original: "Vltima Materia"</note>—the beginning, middle, and end of every body.

<margin>C</margin>
While such things belong more to the knowledge of philosophers than physicians, the reason I point this out is to explain Salt, which is the cause of all open wounds, specifically in this manner: Everything that has a body must be preserved from rotting—whether it be dead or alive—if it is to remain healthy and uncorrupted. If this is to happen, it must occur through the Balsam which God created to sustain every creature. In whichever creature this Balsam is not present, there is the rotting of the entire body, whether in sensible or insensible life. Just as you see that embalmed bodies, which death has overcome, do not rot, you should also know that an innate Balsam is embodied and united within the physical body, which preserves man from rotting. For if the Balsam were not in man, man would rot while alive like a dead carcass <note>original: "Aaß," "Cadauer"</note>, like stinking dead flesh. This Balsam protects his life from such rotting, and no one takes the Balsam away except death alone. The difference between the Balsam of the living body and the Balsam of the dead body is that one belongs to life and the other to death.

To give you an understanding of this Balsam: the Balsam of both life and death is a Salt, which has divided itself into its various species according to how each body is naturally formed. Just as you see meat taken from the butcher is saved from rotting by the power of salt for many years and days—now, such an effect and power is nothing other than the Balsam manifesting itself in the form of a salt. Likewise, it is found that a salt is sensed and tasted in man, by which salt the blood, the flesh, and everything in the whole human being is preserved and maintained. Thus, enough has been said and presented here regarding the Salt that is the cause of all open wounds. The conclusion in summary is this: just as three things make up man—namely Sulfur, Liquor, and Salt—the first two, Sulfur and Liquor, are not cited here as the causes of open wounds. Rather, the third is Salt, which is the Balsam of the physical body, in which lies the cause of the disease that I describe here in this book. <margin>A</margin> [Balsam] hardens stone; it hardens wood; it also hardens man; each according to its proper coagulation <note>The process of becoming solid or firm</note>.

But what has been created so well that it does not contain as much evil as it does good, since we all essentially feel this to be true? The Balsam <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Balsam" is the internal preservative fluid that prevents the body from decaying while alive</note> preserves the body of every creature on Earth. Now, it has two evil parts within it: the first is that it is itself mortal, transient, and fragile. For nothing is so good that it is not subject to destruction, as nothing can outlive its appointed term. So, when a plague comes into the Balsam, such that the Balsam itself is injured, the rot of that specific limb and body follows as far as the injury reaches. For the Balsam is not of just one kind; rather, there are as many kinds as there are limbs in a human, and just as many different locations. Just as there are different types of flesh in a human, so too are there many types of Balsam. Thus, the lung may rot without harming any other limbs, and the liver likewise, and so every limb for itself. This is the first cause in the generation of open sores: when the Balsam injures that specific limb. But the other cause, which is also within the Balsam, is this: the Balsam is a Salt <note>Original: "Salß"</note>; sometimes it is sweet, sometimes sour, sometimes like soot, sometimes sharp, for there are many such tastes. Just as there is a Balsam in honey, one in vinegar, and one in common salt, etc., each thing preserves the body it has "balsamized." Now know this: since destruction is in all things, nothing is good that does not also have as much evil within it. From this destruction and malice, it follows that the Salt generates into a corrosive substance <note>original: "Corrosivum"</note>. From this, it follows that in the places where such things are born, the power of the corrosive Salt causes an etching and eating away of the flesh, along with the accompanying virtues of heat, swelling, burning, etc., according to the properties and nature the Salt holds within itself.

<margin>B</margin> Thus, it has been sufficiently revealed what the "offending matter" <note>original: "Materia peccans"; the physical substance causing a disease</note> is in the generation of all kinds of holes and open sores, as is generally understood. Furthermore, it should be understood that from the study of open sores, a teaching and instruction is given which is derived from the very form of the sores. This shows that there is not just one lineage of Salt, but many, as found in the variety of forms, shapes, figures, and images. The physical body <note>original: "Physicum Corpus"</note> is the same in its specific types. To understand this with a significant explanation, the specific generation of each species follows hereafter. So too does every specific form of an open sore have a specific nature, according to the characteristics of that form. For different physical traits <note>original: "Physionomen"</note> give different meanings; just as different figures have different interpretations, different forms, different essences, different images, and different properties.

But just as the causes of such open sores occur and break in to destroy man, Providence has created the Physician and the Medicine to overcome such destruction; therefore, the wise man does not despise them.

Through their influence and ordained rays, they infect and burn man from above. Such "Impressions" must be highly regarded and recognized. ### Surgery: The Second Treatise

<margin>A</margin> Just as lightning <note>original: "Fulgura oder Straal"</note> strikes down into a tower or a tree—or, as often happens, into a person—there are also certain "impressions" <note>In Paracelsian thought, "impressions" are invisible celestial or atmospheric influences that strike the body like lightning</note> that produce open sores, which are called "lightning strikes" by a similar metaphor.

There is yet another way these sores manifest in man, outside of all the indications previously mentioned, which should be understood through this example: just as springs flow out of a hard rock, naturally ordained by their Creator, so we should also know that a flow like a spring may arise in man. This flow opens its own exit and runs according to its nature, and no one can know its origin or source, just as no one can truly know the origin of these sores or the source of a spring. Therefore, no one can seize the "seed" of either flow or dig out its root. And just as springs have many characters—some cold, some warm—there are also colder and warmer flows in man of this kind. Just as there are many kinds of springs named after different substances—sometimes sulfur, sometimes alum <note>original: "Alaun," a mineral salt used as an astringent</note>, or in other ways—here too, one must distinguish between the different natural flows in man.

Thus, in total, the origins of all open sores have been described in the previous chapters and in this one. And although the ancient writers do not include such things, they did not write the "Gospel" of medicine; nor did they write from the true Art from which a physician should write, as was stated in the beginning.

<margin>B</margin> There are also several other open sores that do not appear and grow according to the order mentioned above, but instead destroy the Balsam <note>The body's internal healing fluid</note> and the Salt. They are destroyed against their own power and health by other foreign accidents. These are of three types: from the pestilence, mucoid sores <note>original: "Schlier," likely referring to glanders or similar ulcerative discharges</note>, and breast abscesses.

Furthermore, there are some that force their way into the Balsam and break it, such as those from corrupted wounds, from burns, and from animal bites.

There is another type that also breaks the Balsam, coming from canine madness <note>original: "Hantzerey," likely rabies</note>. And there are two more types: from St. Anthony’s Fire <note>original: "Wildenfewer," or erysipelas, a skin infection</note> and from leprosy.

These are the types that are counted among the open sores, along with those that have their natural origin. And although a type of open sore also occurs inside the body—such as in the lungs, liver, and the like—even though they are not openly visible on the outside, they are still recognized as sores. Their treatment is handled in a special chapter (or several), because of the difficulty of healing when they occur in the kidneys, bladder, torso, throat, head, etc. For consumption <note>original: "Busichtigkeit," referring to phthisis or wasting diseases</note> requires a higher degree of healing than visible things. Although a chapter is recorded regarding the "deepest holes" <note>fistulas or deep ulcers</note>, it is included for the sake of experience, even though they themselves do not strictly belong in the healing section of this book; however, because the disease carries a similar form, it should not be omitted.

<margin>C</margin> It should further be noted that although much has been written about open sores, their origin has never been properly identified. If we wish to truly and thoroughly learn the foundation of medicine through the origin of diseases—taking these open sores as a specific example—then the *operation* <note>The way a thing acts or functions</note>, *form*, *figure*, and *image* of the diseases must be experienced and recognized. For there is nothing that grows or has grown that is completed without a form, nor is it without an operation; it is in and through both of these that one recognizes what its property and essence are. Nothing grows out of nature—be it in the field, the forest, the air, or the water—that does not give knowledge of its property and essence through the signs of its form and operation, or its figure and image. 

Consider this example of the *operation*: do not the salts of the "open physical body" <note>The external world of minerals and nature</note> demonstrate the same effect as the salts in the Microcosm <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature version of the universe</note> when they work in the operation of open sores? Therefore, the same effect is judged to be one essence—understanding invisible working things through visible ones. We should understand that every external figure represents <note>original: "Figuriret"</note> something similar internally. Just as the operation of external salts prefigures the operation of internal ones, the figure of external salt prefigures the spirit of the internal salt. Thus, every external figure should provide an "imagination"—that is, a comparative image of an internal and external essence that are the same.

Thus, through such operations, one finds through the signs what the species of each open sore is: which comes from vitriolic salt <note>Sulfates, often associated with burning or sharp pain</note>, which from aluminous salt, etc. And they are judged according to this knowledge. To this also belongs a knowledge and understanding of the *form*. In whatever form coagulation brings the external salts, so it also forms them in man, but in a "resolved" <note>liquefied or dissolved</note> form. For form and form correspond to each other: a coagulated form represents a resolved form. By knowing what species the external form is, you judge the resolved form to be of that same form and species. This comparison brings them together, so that one form makes the other known, and one operation is equal to the other. Through such "concordance," you remain unled; you do not have to fantasize or describe medicine out of your own reason, but rather describe it from the Light of Nature <note>The innate wisdom found in the observation of the natural world</note>, which is the form and operation. According to the content of this natural light, give names to those sores based on the corresponding form and operation as they appear in the external physical body, using their distinct names.

# The Second Book of the Great [Surgery]

<margin>A</margin> ...named. Thus, understand in this chapter how open sores grow and how they take their origin, and with that their form, shape, and structure along with their perceptible effects, so that you may not be led into darkness.

We should also note that there is no creature that Nature does not mark with a sign of what is within it. Take man as an example: nothing natural in him concerning natural virtue is not marked on him externally—either in his nature, his proportions, his gestures, or on his tongue, eyes, ears, etc. There are many more that reveal a man’s mind, which are not necessary to describe in this primary work, but are further described in the *Proportions of Physiognomy* <note>original: "Proportionibus Physionomiæ"; the study of determining character from physical features</note>. This is not only true in man (though man has the most emotions <note>original: "Affectus"</note>), but also in every plant. In the Plantain <note>original: "Plantagine"</note>, the veins show what its medicinal powers are; so too the Savin <note>original: "Sauina," a type of juniper</note> shows its virtues through its form. And just as the eyes of men indicate the complete physiognomy of their heart's desire, the ears their mind's pleasure, and the tongues what they are full of internally, all these are found in flowers and in that which stands in place of the tongue. Therefore, one who wishes to be experienced in medicine and recognize what belongs to him should also recognize this art, which Nature presents externally in signs, to know what they signify internally. 
<margin>q. 75. Signature</margin> For everything that is internal carries an external figure of that same essence, in both sentient and non-sentient creatures. Through this figure or other signs, that which is internal may be sufficiently understood. Therefore, every physician should know this well from the ground up.
<margin>B</margin> For these are the first scholarly fundamentals <note>original: "Scolasticalia"</note>. If he does not know the beginning, he will know much less of the end. But if he employs the end without knowing the beginning, how much harm and evil is accomplished by his stubborn head!

### CHAPTER V.
## On Diseases, Especially Those Arising from Atmospheric Vapors
->Explained in detail.<-

Since henceforth each open sore shall be described one after another, first note this example. In Nature, there is an innate quality such that all her ores <note>original: "Erz"</note>—before they reach their destination—show their "weathering" <note>original: "Witterung"; in Paracelsian science, this refers to the vapors or "blooming" of minerals as they form</note>. Each ore according to its nature—which weathering, according to the kind and nature of the ore, is its "bloom." Just as every plant shows its bloom in its own time—one more often and more than the other—so there is also a weathering in ore. This is a "blooming" that indicates the future time and perfection of the ore. Just as this is a general example concerning all ores, the salts <note>original: "Salia"</note> also specifically have a weathering that often reveals itself, by which one can recognize what is also growing at that same place where the salts are born.

As has just been mentioned, the same occurs in man; for whatever the "Greater World" <note>the Macrocosm/Universe</note> is capable of is also contained within the "Lesser World" <note>the Microcosm/Man</note>. For all qualities, characters, and essences that are external are also found perfectly within man. Now, if such a mineral character exists in man, as mentioned above, and it moves toward destruction, then the "weathering" begins to move. In man, this serves only for frailty, whereas externally in the world, it leads to fertility. For although man has all external qualities within him, he has them only in the spirit, not in the matter and body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> as they appear externally. 
<margin>C</margin> And although a body also exists within that same spirit, they differ from one another like flesh and iron; both are a body, yet neither is like the other. From this it follows: when the mineral nature in man "weathers," a movement of the whole body follows from that weathering because of its sensitivity—and because the qualities of the whole world lie enclosed in one small body. And because man is so well-enclosed that nothing can escape him, there follows from this a trembling and an "earthquake" of the whole body.

When such a trembling begins, the nature of every "weathering" is that it is of a cold nature. It enters with coldness, just like the North Wind <note>original: "Wind von Mitternacht," literally "midnight wind," referring to the North</note>. It blows through all the internal members of the body and chills all its parts, from which they receive the shivers—just as when one comes out of the heat into the northern wind <note>original: "Septentrionischen Wind"</note>, it pierces him and brings him a shudder and a frost. This is also the nature of "weathering": it begins with the cold wind and chills all internal members. This lasts as long as the nature of such a wind is consumed. Afterward, a heat follows in all internal members because of the raging they suffered in the aforementioned shaking. And because they stood in such adversity, all of this goes through the whole body. For there is nothing that remains untouched. And such heat of the whole body does not subside until it is all consumed. And if it starts so strongly, the limbs smell upward along with the weathering, and they rob the reason and cause a hard, heavy sleep, because of the stupefying <note>original: "Stupefactivisch"</note> nature that belongs to the "weathering."

But so that you may notice where the disease breaks out, understand it thus: it settles in a limb where it is driven most strongly by the "wind." With heat and its whole nature, that limb swells up and reddens like a cancer <note>original: "Krebs"; can refer to a canker sore, gangrene, or a spreading inflammation</note>, so strong and violent that it could not be stronger. It settles in one place and presses as if it wants to break out. But if it is not so powerful and strong, but rather young and

Therefore, you should henceforth know that since <term>Error</term> <note>original: "Irung"; refers to a metabolic or natural malfunction</note> and <term>Destruction</term> are created and ordained within Nature—and this is what must be considered here—it follows: If such <term>Excrement</term> <note>waste products of digestion/metabolism</note> should turn into <term>Error</term> and <term>Destruction</term> within someone, it enters the urine, but instead of being expelled, it holds itself back and turns into another essence, namely into the sheath of the flesh. Where it settles in this way, it causes a blockage, surrounded by the limit of its own kind. Just as in the earth it produces salt over time by itself, so it also lies in the flesh, and with time it reaches its <term>Effect</term> <note>original: "Effecum"</note>. And as it approaches this state, it creates a double, knotty sort of growth in the skin, which becomes harder over time. And of such knots or pegs that it creates, many are close together, each for itself, just as saltpeter, when it is fused, shoots out into many pegs. Thus, in one place also, many pegs appear next to each other, like unripened sores.
In such a state, if it lies in that place for a long time, it works through the natural heat and through its own sharpness, and it enters into a <term>Corrosive nature</term>. Thus, where there was a peg and a knot, a hole falls in; and for as many pegs as there were, there are as many holes, shaped according to their size. Many appear next to each other, as is the nature of saltpeter, which shoots out many tines in a cluster together. Such holes manifest with a flow or with dryness, according to how the accident <note>the specific medical occurrence</note> happens to fall there; and then it makes its own steady path, and also its own moisture, but works only in dryness. And because they are so many together, they have been called in Latin <term>Scrofula</term> <note>swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis</note>, though it is better that the name should come from that by which it is made and born, which is <term>Ulcers of Saltpeter</term> <note>original: "Nitri Ulcera"</note>.

And although the <term>Salts</term> <note>original: "Salia"</note> have in themselves a hot and awakening nature, nevertheless their heat is often suppressed, as appears here. All things that exist reach their peak, and when they are at that peak, they sink into Death, which takes all things away in the very minute they are at their highest. Therefore, when the <term>Salts</term> go into an <term>Operation</term> <note>a chemical or biological process</note> and wish to increase the destruction: it is their nature that they do not manifest themselves until Death falls upon them and kills their intention; then follows the effect of the same, [though] living. And that which they should have made sensitive, they make insensitive. Such a kind and nature is in everything where the Saline [substances] of an animal nature delay further and make something worse of it. Not that the human dies entirely, but within him something dies, just like a hand that has been cut off; the body must [deal with] the same.
Therefore, regarding this, every physician must take good note that he has an understanding and a conscience regarding all those things that are in man when they are called into their death and follow a living power, but through deadly corruption; so that in such a case nothing is handled against the living power, since it is deadly, nor [otherwise]. If it is in such an undertaking and overcomes its malice, that is to overcome its death: thus it becomes <term>Alum</term> <note>original: "Alumen"</note>, which is called Entali when it has died.

# Surgery: The Second Treatise.

<note>Large decorative initial 'A'</note> Although a disease may take hold of the entire body, nothing shall be written of such cases here. Rather, what concerns the external limbs—provided no internal vital organ is involved—is what is understood and presented in this section. Furthermore, the names of such **Open Sores** <note>original: "Offenen Schäden," referring to chronic ulcers or lesions</note> are never specifically named here. The reason for this is that they are named and described so disorderly in traditional medicine that they are inconsistently maintained and remembered. Instead, these are simply Open Sores that have sprung from *Sal Gemma* <note>Rock salt or common salt in a crystalline form</note>. When it was at its highest potency, its "death" seized it, and through **putrefaction** <note>the process of decay or breaking down</note>, it was born into the shape and form inherent to the nature of *Salis Gemmæ*.

### CHAPTER IX.
Regarding Open Sores that grow out of Physical Vitriol.

<note>Large decorative initial 'A'</note> Likewise, some Open Sores are compared in their form and operation to **Vitriol** <note>Sulfate minerals, often associated with corrosive properties</note>, which is an ore that must be extracted through boiling and similar preparation so that it may be further applied.
In the same way, the cause of these Open Sores is found deep in the lower part of the body, most often below the knees. Now, if it happens that such *Sal Vitrioli* <note>Salt of Vitriol</note> results in destruction through its operation, it first attacks the large veins, which are called **varicose veins** <note>original: "Krampfadern"</note>; these veins are the locations where the vitriol resides. And when the vitriol begins its action in the Open Sores, it opens up the veins and prepares itself within them until it is transformed into a **corrosive** <term>Corrosiff: a substance that eats away at living tissue</term>.

<note>Large decorative initial 'B'</note> When this occurs, it then begins to create a swelling and a hardness.
Because it is corrosive, it subsequently eats holes into the flesh according to its nature—that is, many holes in a circular pattern. In this regard, it should also be noted that vitriol is seldom without pain, unless it has become stagnant; yet it increases continually in its malice and weight, continuing until it has hollowed out and gnawed through the entire thigh. And what it cannot gnaw through, it puts to sleep, turning it into a **decay** <note>original: "Moder"</note> that becomes insensitive. For in every vitriol there is an innate **Sulphur**, which by its nature induces this "sleep" or numbness.

Although it often happens that such vitriol and salts do not reach the point of ulceration because they cannot prepare themselves into the sharpest corrosive state, where this does occur, **cramps** and **stabbing pains** easily arise. This is because the vitriol agitates the "Old-water" <note>original: "Oldwasser," likely referring to waste fluids or lymph</note>, which causes the cramps and stabs. It also frequently happens that the **Spirit** <note>the volatile essence</note> of the vitriol rises upward and follows those same veins until it reaches the root of the veins, introducing localized ulcers and poisoning there. And as is its nature to branch out into many small pieces like capillaries, it creates many **growths** and **lumps** <note>original: "Kröpff vnnd Düpel"</note> on that same leg. And although they are not all of a corrosive nature—and therefore do not all turn into holes—holes only form where the corrosive nature is present. Its action is accompanied by rot or a stench; this is caused by the "smothering" when it becomes entangled in itself. For any salt in the presence of moist heat comes to rot much sooner than in dryness or cold. Thus, the desire of vitriol is to make many holes and to run out quickly.

<note>Large decorative initial 'C'</note> A similar effect is found in **white eye-stone** <note>original: "weissen Augstein," likely zinc sulfate</note>, which is understood to be related to vitriol in every way, except with greater pain, less swelling, and no cramps. And where such Open Sores exist, a yellow-colored water is discharged from that place, sometimes with clotted blood and a fine rot. Where such sores are present, there is no pain, but rather much swelling and lumps, tightness of the chest, stabs in the side, and poor digestion in the stomach—all of which, however, pass away once the sore breaks open. It is not that the "fluids" sink down from above, but rather that the nature of the vitriols rises upward and causes the aforementioned illnesses; this rising ceases once the sore has broken out. Therefore, the breaking out of the sore is the path to health. It should not be healed unless all the vitriol in the thigh has first been resolved and melted away, root and branch.

### CHAPTER X.
Tells of the Open Sores of Alum, and what their nature and properties are.

<note>Large decorative initial 'S'</note> Furthermore, there are open sores that manifest with swelling and a pale appearance, without a corrosive nature. First, they swell the thigh with a "wet" swelling <note>edema</note> that allows itself to be pressed in <note>pitting edema</note>; in time, this rots of its own accord and creates large holes with much stench and drainage. These holes are compared to **Alum** <note>a mineral salt used as an astringent</note>. Although alum itself does not cause swelling or rot, but rather constricts and helps healing, the heat in which it lies causes it to rot. Thus, heat is the mother of all rot. These sores do not form knots or lumps, but they give birth to others through long-lasting putrefaction. Their holes become wide and deep, occupying the regions even over the feet...
